Two fixtures, four visits to the naught column, and a genuine slice of Duck Club history — a sibling double no less. The exclusive zero club welcomes its latest inductees. Saturday 30 May — Old Williamsonians CC (home) - H Clarke walked in at four and walked straight back out, bowled by Farrow without scoring. A debut innings, and therefore an instant, involuntary enrolment onto the Debutante Duck board (rank 222 of 715) — there are faster ways to make your mark, but few so memorable. Splendidly, on this very day in 1943 Frank Sutton was doing exactly the same thing against Home Guard - D Company, en route to two Duck of the Year titles (1940, 1946) across a 24-year Linton career. - Two places later, brother Roy Clarke followed him back, also to Farrow, for his 3rd duck of the season and 10th of a career now standing at 52 innings (rank 19 of 715). Roy currently leads the 1959 Duck of the Year race outright, and carries a Quacking Together credential alongside club legend John Ames. Fittingly, his fall shares its calendar date with Frank Sutton's 1943 effort too — some days are simply built for it. - Arthur Cradduck rounded things off, run out for nought by a mix-up nobody present is owning — his 1st duck of the season and 8th career nought from 47 innings (rank 25 of 715). A past Duck of the Year himself back in 1951, Arthur joins the Sutton parallel for a third time this innings. 🍩 Family honours: a proper Two of a Quack — H and Roy Clarke, brothers both back in the hutch to Farrow inside the same innings. The Duck Club doesn't get to toast a bloodline double often; Saturday obliged in style. Sunday 31 May — Folkestone CC (home) - William Buck opened and closed his account almost immediately, bowled John Spanswick for his 2nd duck of the season and 13th career nought from a substantial 201 innings — a lofty 10th of 715 all time, and half of a standing Quacking Together pairing with John Thirkell. On this same day in 1958, Frank Brattle also made a duck, one stop on the way to an eventual 8-duck career. Week in summary: 4 ducks from 2 matches, the full set courtesy of the 1st XI, topped off by a rare sibling pairing at the top of the order. 🦆 Duck News — 16 to 20 May 1959

5 ducks
Week 3 · 16 May 1959 – 20 May 1959
A middling week for run-scoring turned into rather a vintage one for the Zero Club, five noughts recorded across two fixtures and every last one of them credited to the 1st XI. 🏏 Saturday 16th — Gore Court CC (away) Bob Arnold departed for nought, bowled by David Ledger, his second duck of the young season and 28th of a storied career now spanning 127 innings. That tally keeps him lodged at a magnificent #2 in the all-time standings, second only to the seemingly untouchable John Thirkell, and a proud holder of Ducks in a Row honours besides. Lower down, R- Spillane fell run out for a second successive duck, making it two from two innings for the season and, remarkably, two from two for an entire career so far — a flawless start in the art of not scoring if ever there was one. Already a paid-up member of the Debutante Duck club from his first-ever knock, and carrying Retirement Duck honours from a past farewell, Spillane sits 134th all-time. He shares his on-this-day parallel with Arnold — 1943, Breedon, same tune. 🏏 Wednesday 20th — Tilling Steven (away) A torrid middle order at Tilling Steven, where R- Bailey found something. Michael Fagg went first, caught off Bailey for his maiden career duck from just two innings, Retirement Duck honours already banked from a previous chapter. He walks in step with club legend John Thirkell, who made a duck on this same day in 1950 against Charles Arkcoll — Thirkell sits proudly atop the all-time list on 41, a hoard including three separate Duck of the Year titles. Alan Wilkes followed, bowled by Bailey, his ninth career duck in 42 innings and good for 20th all-time, a man boasting not one but two Only Two Quacks pairings to his name. William Buck went the same way, bowled Bailey, his 12th career duck from 199 innings — a tidy coincidence, 12 ducks and 12th on the all-time list, with a Quacking Together honour alongside Thirkell to boot. Both Wilkes and Buck tip their caps to Thirkell's 1950 vintage. 📊 Week in Summary Five ducks, two fixtures, one common denominator — the 1st XI cornered the market entirely this week, and R- Bailey can consider his afternoon at Tilling Steven a rather good one. 🏆 Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Bob Arnold — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - R- Spillane — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - Brian Mills — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 67% - Roy Clarke — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40% - Michael Fagg — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% Arnold and Spillane share top spot on a perfect record of failure so far this season — early days yet, but the standard has been set. 5 ducks

🦆 Duck News — 2 & 3 May 1959 🦆

6 ducks
Week 1 · 2 May 1959 – 3 May 1959
Six into the book across two outings for the 1st XI this weekend, the exclusive zero club welcoming old faces and one very new one. The art of not scoring, alive and well at Linton Park. Saturday 2 May — Bearsted CC (h) Frank Brattle survived two deliveries before Peter Longley had the last word, bowled for his 1st duck of the summer and 8th of a lengthening career (52 innings, 24th in the all-time table). He now sits level with Alan Wilkes, who played 1953–1959 and reached the same 8 in a brisker 41 innings — and, for the genealogically minded, Frank's forebear Percy Brattle already carries 4 career ducks of his own, so the family name is no stranger to the honours board. Brian Mills provided the day's real occasion — out first innings, first ball faced, first everything, bowled Alan Fagg without troubling the scorers. A genuine arrival into the Duck Club, and he goes straight onto the Debutante Duck board for it. He joins the select company of the 1952 debutant "- Dampier," who also opened his and closed his entire Linton career on a single duck — Brian, one hopes, has rather more cricket ahead of him. Roy Clarke departed caught behind off Ian Lambert for his 8th career duck, and with 1959 barely a month old already sits proudly atop this year's Duck of the Year table — a crown he'll be defending all summer. He too draws level with Alan Wilkes on 8 apiece. Tony Snell rounded off the innings at number 11, bowled by Bryan Elswood for his 14th career duck from just 45 innings — form that earned him the Duck of the Year gong in 1958 and a place in the Ducks in a Row (4 consecutive) hall of infamy. He now stands shoulder to shoulder with Frank Sutton, twice Duck of the Year in the 1940s, who reached 14 in 62 innings. Sunday 3 May — Harrietsham CC (a) Tony Tipples was caught and bowled by C Stitchman for his 7th career duck. Neat historical footnote: on this very date back in 1953, club legend John Ames also trudged off for nought, against Hunton Wanderers CC. And then the headline act. John Thirkell, LBW to D Hampshire, notched his 41st career duck — and yes, that keeps him firmly at number 1 of 712 in the entire Linton Park record book. A three-time Duck of the Year (1952, 1954, 1955), permanent fixture of the Lone Duck, Homebody Duck and Ducks on the Road top tens, Thirkell remains the undisputed monarch of the zero club. Fittingly, he shares his duck's date with the very same John Ames who also fell on 3 May 1953. Week in brief Six ducks, two matches, the entire haul claimed by the 1st XI — the 2nd, 3rd and 4th escaped entirely unscathed this week, which either means discipline or simply that they weren't watching. Nobody managed the ignominy of a golden duck this time round — every one of our six at least troubled the bowler for a delivery or two before departing. Small mercies. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. Brian Mills — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 2. Tony Snell — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 3. Tony Tipples — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 4. Frank Brattle — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% 5. John Thirkell — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% Early days yet in the 1959 campaign, but the leaderboard is already crowded. Next fixture awaits — who fancies joining the club? 🦆🍩0️⃣

6 ducks

Two fixtures, six ducks, and the ghost of John Thirkell walking arm in arm with every one of them — the great man (1943–1958, still an imperious 40 ducks, all-time #1) made his own duck on this very date back in 1952, once at Hunton Wanderers, once at A Levick XI. Then Bob Arnold, caught Farrance bowled Murrell — the same Farrance who'd already pouched Thirkell, evidently having a fine afternoon in the slips. Arnold's 3rd of the season moves him to 25 career ducks, rank 3 of 706, well inside his own Ducks in a Row (4 consecutive) territory, and formally Quacking Together with Thirkell — a partnership the pair have now honoured twice, on this very afternoon. His Quacking Together board names John Ames, a partnership from a different vintage. 5 ducks

Two fixtures graced the calendar this weekend, but only one needed the record book out: Linton's 1st XI capitulated against Tovil on the Saturday for FIVE ducks in a single innings, the kind of collective effort the exclusive zero club exists to celebrate. G Abel edged behind for his 2nd duck of the season, his career tally now 2 from 7 innings — a startling 28.57% strike rate that leaves him 3rd on this season's leaderboard. Bob Arnold was caught off Bailey for his 23rd career duck, a genuinely fearsome tally ranking 3rd of all 706 names in the club's nought-book, and a proud holder of the "Ducks in a Row" honour for four on the spin. Last man Tony Snell was bowled by Bailey for his 2nd of the season, his 10th career duck overall. It puts him firmly in this season's Duck of the Year 1958 conversation, with the ignominious "Runaway Duck" — a whole season without troubling the scorers — still tantalisingly on the cards. Hitchin (2) and Bailey (3) shared the spoils of an afternoon Tovil will remember fondly and Linton would rather forget. 📋 Week in Summary 5 ducks, 2 matches, all five arriving in the same doomed innings. 🦆 Duck Report — Weekend of 19–20 July 1958

2 ducks

Two Linton fixtures across the weekend, and the club's enduring gift for the naught stayed firmly switched on for one of them. Saturday's outing passed off disappointingly duck-free, but Sunday's visit from J G Larkings more than made up for it, with two names freshly inked into the ledger of dubious distinction. 🏏 1st XI v J G Larkings (Sunday 20th, home) First up was Tony Levick, trapped lbw by D. Goodliffe without troubling the scorers. His first duck of the summer, and his sixth for the club in 108 innings, which lodges him 34th of 706 in the all-time table — respectable company for a man who otherwise knows which end of the bat to hold. Splendidly, this very fixture falls on a haunted date: on this day in 1906, R W Mitchell (1903–1909) also strolled back for nought, against the Royal West Kent Regiment CC Officers XI, en route to 2 career ducks and 130th on the all-time list. Fifty-two years apart, same calendar square, same outcome. Not long after, Goodliffe struck again, bowling John Thirkell outright for his second duck of the week — and, with rather greater ceremony, his 39th career duck in 263 innings. That is enough to make John the club's outright record holder, sitting at #1 of 706 all-time, a throne he has occupied with some style having already been crowned Duck of the Year in 1952, 1954 and 1955. He also holds permanent residency in the Lone Duck, Homebody Duck and Ducks on the Road top tens, and carries Quacking Together honours alongside old teammates Bob Arnold and William Buck — a man who has mastered failure from every conceivable angle. Fittingly, he too shares this weekend's ghostly echo of R W Mitchell's 1906 duck, out on the same date 52 years prior. Two wickets, one bowler, no complaints from D. Goodliffe, who evidently fancied his afternoon's work against the Linton middle-to-lower order. 📊 Week in Summary Two matches, two ducks, both claimed by the same bowler in the same innings — a rare case of Larkings doing the club's collecting for it. Saturday's fixture, by contrast, saw every batsman get off the mark, to nobody's great excitement. 🏆 Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard — Top 5 - J Lea — 2 ducks from 4 innings (50%) - Frank Brattle — 2 ducks from 7 innings (28.57%) - G Martin — 2 ducks from 8 innings (25%) - John --'s Taylor — 2 ducks from 9 innings (22.22%) - Robert Murray — 2 ducks from 13 innings (15.38%) J Lea leads on strike rate alone, though with the season still developing there's ample time for the chasing pack — and for Goodliffe's happy hunting ground at Larkings — to reshuffle the order. 🦆 More cricket to come, and with it more scope for glorious failure. A rare and troubling weekend for the club's most dedicated observers: two full fixtures played, and not a single nought to show for it. 3 ducks

🦆 Duck Report — Weekend of 14–15 June 1958

2 ducks
Week 8 · 14 Jun 1958 – 15 Jun 1958
Two fixtures on the fixture card this weekend, and only one of them fancied feeding the exclusive zero club. Headcorn CC away proved the happy hunting ground, claiming two scalps to a single bowler in the same innings — a fine afternoon's work for L- Murrell, rather less fine for the men at the other end. 🏏 Saturday 14 June — 1st XI at Headcorn CC First to fall was John --'s Taylor, bowled by L- Murrell at number five. This is his second duck of the summer and his 15th in a Linton career now standing at 139 innings — a tally that plants him a lofty 4th of 705 in the club's entire scoreless history, a position few will ever trouble. On this very day back in 1882, C Gibbs was busy doing much the same thing against 1st Innings Boxley CC during his own brief 1881–1882 spell in the whites — proof, if any were needed, that the art of not scoring transcends the century. Murrell wasn't finished. Down at number eight, debutant Robert Wood became his second victim of the day, departing without troubling the scorers on his very first outing for the club. A baptism of fire if ever there was one, and it earns him immediate, permanent enrolment onto the Debutante Duck board — a place of dubious distinction reserved for those whose Linton career begins precisely as it means to go on. Curiously, Robert shares his moment in history with the very same C Gibbs, who was also dismissed for nought on 14 June 1882 against Boxley CC — separated by 76 years, united by the identical fate. The weekend's second fixture, mercifully for whoever was in it, returned home without adding to the tally. 📊 Week in Summary Two matches, two ducks, one bowler doing the damage twice over. No further casualties elsewhere across the weekend's second fixture — a rare mercy for the bowlers, and a quieter entry than most for the Duck Club minute book. Week in Brief Two matches, one duck. 8 ducks
Week 23 · 29 Sep 1956 – 30 Sep 1956
The season winds down but the Duck Club never clocks off. Snell's XI Frank Brattle, in at 3, was bowled by S Capon for his 3rd duck of the season and 4th career, from 20 innings — rank 49 of 683. He joins C Amies, who played 1867–1870, on exactly 4 career ducks. A family trait, too — kinsman Percy Brattle also sits on 4 for his career, so the naught clearly runs in the blood. S Capon then struck again lower down, accounting for Tony Tipples at 5 — his 2nd of the season, 5th career from 33 innings, rank 29 of 683. He joins Alan Wilkes (1953–1956), himself a veteran of the "Only Two Quacks" honours with both Bob Arnold and John Ames. Tony wasn't finished for the weekend, as we'll see. ⚭ Sunday — the annual Married v Singles duel, Linton Park The old fixture did what it always does, contributing six of the weekend's eight ducks, three of them to one bowler. For the Married side, Basil Sears opened and fell lbw to John Ames — his 1st duck of the season but 8th of a long career spanning 128 innings, rank 17 of 683. On this very day in 1951, Don Hartridge (1940–1952, 10 ducks, rank 11) also made a duck against Linton Park CC — history repeating five years to the date. Peter Weedon, at 7, became Ames's second victim, bowled for his 1st season duck and 11th career nought from just 56 innings — rank 10 of 683 and closing in on the elite. A paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club from a past farewell, though today he's very much still in the fight. Monty Deakes at 10 fell caught Wright bowled Howard, his 1st of the season and 3rd career in only 11 innings, rank 76. A Debutante Duck and Quack-to-Quack alumnus of old — a short career, but never a dull one. Completing Ames's hat-trick of scalps, Tony Snell was stumped down the leg side for his 2nd season duck, 6th career from 29 innings, rank 28. A proud member of the "Ducks in a Row" board for four on the spin — he clearly knows a rhythm when he finds one. For the Singles, Tony Tipples returned to complete a grim weekend double — out Saturday for the 1s, out again bowled here for his 3rd season duck and 6th career, from 33 innings, rank 29. A proper weekend tour of Linton's duck-getting grounds. C- Haylor fell lbw for his 3rd of the season and 5th career from just 16 innings, rank 34 — another Retirement Duck board member from years gone by. All four Married/Singles duckers can toast a shared moment — on this day in 1951, Don Hartridge also walked back for nought against Linton Park CC. Some traditions run deeper than the fixture list. 📊 Week in Summary Eight ducks, two matches, one bowler (John Ames) doing the lion's share of the damage with three scalps in an afternoon. Tony Tipples's weekend pair is the standout feat — turning out for two different sides in two days and finding the same fate in both. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. Completing Fairweather's set, C Sandford departed for nought at number ten — bowled, same bowler, his 1st duck of the season and 2nd of his career in 17 innings, ranking 90th overall. Another name for the 1897 ledger alongside H G Smith. 🌱 Sunday 22nd — v John Larkings (home) John Abnett kept the family tradition of Sunday sacrifice going, stumped by R- Dollymore off the bowling of Hughes for a duck at number ten. It's his 2nd of the season and a brisk 5th of his career from just 15 innings — 35th on the all-time list, and a proud member of the exclusive Ducks in a Row club (4 consecutive). Abnett's fall echoes W Edwards, who made a duck against Maidstone CC on this same date back in 1896. 📋 The Week in Nought Four ducks from two matches, all courtesy of the 1st XI, with three of them gifted to a single bowler in a single innings — Fairweather will be dining out on that one for a while. The art of not scoring remains alive and well at Linton Park. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 🥇 Michael Morton — 4 ducks, 9 innings (44.4%) 🥈 Bob Arnold — 3 ducks, 11 innings (27.3%) 🥉 Richard Harris — 3 ducks, 12 innings (25.0%) 4️⃣ John Abnett — 2 ducks, 4 innings (50.0%) 5️⃣ R- Waters — 2 ducks, 5 innings (40.0%) Next fixture looms, and with it the inevitable next round of applicants to the exclusive zero club. Bring your bats, gentlemen — or don't bother, some of you clearly aren't using them anyway. 🍩🦆

🦆 Duck Club Bulletin — Weekend of 14–15 July 1956 🦆

3 ducks
Week 12 · 14 Jul 1956 – 15 Jul 1956
Two fixtures, three ducks, and the exclusive zero club welcomes fresh blood while an old hand extends his terrifying lead at the top. Let's have it. 🏏 Saturday 14th — 1st XI v A. Trembeths (home) First up, A Hughes, walking out at number 7 on his very first senior appearance and walking straight back again, bowled by v- Chance without so much as troubling the scorers. A debut duck is cricket's cruellest welcome mat, and Hughes takes his rightful place on the Debutante Duck board — membership secured before he'd even worked out where the sightscreen was. Career duck number 1 of 1, straight in at 139th of 678 all-time. Fittingly, on this very day back in 1900, H F Morris was doing exactly the same thing against Yalding CC — some traditions span the centuries. Then Bob Arnold, at 8, caught behind off C- Rye for his 3rd duck of the season and 18th of an illustrious career — a career now sat at a staggering 3rd of 678 in the all-time charts, a position most club legends only dream of troubling. Arnold's honours board reads like a rap sheet: Ducks in a Row (4 consecutive), Only Two Quacks (with Alan Wilkes), and Quacking Together (with John Thirkell) — a man who has made the art of not scoring into a genuine team sport. And, extraordinarily, he shares his on-this-day company with young Hughes — H F Morris was clearly a busy man in July 1900, ducking twice over for two different Linton men fifty-six years apart. 🌱 Sunday 15th — 1st XI v Selsted CC (away) Away at Selsted, John Waters came in at 6 and departed bowled by S-v- Smith, his 1st duck of the season and 1st of a career now standing at 4 innings — 230th of 678 all-time and freshly on the board. Waters joins a quiet fraternity sat on exactly one career duck, level with the long-retired Dampier of 1952, a paid-up member of the Debutante Duck and One and Done clubs, and — appropriately enough given nobody's seen him since — the Retirement Duck honour too. 📊 Week in Summary Three ducks, both from the 1st XI, and both matches happy to oblige with a soft dismissal for the middle-to-lower order — numbers 6, 7 and 8 doing the honours between them. A quiet weekend by Duck Club standards, but quality over quantity: a debut duck, a top-3 all-time entry extended, and a fresh face added to the rolls. The engine keeps turning. 🥇 Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Michael Morton — 4 ducks in 8 innings (50.0%) 2. Bob Arnold — 3 ducks in 11 innings (27.27%) 3. Richard Harris — 3 ducks in 11 innings (27.27%) 4. C- Haylor — 2 ducks in 5 innings (40.0%) 5. Frank Brattle — 2 ducks in 6 innings (33.33%) Morton sits handsomely clear at the summit, but with Arnold and Harris breathing down his neck on the percentage charts, this Duck of the Year race is far from settled. 4 ducks

0 ducks

5 ducks

4 ducks

A three-time Duck of the Year (1952, 1954, 1955) and fixture of the Ducks on the Road, Homebody Duck and Lone Duck top tens, Thirkell's "Quacking Together" board now ticks over nicely alongside Buck. Completing the Allsworth treble was Michael Morton, bowled at five for his 2nd duck of the season already — 8th of his career (17th of 670, 46 innings). Morton draws level with George Champion, who mustered the same eight across a marathon 1886–1912 stint. With a live Duck of the Year 1956 board to his name, Morton is very much one to watch in this year's race for scoreless glory. 🌱 Sunday 27th — Ron Aiston XI (Home) C- Haylor continued a lean run, run out for nought at number eight — his 2nd duck of the season and 4th of his career (39th of 670, just 9 innings — a rate that raises eyebrows). A paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club from a past farewell, Haylor can at least take comfort that on this very day in 1950, John --'s Taylor was also trudging back for nought, against Hunton Wanderers CC no less. History does love to rhyme. 📋 The Week in Brief Four ducks, two matches, and one bowler doing the lion's share of the damage. 🦆 Duck Club Dispatch — Weekend of 12th & 13th May, 1956

3 ducks
Week 3 · 12 May 1956 – 13 May 1956
A modest but perfectly formed haul this week — three noughts across two 1st XI outings, the exclusive zero club welcoming its latest inductees with the usual pomp. Saturday 12th May — 1st XI away at Bearsted CC R- Piercy, walking in at number seven, fell lbw to Vic Pound to open his account for the season and his career in one stroke — his maiden duck in just 2 innings, installing him at 261st of 668 in the all-time roll of dishonour. Neatly enough, on this very day back in 1906 D H Luck was performing the identical ceremony against Town Malling CC, so Piercy joins good company exactly half a century behind. Then came the main event. Richard Harris, in at eight, was caught and bowled by E "Ted" White for his second duck of this very season — a flawless 2 from 2 so far, a perfect 100% strike rate in the art of not scoring. More strikingly, this is career duck number 24 from 118 innings, which plants him at a formidable 2nd of 668 on the all-time list — one of the most decorated members the club has ever produced, and he isn't finished yet. Like Piercy, Harris shares his duck-day with D H Luck's 1906 vintage against Town Malling — Saturday the 12th evidently has previous. Sunday 13th May — 1st XI at home to West Farleigh CC Ray Howard, batting four, was trapped lbw by R- Kemp for his first duck of the campaign and his first in senior colours — 1 from 16 career innings, ranking 262nd of 668. On this same date in 1950, D Simmons was similarly dismissed for nought against Bearsted CC, racking up what would become 4 ducks across his 1949–53 career and a rank of 39th — Howard has some catching up to do if he fancies that company. Week in summary Three ducks, two matches, one common thread — the 1st XI carried the weekend's entire quota single-handedly. Richard Harris' back-to-back pair of noughts is the standout, a serious early marker in the race for this season's crown, while Piercy and Howard both open their season accounts in style — or rather, in its total absence. Down in the record books he settles on 1 career duck from 1 innings, ranked 258th of 666 all time, drawing level with - Dampier, who managed the identical feat back in 1952 before promptly retiring on it — a cautionary tale Vincent will hopefully decline to follow. Can't win them all. Then O Barden got to work, and got to work thoroughly. Number six John Thirkell fell to him for a 7th duck of the season, his 26th in an LPCC career now 150 innings deep — a total that keeps him imperiously parked at #1 on the all-time chart. Thirkell already carries Duck of the Year honours from 1952 and, on this season's evidence, is mounting a serious defence of the 1954 crown too. He's a fixture of the Ducks on the Road, Homebody Duck and Lone Duck top tens besides, with shared quacking history alongside Bob Arnold and William Buck. On this same day in 1953, J Barclay was likewise dismissed for nought against Yalding — Barclay finished his short career on exactly 7, precisely where Thirkell now sits for the season alone. O Barden wasn't done. Richard Harris, in at seven, followed his captain back for a 5th duck of the campaign, taking him to 19 career ducks from 96 innings and into 2nd place all-time — Thirkell's shadow lengthens behind him. Like Larking, Harris finds company on this calendar date in Thirkell's 1953 effort at Yalding. And to complete the set, John Abnett went at eight, O Barden's third scalp in a row, for his 1st career duck in only his 2nd senior innings. He arrives with a "Ducks in a Row" board credit already to his name for a run of four in swift succession — a man clearly not afraid of type-casting. Another entry for the 5 September file, joining Thirkell's 1953 quack at Yalding. Week in brief: one match, four ducks, and O Barden helping himself to three victims on the spin — Thirkell, Harris and Abnett walking back in convenient single file. A tidy afternoon's work for Gillingham, a less tidy one for the LPCC top order. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - John Thirkell — 23 inns, 7 ducks, 30.43% - Richard Harris — 19 inns, 5 ducks, 26.32% - Bob Arnold — 15 inns, 4 ducks, 26.67% - William Blight — 20 inns, 4 ducks, 20.0% - Gerald Wright — 7 inns, 3 ducks, 42.86% Thirkell holds the top spot but Gerald Wright's strike rate should worry him. 🦆 DUCK NEWS — Week of 29 May 1954

1 duck
Week 5 · 29 May 1954
A modest catch for the Duck Club this week — one match, one nought — but what a nought it was. 🏏 1st XI v Old Williamsonians CC (home) Batting at four, John Thirkell fell to G- Trower for the first duck of his 1954 campaign. Modest as one duck sounds, this is no ordinary quacker — Thirkell already sits 1st of 643 in the all-time charts, a colossal 20 career ducks from 133 innings, comfortably the most decorated failure in Linton's history. A two-time Duck of the Year already, having taken the crown in 1952, and with a 1954 entry already sitting on that same board, the smart money says he's chasing it again this season. Throw in card-carrying membership of the Lone Duck top 10, the Homebody Duck top 10 and the Ducks on the Road top 10 — proof he can find nought whichever ground he's stood on, home or away — plus twin honours in Quacking Together, alongside both Bob Arnold and William Buck, and you have something close to the complete works of noughtdom in one man. Neat symmetry too: on this very day in 1937, E Hayes also made a duck against Charles Arkcoll — a name from the 1935–1939 era who finished with 3 career ducks and his own brace of Duck of the Year titles, in 1937 and 1939, sitting 52nd of 643 all time. Seventeen years apart almost to the day, same fate, same long walk back. 📅 Week in Summary One match, one duck — but it belongs to the man who owns the record book anyway, so quality trumps quantity this week. A quiet start, with the season proper still to come. 2 ducks

A quiet weekend by Duck Club standards, but the exclusive zero club still found two new inductees, both from the 1st XI, both away at Bearsted CC. 🏏 Saturday — 1st XI at Bearsted CC The top order held firm, but the lower middle order found batting rather harder work. In at number seven, Richard Harris was undone by a mix-up in the middle and run out for his side's trouble — his 1st duck of the 1954 season, and the 15th of a long and increasingly distinguished ducking career. That tally is no small thing: it plants him 2nd in the entire 642-strong all-time standings, a position most club members will never get close to, for better or worse. At number ten, J Barclay departed bowled by Gordon A Hawkins, chalking up his 1st duck of the season and 7th of his Linton career, good enough for 14th on the all-time list. That total draws him level with A Startup, who put together the same seven ducks across a positively economical 11 innings back between 1868 and 1882 — proof that quality ducking is timeless. Barclay is no stranger to the honours board either, having been crowned Duck of the Year back in 1953, and carries a paid-up membership of the Retirement Duck club from a previous, apparently premature, farewell. Evidently retirement didn't take — he's still very much in the runs-avoidance business. The weekend's other fixture passed off without incident for the Duck Club — runs, regrettably, for everyone involved. 📋 The Week in Noughts Two matches, two ducks, both surrendered by the 1st XI's lower order — a timely reminder that batting gets no easier as the tail wags on and the tea urn starts calling. 🏆 Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - J Barclay — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) - Richard Harris — 2 innings, 1 duck (50%) Early days in the 1954 campaign, plenty of season left for these standings to be shuffled, reshuffled, and shuffled again. A single fixture out on the park today, and for once the Duck Club has nothing whatsoever to show for it. Not a nought, not a nick, not so much as a nervous single turned into a run-out scare. 2 ducks

🦆 A modest afternoon at the crease for the Married eleven against Linton Park CC, but modesty is, as ever, our stock in trade. He takes his place at 257th of 640 in the club's all-time reckoning, and joins the shade of - Dampier on a career tally of exactly one, though Dampier, it should be noted, took the more decisive step afterwards of never batting again. - John Ames, following him to the wicket at first drop, fell to Michael Morton for the fifth time this season — a figure that also happens to be his career total from 33 innings, and good enough for 28th of 640 on the honours board. Mr Ames arrives, moreover, as a gentleman of substance in these matters: four consecutive ducks already to his name, a fixture of the Homebody Duck top ten, and a familiar face in the club's pairing books alongside Alan Wilkes, Roy Clarke and Stan Wratten. He now stands level on career ducks with Allan Peach of the 1900s vintage — kindred spirits separated by half a century but united in the art of not scoring. The Week in Brief One match, one innings apiece for our two unfortunates, and both ducks fell to the bowlers of Linton Park CC — a side evidently in fine order with the ball. No golden ducks this week, no pairs, no family affairs to report — merely the eleven's usual steady contribution to the exclusive zero club. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. The Duck Club Gazette — 12th and 13th September, 1953

0 ducks
Week 20 · 12 Sep 1953 – 13 Sep 1953
A quiet week, and a disappointing one for connoisseurs of the duck's egg. Across both fixtures played this weekend, the club's watchful eye — ever hopeful, pencil poised over the honours board — found not a single nought worth the recording. Every man who walked to the crease departed, sooner or later, with at least one run to his name, which is all very well for the scorebook but leaves this correspondent with precious little to celebrate. One might almost suspect a conspiracy of straight bats and watchful footwork about the ground this week, though it is more likely simple ill fortune for the Duck Club, whose members hunt in vain whenever an eleven insists on playing sensibly. The tail, we are reliably informed, wagged rather than folded, and not a man among either side troubled the exclusive zero club these two days. Still, one barren weekend does not empty the trophy cabinet, nor dim the lustre of those already enrolled in the club's dubious distinction. The season's leading exponents of the art of not scoring remain handsomely in credit, and the list below stands as testament to sterner, more fruitful days for the pursuit of nought. The Duck Club Gazette — 5th and 6th September, 1953

4 ducks
Week 19 · 5 Sep 1953 – 6 Sep 1953
A brace of fixtures this week, and the eleven found four ways to depart without troubling the scorer. The exclusive zero club, ever discerning in its membership, drew its new candidates from both ends of the county this week. 1st XI At Yalding, John Thirkell strode out first wicket down and returned bowled by D. Brooker, his fifth duck's egg of the summer and the nineteenth of a long and eventful career — a career distinguished chiefly by its studious avoidance of runs. He sits alone at the head of the club's roll of honour, first of 639, and carries into every innings the laurels of Duck of the Year 1952, a place among both the Ducks on the Road and the Homebody Duck top tens, and shared quacking honours with Bob Arnold and William Buck besides. A gentleman for whom the long walk back has become almost a habit of residence. Further down the order, J Barclay followed him to the pavilion, bowled by G. Davis, his sixth duck of the season and sixth of his career, good enough for twentieth on the all-time list and this year's Duck of the Year honour already resting on his shoulders. He is besides a paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club from a past farewell. He now stands level on six career ducks with D Sells, who played his own quiet innings of failure between 1943 and 1944 — kindred spirits separated by a decade but united in arithmetic. At Gillingham the following day, the eleven suffered a curious symmetry: Richard Harris and Gordon Fenner, batting at six and seven, were both bowled by R. Beckenham within the same innings. Harris departed for his second duck of the season, his thirteenth in a career of seventy-six innings and fourth on the club's roll of shame. Fenner followed directly behind him, his fourth duck of the summer and also his thirteenth for his career, third all-time — and now drawing level with Harris himself, the two gentlemen sharing both a bowler's figures and a lifetime tally within the space of a single over. Fenner, it may be added, keeps failure rather in the family, his brother Joe carrying five ducks of his own. The Week in Brief Two matches, four ducks, and something of a pattern: three of the four fell to the bowled dismissal, and Gillingham's R. Beckenham managed the rare distinction of accounting for two Duck Club members in a single innings. A sticky wicket for the top and middle order alike, and no mistake. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - J Barclay — 20 innings, 6 ducks, 30.00% - John Thirkell — 28 innings, 5 ducks, 17.86% - Gordon Fenner — 12 innings, 4 ducks, 33.33% - John Ames — 15 innings, 4 ducks, 26.67% - Gerald Wright — 13 innings, 3 ducks, 23.08% The season's honours board continues to fill most satisfactorily, and the eleven take the field again next week with every confidence that fresh candidates will present themselves. A modest week for the eleven, home to Charles Arkcoll, yielding but a single fresh entry to the Zero Club's ledger. Modest in number, never in ceremony — the club has always held that one duck properly honoured is worth more than a dozen let pass unremarked. 1st XI J Barclay, promoted to number eight, offered a return catch that Stan Wratten was only too glad to accept — c & b Stan Wratten, and back to the pavilion without troubling the scorers. It is his fifth duck of the season and stands as the twenty-fourth entry on the club's all-time roll of dubious distinction, a list now numbering 638 names in all. With the season itself bearing the same number, 1953, Barclay's effort must be counted toward this year's Duck of the Year — a title awarded not for runs made but, in the club's own particular reckoning, for runs conspicuously not made, and he goes into the reckoning as a serious contender. He remains besides a long-established member of the Retirement Duck fellowship, a past farewell recorded on the honours board from an earlier chapter of his cricketing life, and no reflection upon this week's proceedings. Most curiously of all, on this very date in 1903, a full half-century before, one W Peach fell in precisely the same manner against the 1st Innings of the Kent County Constabulary — the art of not scoring, it seems, keeps a faithful calendar. The Week in Summary One match, one duck, and a single name added to the ledger — the eleven played a generally straight bat this week, leaving the Zero Club's secretary with rather less to record than usual. Whether this reflects improved batting or merely a quiet fixture, the committee declines to speculate. The Duck Club Gazette — the 2nd and 3rd of August, 1953

2 ducks
Week 14 · 2 Aug 1953 – 3 Aug 1953
Two fixtures over the weekend, and two subscriptions paid into the exclusive zero club, that place of dubious distinction where consistency of a very particular kind is celebrated rather than mourned. 1st XI - J Barclay, turning out against Birchington Wanderers on the Saturday, came in at number six and was bowled by J Ince without troubling the scorers unduly — hardly the straight bat the eleven had hoped for. It is his fourth duck of the season and the fourth of a career of fifteen innings, placing him thirty-seventh in the club's all-time roll of the dismissed for nought. As it happens 1953 is very much his season for it, and this latest nought keeps him snugly inside the Duck of the Year honours he already carries for the year in question. He remains, besides, a long-standing member of the Retirement Duck club, having bowed out on a duck in an innings some while back — a badge worn with the quiet pride of the veteran. Curiously enough, on this very date in 1944 one E- Humphreys performed the identical trick against the National Fire Service Overseas Contingent, proving that some anniversaries keep themselves. - John Thirkell, a day later against the Lord Cornwallis XI, came in at the same number six and departed caught by a- Milsted off the bowling of K- Goodwin, for nought. It is only his second duck of the present season, but a rather more imposing sixteenth in a career now standing at one hundred and fifteen innings — figures that install him, with a certain grim majesty, at the very summit of the club's all-time table: first of six hundred and thirty-seven, a record the rest of the eleven can only regard from a respectful distance. A fixture of the Ducks on the Road, Homebody Duck and Lone Duck top tens, and a name twice bracketed under Quacking Together, with Bob Arnold and with William Buck besides, Thirkell wears his Duck of the Year 1952 as history now rather than news. Fittingly, on this same day in 1952 Gordon Fenner — no mean hand at the art of not scoring himself — was also making his own quiet way back to the pavilion. A modest week by the club's usual standards: two matches, two ducks, one apiece between Saturday's and Sunday's elevens, and neither a pair nor a family affair to report. The ducks came singly this time, which by this club's lights counts almost as restraint. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - J Barclay — 15 innings, 4 ducks, 26.67% - Gordon Fenner — 10 innings, 3 ducks, 30.00% - John Ames — 13 innings, 3 ducks, 23.08% - Michael Morton — 15 innings, 3 ducks, 20.00% - Gerald Wright — 7 innings, 2 ducks, 28.57% The wicket will doubtless prove sticky again before the season is out, and the honours board never wants for fresh names. Members are warmly invited to attend the next fixture, bat in hand and hope undimmed, and to make their own contribution to the ledger in the usual manner.

The Duck Club Gazette — 25th to 26th July, 1953

2 ducks
Week 13 · 25 Jul 1953 – 26 Jul 1953
🦆 Two more names are inscribed upon the ledger of the scoreless this week, both from the 1st XI's excursion to Folkestone, and both, it must be said, achieved by rather more decorous means than the customary golden blob. No first-ball ignominy here — merely two batsmen undone after settling their guard, which the club regards as scarcely better consolation. 1st XI — away to Folkestone CC, 26th July Tony Levick, at number five, played on to a leg-before decision off D Morton and trudged back having troubled the scorers not at all. This is his second career duck in five-and-thirty innings for the 1st XI, placing him 104th of 637 in the club's all-time roll of the dismissed-for-nought — a position he now shares, at exactly two apiece, with a positively distinguished company including Arthur Ash, B Lloyd of the Debutante Duck club, and B- Vince, who once carried off the Duck of the Year honour itself in 1941. By curious coincidence of the calendar, on this very date in 1940 one J Short likewise trudged home for nought against Boughton Monchelsea CC — proof, if any were needed, that the ducks of Linton Park stretch back through the decades in unbroken and faithful procession. Bill Hall, sent in at number eight, was stumped by Len Godden off the same D Morton — a dismissal requiring, one notes, rather more effort from the opposition than the standard variety, though the result upon the scorecard is identical. It is his maiden duck of the season and of his one-and-twenty-innings career, seating him 130th of 637 on the all-time list, level on a single career duck with a full company of one-time offenders, several of them Debutante Duck men and one-season wonders besides. Mr Hall is additionally a paid-up member of the club's Retirement Duck honours board, a distinction earned on some past and presumably dignified departure from the crease — not, it should be stressed, this week's affair, upon which no comment as to his continuing career shall be ventured. He too finds his name matched against J Short's duck of the 26th of July, 1940, against Boughton Monchelsea CC. The week in summary A modest haul: two ducks from two fixtures, both from the 1st XI, both at Folkestone, and both, pleasingly, struck by different means of dismissal — the straight bat undone by swing, and the wandering foot undone by wicketkeeper's swiftness. No pairs, no golden ducks, and no family gatherings at the crease this week — the ducks, for once, kept to their own company. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - Gordon Fenner — 8 innings, 3 ducks, 37.5% - John Ames — 11 innings, 3 ducks, 27.27% - J Barclay — 14 innings, 3 ducks, 21.43% - Michael Morton — 15 innings, 3 ducks, 20.0% - Gerald Wright — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.33% Gordon Fenner sits proudly atop the season's table of dubious distinction, though with matches yet to be played, no man's place upon it may be considered safe. The eleven return to action shortly, and the Gazette shall be watching the close of every innings with its customary keen and slightly malicious interest — for the exclusive zero club never wants for fresh applicants. Until then, may your bats stay straight and your stumps stay standing.

The Duck Club Gazette — 19th July 1953

3 ducks
Week 12 · 19 Jul 1953
A single fixture against John Larkings, and the home eleven contrived to lose three wickets without troubling the scorers at all. The zero club welcomes its latest subscribers. The 1st XI - Tom Osborn, in at first wicket down, played across a good length ball from J- May and was taken by R- Dollymore for his customary nought — his first duck of the season, and the first of a career now twenty innings old, placing him a modest 247th of the club's 637 all-time duck-holders. Curiously, on this very date in 1902, one F M Hills also strolled back for nought against Boxley CC — the calendar, it seems, has a long memory for failure. - Gordon Fenner, promoted to number seven, edged J- Larking's bowling into the gloves of M- Varcoe and departed for his third duck of the season — a lean spell even by the standards of a man who now stands third on the club's all-time roll of dishonour with a dozen career ducks from seventy-five innings, level with the venerable Jack Fryer and with Richard Harris. His brother Joe, himself no stranger to the zero club with five career ducks to his name, will doubtless offer what sympathy the tea urn allows. And once again the shade of F M Hills walks abroad, his 1902 duck against Boxley falling on this very date. - Frank Wright, sent in at number ten, was bowled by J- May without troubling the scorers — a debut innings and a debut duck in the very same breath, earning him instant and undisputed membership of the Debutante Duck club, and a starting berth 170th of the club's 637 all-time subscribers. The weightier honours of the Quack-to-Quack and the Retirement Duck must wait upon further innings, and further seasons, before either can be fairly claimed. He too walks in step with F M Hills, whose Boxley duck of 1902 falls on this same calendar day. The Week in Brief Three ducks from one match, and John Larkings' bowlers plainly found Linton Park's order much to their liking. No pairs this week, and no families united in shared misfortune — merely three gentlemen, each dismissed without addition, doing their part for the club's proudest and most peculiar tradition: the fine art of not scoring. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Gordon Fenner — 7 innings, 3 ducks (42.86%) 2. John Ames — 10 innings, 3 ducks (30.00%) 3. Michael Morton — 13 innings, 3 ducks (23.08%) 4. J Barclay — 14 innings, 3 ducks (21.43%) 5. Gerald Wright — 6 innings, 2 ducks (33.33%) The season's summit of failure remains keenly contested. Members are cordially invited to the next fixture, where the eleven will no doubt furnish further candidates for these pages.

LPCC Duck Club — Weekly Gazette, 11th July 1953

0 ducks
Week 11 · 11 Jul 1953
🦆 A quiet week at the crease, ladies and gentlemen. For once the eleven kept their bats straight and their heads down, and not a single member of the club presented himself for induction into the exclusive zero club this week. Whether by sound technique, good fortune, or the bowling simply not being up to the task of separating a batsman from his wicket without troubling the scorer, the ducks evaded capture entirely. One match was played in the period, and it passed — remarkably — without incident. The committee notes this with a mixture of relief and mild disappointment, for a week without a nought is a week without a story, and this gazette rather prefers its heroes fallen. Let it be recorded, all the same, that the season's stalwarts of self-inflicted misfortune remain hard at work elsewhere, quietly compiling the sort of figures that keep this column in business. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - John Ames — 10 innings, 3 ducks, 30.0% - Michael Morton — 12 innings, 3 ducks, 25.0% - J Barclay — 14 innings, 3 ducks, 21.43% - Gerald Wright — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.0% - Gordon Fenner — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.33% Mr Wright leads the percentage table with a positively alarming 40 per cent strike rate for nought, a consistency of a very particular kind that the rest of the eleven would do well to study, if only to avoid. Ames and Morton press on with quiet determination toward their fourth ducks of the summer, while Barclay's fourteen innings suggest a batsman rather too often given the opportunity to fail. The tail, as ever, wags on regardless. The eleven take the field again next week, and this correspondent, ever the optimist in matters of pessimism, fully expects the zero club to welcome fresh blood before long. Until then — mind the sticky wickets, and keep an eye on the scorebook.

THE DUCK CLUB GAZETTE — for the week of the 4th and 5th of July, 1953

3 ducks
Week 10 · 4 Jul 1953 – 5 Jul 1953
Two fixtures were played this week, and though the exclusive zero club is rarely quiet for long, it was the 1st XI alone who furnished business for the honours board — three names added in a single afternoon away to Charles Arkcoll. The 1st XI, away to Charles Arkcoll — 4th July In at five, Bob Arnold played across one from Randolph Thompson and was bowled without troubling the scorers — a first duck of the season, and the eighth of a career now run to two-and-forty innings, placing him tenth of six hundred and thirty-six in the club's long and dubious roll. A charter member of Ducks in a Row, four in unbroken succession, and party to two companionable pairings, Quacking Together with John Thirkell and Only Two Quacks with Alan Wilkes — Arnold's is consistency of a very particular kind. It may interest him to learn that on this very date in 1904, Arthur Cornwallis also made his way back for nought against Sutton Valence School; the calendar, it seems, has long had a taste for the art of not scoring. At seven, G- Neighbour fell to John Ames, likewise for nought — a maiden season's duck, and but the first blot on a young ledger of three innings, 179th of the 636. He carries already the Retirement Duck honour from a past farewell of his own, a solemn distinction best left where it belongs, in history rather than this week's account. He, too, finds himself keeping company with Cornwallis, who trod the same lonely path back to the pavilion on this date in 1904. And at eight, Michael Morton went the same way — bowled John Ames — for the third time this season, and the third duck of a career built upon a dozen innings, 58th of the all-time company. Two wickets to Ames inside the same short spell was triumph through adversity for the bowler and a sticky wicket indeed for the middle order. Morton, like his colleagues above, shares his date with Cornwallis's duck of 1904 — a coincidence the honours board will note with quiet satisfaction. Week in summary Three ducks from two matches, all struck from the one innings against Charles Arkcoll, with John Ames doing for two batsmen what most bowlers manage only once in an afternoon. The tail, it must be said, did not so much wag as fold quietly. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - John Ames — 10 innings, 3 ducks, 30.00% - Michael Morton — 12 innings, 3 ducks, 25.00% - J Barclay — 13 innings, 3 ducks, 23.08% - Gerald Wright — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.00% - Gordon Fenner — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.33% The season's leading names sit close together, and there is no reason to suppose the gap will widen before the next fixture is played. Members are cordially reminded that the eleven takes the field again shortly, and the club's honours board, ever hospitable, keeps a place set for whoever should care to walk in and straight back out again.

THE DUCK CLUB GAZETTE

2 ducks
Week 9 · 27 Jun 1953 – 28 Jun 1953
A Chronicle of Noughts — 27th and 28th June, 1953 Two fixtures played across the weekend, and the exclusive zero club receives two new subscriptions, both from the 1st XI, both furnished in the same understated fashion. 1st XI - R- Fermor came in at number seven against Bearsted CC on the Saturday and was back in the pavilion directly, bowled by V. Pound before he had troubled the scorers to any degree. A maiden innings met by a duck's egg is a debut of the rarest sort, and he is enrolled at once into the Debutante Duck club. The books, as they presently stand, place him upon the One and Done board for 1953 — a career of a single nought so far recorded — and should the eleven see no more of him, a place waits quietly among the club's Retirement Ducks, though we trust the books prove premature. He takes his station 230th of 636 in the club's long roll of honour. A pleasing coincidence attends him: on this very date in 1936, one E. Godden likewise walked back for nought against Bearsted CC, so the fixture appears to have a memory of its own. - Gordon Fenner followed him to the pavilion the very next afternoon, caught G. Parker off the bowling of B. Fletcher while playing for Selstead at number four. No novice's misfortune, this — it is his eleventh career duck in seventy-four innings, a lofty sixth of 636 all-time, and his second of the present season besides. The art of not scoring runs in the family, it might be said, his brother Joe Fenner carrying five noughts of his own upon the club's books. And by a curious turn of the calendar, on this same date in 1882 one J. Sedgwick made a duck against Marden CC, Kent — the ducks of history keeping, it seems, their own fixture card. A quiet weekend by the club's usual standards — two matches, two ducks, no pairs and no family gatherings at the crease this time, though the season's tally continues its patient accumulation regardless. Stan Wratten — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.33% The eleven takes the field again next week, and the club stands ready, as ever, to welcome whichever gentleman the bowlers next persuade into its dubious fellowship.

The Duck Report — 20th to 21st June, 1953

0 ducks
Week 8 · 20 Jun 1953 – 21 Jun 1953
A curious week to set before you, gentlemen, for the eleven took the field twice over these two days and not a single batsman was persuaded to walk back for nought. The zero club, that most exclusive of pavilions, reports no new admissions. Whether this reflects a sudden and regrettable outbreak of good batting, or merely that the bowlers of the opposition were having an off week of their own, the committee declines to speculate. It happens, now and again, that the ducks give the fielders the slip entirely — a fortnight's respite from the art of not scoring, and no doubt a source of quiet disappointment to those who follow this report chiefly for its casualties. Let it be recorded, in the spirit of honest chronicle, that on this occasion every man who came to the crease left it having troubled the scorers for at least one run. A sticky wicket for the Duck Club correspondent, if for nobody else. We shall not want for material long. The season's leading exponents of the golden art remain very much in form, and a glance at the honours below should reassure members that ignominy is never far away. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - John Ames — 8 innings, 3 ducks, 37.5% - J Barclay — 13 innings, 3 ducks, 23.08% - Gerald Wright — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.0% - Stan Wratten — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.33% - Michael Morton — 9 innings, 2 ducks, 22.22% Mr Wright's figure of two ducks from a mere five innings places him on a striking 40 per cent, a rate of failure so committed it borders on the professional, and Mr Ames is not far behind him for sheer consistency of a very particular kind. The rest of the eleven would do well to remember that reputations built over a season are not undone by one blameless fortnight. So: a week without a casualty, and the club's records unchanged for it. Enjoy the respite while it lasts, gentlemen — the next fixture is rarely so obliging, and the pavilion steps have a way of calling a man back sooner than he expects. Until then, straight bats all round, and may your luck hold a little longer than your opponents'.

The Duck Club Gazette — Sunday, 14th June, 1953

2 ducks
Week 7 · 14 Jun 1953
A quiet afternoon at home to Old Colfeians CC furnished the Club with two fresh members of the exclusive zero club, both from deep in the order, both dismissed without addition to the total. The art of not scoring remains, as ever, alive and well among the lower reaches of the 1st XI. 1st XI - Gordon Fenner, in at number seven, was taken by E. Evans off the bowling of G. Keeble and returned to the pavilion with nothing to show for his trouble — his first duck's egg of the 1953 season, and the tenth of a career now well stocked with them, 72 innings deep. He sits eighth of all 634 names on the Club's all-time roll of the dismissed, a standing not easily disturbed. He may take some comfort, or none at all, in kinship — his brother Joe Fenner already carries five ducks of his own, so the family name is no stranger to this particular honours board. Curiously, on this very day in 1882, one C. Gibbs also walked back for nought against the 1st Innings of Boxley CC — proof, if proof were needed, that the fourteenth of June has long had a taste for these things. - J. Barclay, sent in at number nine, was bowled by D. Beddows for the third time this season, a plucky knock undone before it began. Thirteen innings into his career, three of them now ducks, he stands fifty-fourth of 634 on the all-time list, and finds himself, this very season, in contention for the Duck of the Year 1953 honour — a distinction he seems in no hurry to relinquish. His name is also inscribed, from some earlier and quite separate farewell, upon the Retirement Duck board, though nothing in Sunday's play suggests he has any present intention of bowing out. He too shares his duck's day with C. Gibbs of 1882, against Boxley CC, a coincidence the Club records rather than explains. A modest week, then — one match, one pair of ducks, both from the tail, and both proof that adversity, when it comes, comes with a certain regularity to the lower order. The Duck Club Gazette — 6th and 7th June, 1953

1 duck
Week 6 · 6 Jun 1953 – 7 Jun 1953
A modest despatch this week, for the ducks proved shy quarry across both fixtures, yielding but a single egg to the collector's net. 1st XI At the wicket on the 7th, in the match against Old Shooterhillians, Richard Harris came in at number seven and departed without troubling the scorers, caught J Cooper, bowled G Bird. A tidy piece of bowling and a plucky if fruitless knock, and so the season's first duck's egg is chalked up against his name. It is, mind you, no stranger to him — his twelfth for the career now, in sixty-two innings, which places him a most distinguished fourth of six hundred and thirty-three in the club's roll of honour, a perch few gentlemen ever reach and fewer still would boast of. In doing so he draws level on that very tally of twelve with one Jack Fryer, who wore the same figure with equal good humour between 1881 and 1906 across sixty-seven innings, and who twice carried off the Duck of the Year, in 1891 and again in 1900. Mr Harris now walks in distinguished if unscoring company. The Week in Brief Two matches played over the weekend, and only the one duck laid between them — the eleven, on the whole, kept a straight bat and the tail need not have wagged at all. A quiet week for the club's own particular scoreboard, though the season's leading exponents of the art of not scoring continue to press their claims below. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Gerald Wright — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67 per cent - John Ames — 6 innings, 3 ducks, 50.00 per cent - Stan Wratten — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.00 per cent - Michael Morton — 9 innings, 2 ducks, 22.22 per cent - J Barclay — 12 innings, 2 ducks, 16.67 per cent Gerald Wright leads the field by some distance, though John Ames's three eggs in half a dozen visits to the crease is a rate of failure not easily bettered, and the whole quintet may consider their positions far from safe with the season yet young. The eleven take the field again shortly, and the club's honours board stands ever ready to welcome whichever unfortunate soul the bowlers next dispatch for nought. Until then, keep a wary eye on the sticky wickets.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the days of the 30th and 31st of May, 1953

2 ducks
Week 5 · 30 May 1953 – 31 May 1953
A quiet couple of days for the exclusive zero club — only the First Eleven troubled the scorers with their particular brand of nothing, but they made it count with a fine display of team spirit in adversity against the Old Williamsonians. 1st XI — v Old Williamsonians CC, 30th May Opening the innings and opening the account for the wrong side of the ledger was Basil Sears, caught Saunders, bowled Trower, for his 1st duck of the season and the 4th of a career now standing at a very respectable 28th of 630 on the all-time roll — a batsman who has, over 63 innings, made a habit of occasionally forgetting to trouble the scoreboard. He finds himself level on career ducks with a whole gallery of old and new names alike, joining the likes of Gerald Wright and the long-serving John --'s Taylor on exactly four apiece — kindred spirits in the art of not scoring. And by happy coincidence of the calendar, on this very day in 1943 one Frank Sutton, twice Duck of the Year and second on the all-time list with fourteen to his name, was himself walking back for nought against Home Guard - D Company — the ghosts of duck-outings past keeping Basil fine company. Following him back to the pavilion in short order was John Thirkell, bowled Trower without troubling the scorers, his 1st duck of this season but the 15th of an extraordinary career that sits him proudly — or perhaps not so proudly — at the very summit of the all-time table, 1st of 630. A paid-up member of the Duck of the Year honours board for 1952 and a fixture of the Lone Duck, Homebody Duck and Ducks on the Road top tens, Thirkell also shares the rare distinction of Quacking Together with both Bob Arnold and William Buck in seasons past. Like his opening partner, he too finds himself keeping step with history — for on this same 30th of May in 1943, Frank Sutton was again making his own duck's egg against Home Guard - D Company, proof that some dates simply attract the duck. A sticky sort of morning for the top of the order, then, with the innings undone before it had properly begun — but a straight bat and better fortune will surely follow at the crease before long. A brief accounting: two ducks recorded across two matches this week, both falling to the bowling of Trower and both from the top of the 1st XI order — a fine piece of new-ball work by the visitors, and a sobering reminder to Linton Park's openers that the art of not scoring requires no invitation. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard — 1953 - John Ames — 3 ducks in 5 innings (60.0%) - Gerald Wright — 2 ducks in 3 innings (66.67%) - Stan Wratten — 2 ducks in 4 innings (50.0%) - Michael Morton — 2 ducks in 8 innings (25.0%) - J Barclay — 2 ducks in 10 innings (20.0%) The season presses on, and with it the Duck Club's ever-watchful ledger. Members of the Eleven are respectfully reminded that the next fixture offers every opportunity for fresh nominations to this most singular of honours boards — until then, may your bats stay straight and your stumps stay standing.

The Duck Report — 23rd to 25th May, 1953

3 ducks
Week 4 · 23 May 1953 – 25 May 1953
A quiet week for the eleven, yet not so quiet as to spare the honours board a fresh entry or two. Three ducks fell across three fixtures, and one gentleman contrived to visit the pavilion twice in as many days. The First Eleven Gerald Wright made unwanted history this week, twice undone for nought inside two days — a feat the club's ledger records plainly as a pair, that grim double which no batsman sets out to achieve. On the Saturday, at home to Gore Court CC, he was bowled by Peter Holmes batting at number ten, his first duck of the season and the third of a career now numbering seven innings. Curiously, on this very day in 1943, one K- Symonds likewise departed for nought, against Royal Artillery Wing 48. Wright returned to the crease on the Sunday against Halfway House, in at number eleven, and was run out without troubling the scorers — his second duck in as many days and his fourth for the career, a tally that places him 34th of the 628 gentlemen who have made this particular journey. By a pleasing coincidence, this same 24th of May in the year 1882 saw F Foster fall for nought against Collier Street CC — proof, if any were needed, that the art of not scoring respects no calendar. William Buck, opening at number two against Halfway House on the Sunday, was likewise run out without scoring — a plucky enough start undone by a mix-up in the running. It is his second career duck in a lengthy innings of sixty-five, and places him 107th of the 628 in the club's all-time reckoning. Buck is, besides, a paid-up member of the "Quacking Together" fellowship alongside John Thirkell, two names forever bound by shared misfortune on the honours board. And here too the calendar plays its game — on this same 24th of May back in 1882, F Foster made his own duck against that same Collier Street CC. The Week in Brief Three matches, three ducks, and a certain want of communication in the running between wickets seems to have been the villain of the piece — both Sunday dismissals at Halfway House came by the run out, a sticky wicket of a different sort. Gerald Wright's pair is the week's chief curiosity, two ducks laid inside a single weekend being a distinction few would seek and fewer still achieve twice running. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - John Ames — 5 innings, 3 ducks, 60.0% - Gerald Wright — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100.0% - Stan Wratten — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.0% - Michael Morton — 7 innings, 2 ducks, 28.57% - J Barclay — 8 innings, 2 ducks, 25.0% The eleven takes the field again shortly, and the club has every confidence that fresh candidates will present themselves for the honours board in due course. Until then, the exclusive zero club extends its sympathies, and its congratulations, in equal measure.

The Duck's Egg Gazette — 16th and 17th May, 1953

5 ducks
Week 3 · 16 May 1953 – 17 May 1953
Two fixtures, one melancholy thread running through both: five eggs laid for the 1st XI across Gore Court and Mote A, and the exclusive zero club welcomes its members back with the usual solemn ceremony. Gore Court CC, 16th May Michael Morton, at four, was undone by a smart catch from Peter Holmes off T Clinch's bowling — his second duck of the season, and the second of a career now five innings long. He stands 92nd of 627 in the club's grand and dubious ledger. Curiously, on this very day in 1943, one L- Breedon walked back for nought against the Royal Army Service Corps 533 Division — the calendar, it seems, has a long memory for the art of not scoring. J Barclay, at seven, was caught and bowled by Peter Holmes for his maiden career duck — though the celebrations proved premature, as the reader shall discover below. Barclay already carries this season's Duck of the Year honours, and is a paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club from some past and presumably final innings, though nobody present this week saw him bow out for good, so we shall say no more on that score. His fall, too, echoed L- Breedon's 1943 vintage against the Service Corps. Mote A, 17th May The very next day brought Stan Wratten to the crease as opener, only to be bowled by Mac Harden without scoring — his second duck of the summer, and the seventh of a career that has now seen him dismissed for nought seventy-seven times over, fourteenth on the club's all-time list of the ignominious. Wratten holds his "Quacking Together" honours jointly with John Ames, and fittingly the pair renewed the acquaintance this very afternoon, Ames following him back to the pavilion at four, bowled by J- Coomber for his third duck of the season and his third of a career now eighteen innings long. Ames, a fixture of the Homebody Duck top ten and no stranger to four ducks in a row, continues to prove that consistency in this club comes in more than one flavour. Both men might reflect that on this same date in 1941, Herbert Rayner made his own duck against the Royal Army Ordnance Corps — some anniversaries simply will not be shaken off. And J Barclay, not content with Saturday's disappointment, returned at number eight to be caught by J- Waters off Mac Harden for his second duck of the week and his second of the season — a grim pair across the two fixtures that places him firmly among the week's most decorated failures. The Week in Brief Five ducks fell across two matches, both played away from home, and Mote A alone accounted for three of them — a sticky afternoon for top and middle order alike. Barclay's pair was the week's sternest reminder that misfortune, like rain, rarely falls but once. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. John Ames — 3 innings, 3 ducks, 100 per cent 2. Stan Wratten — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67 per cent 3. J Barclay — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40 per cent 4. Michael Morton — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40 per cent The eleven takes the field again next week, and the zero club stands ready, as ever, to welcome whichever gentleman finds the art of not scoring rather too easy to master.

The Duck Club Gazette — 9th to 10th May, 1953

2 ducks
Week 2 · 9 May 1953 – 10 May 1953
Two fixtures graced Linton Park this weekend, and though bat generally had the better of ball, the eleven surrendered a brace of duck's eggs to keep the Club's ledger in its accustomed good order. 1st XI On the Saturday, against Bearsted CC, Michael Morton came to the wicket at number four and departed without troubling the scorers, bowled by G. Hawkins. A first duck's egg of the season for him, and the third innings of a still-young career — the 212th such dismissal on the Club's long and honourable roll. He now keeps company with the departed - Dampier, who managed exactly one duck in his single season of 1952 before quietly retiring the bat for good, a paid-up member of both the Debutante Duck and the Retirement Duck fraternities, though Morton, one trusts, has rather more cricket left in him yet. The Sunday brought Folkestone CC to the Park, and with them the second instalment of John Ames's week, bowled by Jim Gordon at number five for his second duck of the season and second of a seventeen-innings career — a tidy 87th on the all-time roll. Ames arrives in distinguished if faintly cursed company: he sits within the Ducks in a Row quartet, keeps a place among the Homebody Duck top ten, and shares his solitary quacks with Alan Wilkes, with Roy Clarke, and with Stan Wratten besides — a man who rarely ducks alone. Curiously, on this very day a twelvemonth before, in 1952, Bob Arnold too strolled back for nought against Bearsted CC, a small coincidence of the calendar the Club notes with quiet satisfaction. The Week in Brief Two matches, two ducks, one apiece — a modest yield by the Club's exacting standards, but honest toil against two visiting sides, and proof enough that the art of not scoring remains very much alive at Linton Park. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard, 1953 1. John Ames — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% 2. Stan Wratten — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% 3. Michael Morton — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33% The season is young yet, and the wicket at Linton Park has shown no particular favour to anyone this week. The Club awaits, as ever, the next fixture's certain further contributions to the honours board. --- Separately, and only mentioning this once: one of the team's machines is well behind on shared skills/config — worth telling that colleague to start a session sometime so it pulls automatically, nothing needed from you here.

The Duck Report — 3rd May, 1953

2 ducks
Week 1 · 3 May 1953
🦆 A fine Sunday at Linton Park, and the eleven welcomed Hunton Wanderers CC to the home ground — a fixture that, for two of our number, will be remembered less for runs scored than for runs decidedly not scored. The art of not scoring was practised with quiet distinction. 1st XI John Ames, sent in at five, played a firm enough looking guard before M Owen had him bowled without troubling the scorers — his first duck's egg of the 1953 season, and the sixth of a career now sixteen innings long. He takes his place at 198th of 627 in the club's long and honourable roll of failure, and does so as a paid-up member of several standing societies of the nought — the Homebody Duck top ten among them, and a fellow traveller in "Quacking Together" with both Roy Clarke and Stan Wratten, which made for interesting company in the pavilion this week. Curiously, on this very date last year, the redoubtable John Thirkell — second on the all-time list with fourteen ducks to his name — was likewise dispatched, against West Farleigh CC. History, it seems, keeps a calendar. Not to be outdone, Stan Wratten followed him back to the pavilion one place down the order, also bowled by M Owen, also for nought. A sticky wicket for the middle order, evidently. This was Wratten's first duck of the season but his sixth in a career of seventy-five innings, lodging him firmly at 19th of 627 on the all-time roll — rarefied air indeed, and he now stands level on career ducks with the venerable W H Fryer of 1867-85 vintage, among other distinguished company. Fittingly, he too shares the on-this-day misfortune with Thirkell's 1952 duck against West Farleigh. Two batsmen, one bowler, one unhappy coincidence of dates. The Week in Brief A single fixture, a brace of ducks, and one bowler — M Owen of Hunton Wanderers — who may fairly claim to have enjoyed his afternoon rather more than the home order did. No pairs, no king pairs, and no family affairs to report this week, the ducks arriving individually rather than in convenient bundles. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - John Ames — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Stan Wratten — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A perfect start to the season's ignominy for both, and plenty of fixtures yet to come in which either might improve his figures — or, this being the Duck Club, cheerfully fail to. The eleven return to the field next weekend, and the Club awaits its next candidates for the exclusive zero club with its usual warm and undiscriminating welcome.

He now sits level with A Kent, who compiled his own three ducks in a brief season of 1893 and was that year's Duck of the Year, kindred spirits separated by the better part of sixty summers yet united upon the very same tally. The Week in Summary One match, one wicket falling for nought, and the credit goes to Gordon Fenner — a name that will be seen again below, for he numbers among this season's most industrious duck-hunters, having evidently dispensed more trouble with the ball than he has met with the bat. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the week ending the 31st of August, 1952

3 ducks
Week 19 · 30 Aug 1952 – 31 Aug 1952
A modest week for the exclusive zero club, but a memorable one, for one member of the 1st XI contrived to visit us twice inside a single weekend. 1st XI John Thirkell opened proceedings on the 30th, away to Hunton Wanderers CC. Sent in at four, he was bowled by R Venner without troubling the scorers — his seventh duck of the season and the thirteenth of a career that stands second in the whole Club register of 625 hopefuls. He was not to be outdone by himself. The very next afternoon, at home to A Levick's XI and promoted to first wicket down, he was bowled again, this time by John Ames, for his eighth of the summer and fourteenth for his career — a grim pair taken across two days and two grounds, the sort of feat that asks a great deal of a man's patience and rather more of his sense of humour. In arriving at fourteen he draws level with the great Frank Sutton, who carried the same tally through a career from 1925 to 1949 and was twice crowned Duck of the Year for his trouble. Thirkell, for his part, already wears this year's Duck of the Year sash, sits proudly among the top ten Lone Ducks, the top ten Homebody Ducks and the top ten Ducks on the Road, and shares the honours board twice over in Quacking Together, with both Bob Arnold and William Buck. H Newport followed him back to the pavilion on the same afternoon, number ten, caught D Latham off the bowling of the ever-busy R Venner, for nought — his second duck of the season and sixth of a career now twenty-four innings long, good enough for seventeenth place in the Club's grim ledger. He sits on precisely the same career total as D Sells, who plied his trade between 1943 and 1944, gathered his own six ducks in fourteen innings, and was Duck of the Year in 1943 besides. Newport is, we might add, a long-standing member of the Retirement Duck club, an honour recording some distant and presumably premature farewell rather than any valediction of his own this week. The week in brief Two fixtures, three ducks, and one gentleman of the 1st XI shouldering two of them single-handed — proof, if proof were wanted, that the art of not scoring is best practised with commitment. R Venner of Hunton Wanderers CC may fairly claim the ball of the week, having accounted for both of Saturday's victims.
