Members are warmly encouraged to attend the next match, bat straight, and, failing that, to fail with style.

The Duck Club Gazette: 23rd–24th August, 1952

4 ducks
Week 18 · 23 Aug 1952 – 24 Aug 1952
Two fixtures took the field this week, and one of them proved uncommonly generous to the exclusive zero club. Four eggs were laid in a single innings against Charles Arkcoll on the Saturday, while Sunday's match passed the ducks by entirely, to the quiet relief of at least eleven gentlemen. The First Eleven - D Simmons, in at first wicket down, was caught by Humphrey Morris off the bowling of Stan Wratten — a plain enough dismissal, honestly earned. His third career duck in fifteen innings settles him at 48th of 624 on the club's roll of dishonour, drawing him level with the venerable A Kent, whose own trio of noughts were gathered in a single unhappy season back in 1893. - Three places along, Gordon Bugge fell to the very same Stan Wratten, whose afternoon was plainly a rewarding one for all the wrong reasons. This too was his third career duck, and he joins Simmons in keeping curious company with A Kent on that count — two members of the present eleven, fifty-nine years and one bowler apart, arriving at the identical figure by rather different roads. - At number six, Bob Arnold was bowled by Gordon Fenner for his third duck of the season and his seventh of a career that continues to write itself firmly into the honours boards. He remains a proud holder of Ducks in a Row for four consecutive eggs laid without troubling the scorer, and stands paired for perpetuity in Only Two Quacks with Alan Wilkes and in Quacking Together with John Thirkell — evidently a man who prefers not to fall alone. His seventh career duck draws him level with the formidable A Startup, whose own seven noughts between 1868 and 1882 earned three Duck of the Year honours and a place in the five-consecutive company of Ducks in a Row — a target Arnold may yet have designs upon. - Last man in, Gerald Wright was bowled by John Ames for his second duck of the season and his second in a mere four innings played, a strike rate for failure that would give a lesser man pause. He joins A S Day on that same tally of two. In sum, four wickets fell to nought in the one innings on Saturday — Messrs Simmons, Bugge, Arnold and Wright strung from number two clean through to number eleven, wanting only the middle order to make the collapse entire. Gordon Fenner, who appears further down this very report as a leading light of the season's duck-getting, spent his Saturday afternoon adding to the ledger from the bowling end instead, claiming Arnold's wicket while presumably hoping his own name might rest quiet a while longer. The Duck Report — the weekend of the 3rd and 4th of August, 1952

2 ducks
Week 15 · 3 Aug 1952 – 4 Aug 1952
A quiet weekend for the exclusive zero club, but what it lacked in numbers it made up for in doggedness. Two matches, two ducks, and both laid by the same unfortunate hand. 1st XI Number ten Gordon Fenner opened proceedings on the Saturday, stumped by E Webb off the bowling of D Thomas — undone not by rash stroke but by a wandering foot outside his ground. His second duck's egg of the season, and the eighth of a career now stretching to sixty-three innings, which places him level with the venerable George Champion (74 innings, 1886–1912) on exactly eight career ducks — fine company for a fine failure. Curiously, on this very day in 1903, one H G Smith trudged back for nought against the same opposition, 1st Innings Rochester CC, a reminder that the club has been repeating itself for the better part of fifty years. A day was not enough to shake the habit. Sent in last man on the Sunday against Lord Cornwallis's XI, Fenner was bowled by J Larking for his third duck of the season and his ninth of a career that now stands ninth on the all-time list of some six hundred and twenty-three names — drawing level, by neat coincidence, with B Westover's wartime tally of nine. The scorebook records the weekend plainly as a pair, that grimmest of doubles, two ducks laid within twenty-four hours of one another, though happily neither was a golden one — Fenner played himself in each time before the axe fell, triumph through adversity of a very particular kind. It may be noted, for those who like their history layered, that on this same date back in 1869 one W H Fryer made his own duck against Horsmonden CC — the ritual, it seems, is older than the club itself. Members with long memories will also recall that Fenner's brother Joe carries five career ducks of his own — evidently a family with an inherited gift for the art of not scoring. The week in brief Two matches, two ducks, one player — a rare instance of a gentleman keeping the whole week's dismissals entirely to himself. Whether this counts as generosity or simple bad luck is left to the reader's judgement, though the sticky wicket of consistency clearly runs in the Fenner blood. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. Three eggs were laid this week, gentlemen, all by the 1st XI, and all away from home — which will not surprise those who hold that a duck travels better than it bats. Folkestone CC, Sunday the 11th John Thirkell, at five, played on to J Court without troubling the scorers — his third duck of a summer already generous with them, and the ninth of a career placing him a lofty seventh on the all-time roll. He draws level on nine with B Westover, who played between 1940 and 1945. One place below him, Don Hartridge fell to the very same J Court without scoring — the two gentlemen departing in harness to a bowler plainly in irresistible form that afternoon. It was Hartridge's second duck of the season and his ninth in a career of sixty-six innings, sixth of all time, and he too finds himself keeping company with B Westover on nine. The week in summary Two matches, three ducks, and Folkestone CC may fairly claim the day's honours — J Court removing two LPCC batsmen without a run between them inside a single innings, a sticky wicket indeed for numbers five and six. 0 ducks
Week 21 · 16 Sep 1951
🦆🏏 Well now, members. A curious thing has happened, and it happened by not happening at all. Not a single batsman troubled the exclusive zero club this Sunday. Not one plucky soul walked out, faced his ball or balls, and walked straight back without so much as a single to show for the journey. The eleven, on this occasion, kept their bats and their dignity intact from top to tail — a state of affairs the Committee finds almost unsporting in its rarity. Whether this speaks to a sound wicket, a merciful bowling attack, or simply an afternoon when fortune smiled on Linton Park's willow-wielders, the Gazette cannot say. What we can say is that the season's duck hunters will have watched from the boundary with folded arms and nothing whatsoever to add to their ledgers this week. The nought, it seems, took Sunday off. Let it not be said, however, that the record book has gone hungry this season. Far from it. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - 🥇 Arthur Cradduck — 18 innings, 5 ducks, 27.78% — the season's most reliable early return, and no mistake - 🥈 Richard Harris — 12 innings, 3 ducks, 25.00% — a sticky wicket seems to follow the man about - 🥉 John Thirkell — 26 innings, 3 ducks, 11.54% — plenty of innings between his duck's eggs, which rather counts as restraint - J Enfield — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.00% — a coin-toss of a batting record if ever there was one - E Lockyer — 7 innings, 2 ducks, 28.57% — quietly building a case for the honours board yet A fine collection of gentlemen who know the art of not scoring better than most know the art of scoring, and to whom the Committee extends its warmest and most solemn congratulations, in absentia this week. So there it is, members — a blank page in the club's book of ignominy, though we harbour no illusions it shall stay that way for long. The next fixture will surely furnish the zero club with fresh recruits, and the Gazette will be waiting, pen in hand, to record every last one of them. Until then — mind the sticky wickets, and good batting to you all. 🍩0️⃣

A modest instalment this week, but not without its charm: two eggs laid in the match against Gillingham CC of Kent, both by the home eleven's lower order, both accounted for by sharp work in the field. 1st XI - Tony Levick, sent in at number seven, was caught by F Saunders off the bowling of R Beckenham without troubling the scorers. It is his first duck of the season, and stands as his solitary entry in the Club's ledger of failure to date — one duck now sits against ten innings, placing him 234th of 613 in the club's long and honourable roll. He joins - Gaskin, a name from the 1949 season, on exactly one career duck apiece — kindred spirits separated by two years and joined in nothing. - Richard Harris, one place further down the order at eight, edged behind to R Davies off A Fairbrass and walked back for the third time this season without scoring — a sequence that speaks less of misfortune than of a settled and particular consistency. It is his eighth career duck from thirty-six innings, and it lifts him to a lofty seventh of 613 on the all-time list, a position most members can only dream of and rather fewer would wish for. In doing so he draws level with George Champion, who plied his trade between 1886 and 1912 and whose own eighth duck, taken in his 74th innings, earned him the Duck of the Year honour in 1897. The Week in Brief Two matches, two ducks, both claimed in the same fixture against Gillingham — the lower order once again shouldering the burden while their colleagues, presumably, looked on from the safety of the pavilion. A quiet week for the Club, but an instructive one: consistency, as ever, comes in many forms. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Arthur Cradduck — 5 ducks in 18 innings (27.78%) 2. A quiet week, then, for the connoisseur of the collapsed stump — two matches yielding but one sacrifice to the great cause, and the tail, on this occasion, wagging rather less than it fell. A record of the week's visits to the exclusive zero club, 18th–19th August, 1951 Two fixtures at home this week, and the eleven contributed three names to the ledger of the scoreless — the tail, as so often, doing its own quiet wagging. 1st XI Saturday, 18th August, host to F R Sutton's XI: Peter Weedon, promoted to number eight, played around one from J Toyer and was given lbw for nought. Not a first-ball dismissal by the record, merely a straight bat that found no runs behind it. It is his second duck of the summer and the fourth of a career now 22 innings deep, holding him at 34th of 613 on the club's roll of dubious distinction. Mr Weedon remains, and has long been, a paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club — that solemn honour reserved for a career's presumed final innings ending on a duck's egg — though nothing this week suggests his innings with the club are done, only that the board awaits its moment. A pleasing coincidence attends him: on this very date in 1893, one Jack Fryer, twice Duck of the Year and twelve times a visitor to nought, was likewise trudging back to the pavilion, his against Eton Ramblers CC. Sunday, 19th August, host to Mote A, proved a sticky wicket for the lower order twice over. Richard Harris, at number eight, was trapped lbw by C. Horton without troubling the scorers — his second duck of the season and seventh of a career spanning 35 innings, a tally lofty enough to rank him eighth of 613, rarefied company indeed. At number eleven, E Lockyer followed him back, bowled by H. Hawkins for nought — also his second duck of the season, and the fourth in a brisk career of fifteen innings, 28th on the club's roll. Both gentlemen share good company across the years: on this same date in 1944, Herbert Rayner made his own duck against the R.A. Training Wing, Wrotham, a fellow traveller separated from them by seven summers exactly. The Week in Brief Two matches, three ducks, and the home dressing room rather better acquainted with nought than it might have wished — Sunday's Mote A fixture alone accounting for two of the week's three, a plucky lower order undone twice in an afternoon. 🏏 Good evening, members. The 1st XI took the long road to Old Williamsonians on the 28th and came home with three names for the register — a sound reminder that a straight bat is no guarantee against a straighter ball. Arthur Cradduck, sent in at eight, fell to the same Bowring for his 4th duck of a rampaging season and his 5th career duck in a mere 19 innings — form that has already earned him the Duck of the Year 1951 board, and at this rate he may retain it by Michaelmas. He too shares the curious distinction of a duck on the 28th of July matching Cruttenden's 1897 vintage — a date, it would seem, with a certain reputation. No pairs, no king pairs, and no family affairs this week, though with Cradduck's rate of return one wonders how long that can last. A modest week for the exclusive zero club, but a week nonetheless, and the eleven's opening pair supplied both entries between them. The First XI Against Town Malling CC on the 21st, the innings began in the poorest of fashions. Basil Sears, opening the batting, and William Buck, sent in first wicket down beside him, were both undone by the identical hand — b M- Wheatley to each — the pair back at the pavilion gate almost before the scoreboard had properly turned over. A sticky start to any innings, and Wheatley may fairly claim the morning's honours, though it is not a wicket the club enters in its own book. For Sears this is the season's first duck's egg, and the second of a career now standing at thirty-three innings, a tally that lodges him sixtieth of six hundred and thirteen in the club's long and undistinguished roll of nought-getters. On this very day in 1897, one H G Smith performed the identical feat against Maidstone CC, so Sears keeps rather venerable company down the years. For Buck the story is briefer but no less final, his very first career duck in twenty-one innings, placing him two hundred and forty-second of six hundred and thirteen upon the all-time list. He is besides a paid-up member of the Quacking Together honours board, sharing that distinction with John Thirkell from an earlier occasion, and needs no repeat performance this week to keep his place there. Buck too finds himself in Smith's 1897 anniversary company, the same duck against Maidstone recalled once more, fifty-four years on almost to the day. The Week in Brief Two matches were played in the period, and the zero club received exactly two new subscriptions, both from the same Saturday afternoon at Town Malling and both from the same bowler's hand. A sticky wicket for the top of the order, though the remainder of the innings, mercifully, falls outside this correspondent's remit. A quiet week at Linton Park, and one must report it plainly: not a single duck was laid across the fixture played in this period. The pitch remains sticky in patches, and reputations built on adversity are not undone by a single week of runs. Week 6 · 2 Jun 1951 – 3 Jun 1951
A quiet weekend at the crease, gentlemen. Two fixtures were played across the period and, we regret to report, not a single duck's egg was laid at either ground. Every man who walked to the wicket contrived, by hook, by edge, or by the grace of a generous umpire, to trouble the scorers at least once. The exclusive zero club held no induction ceremony this week, and its honours board gathers not a single new name. Whether this speaks of straighter bats up and down the order, or merely of bowling below its best, history alone will judge. The Duck Club, ever a patient institution, notes only that the art of not scoring was, for once, left unpractised. We trust it is a lapse swiftly corrected. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - J Enfield — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100.0% — a perfect record of imperfection, sir, and none in the eleven presses him closely - Gordon Bugge — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.0% — a steady contributor to the cause, level of head if not of average - E Goodall — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% — early days yet, but a flawless start in the wrong direction - Gordon Fenner — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% — keeping his name warm on the honours board without undue exertion - E Lockyer — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33% — the most reluctant member of this distinguished company, and rightly proud of it The season standings remain unchanged this week, gentlemen, for want of fresh material. Mr Enfield sits atop the table still, his average a model of consistency that the rest of the eleven might do well, or ill, to emulate. The Duck Club awaits the next fixture with its customary patience and its customary confidence that the ducks, though they evaded the net this week, will not stay away for long. Pads on, gentlemen — the season is far from finished, and neither, we suspect, is the list.

The Duck Club Gazette — for the week of 26th to 27th May, 1951

0 ducks
Week 5 · 26 May 1951 – 27 May 1951
A curious thing occurred over the weekend's two fixtures, and it is this: nothing occurred at all. Not a single member of the eleven, on either side of the ropes, contrived to walk back for a duck's egg. The bowlers toiled, the fielders crouched in expectant hush around the bat, and still the naught eluded every hand that reached for it. One almost suspects the batsmen of having taken instruction, though the Club trusts this is merely a passing aberration and not a change of habit. It falls to your correspondent to report, with as much good grace as can be mustered, that the ducks have gone to ground. Two matches played, and not one egg laid. The exclusive zero club, so accustomed to welcoming new and returning members most weekends, must this week close its doors for want of custom. Consistency, it seems, took the week off along with the ducks. We are assured this dry spell is temporary. The wicket will turn sticky again in due course, a promising young batsman will play across a straight one, and the roll of dishonour shall resume its stately growth. Until then, we record the quiet with the same solemnity we would a triumph, for the art of not scoring a duck is, after all, still a species of cricketing accomplishment. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard, 1951 - J Enfield — 2 innings, 2 ducks, a scarcely believable 100 per cent. A batsman playing a lone and unrelenting hand against fortune. - Gordon Bugge — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67 per cent. Two eggs from three visits to the crease, and a name the bowlers must relish seeing walk out. - E Goodall — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent. A short career thus far, and a naught to show for the whole of it. - Gordon Fenner — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent. Cut from similar cloth to Mr Goodall, and welcome to keep him company. - E Lockyer — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33 per cent. The most restrained of this company, and rather better for it. The Committee extends its compliments to these five gentlemen, who between them have kept the season's honours board from gathering dust while the rest of the eleven behaved themselves. We trust the coming fixture will furnish fresh candidates for the register, and members are respectfully reminded that a straight bat is no guarantee against a wandering one. Until the next match, the Club remains, as ever, at the batsman's peril.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 19th and 20th May, 1951

1 duck
Week 4 · 19 May 1951 – 20 May 1951
A gentle week, this, for the connoisseurs of the duck's egg. Two fixtures were played between the 19th and the 20th, and for once the bowlers of the district found the Club's collectors uncommonly hard to catch out. Only one nought was recorded in the whole of the period, and it fell, as these things generally do, to a man already well acquainted with the pavilion steps. The First Eleven On the Saturday, against Aylesford Paper Mills CC, Mr Gordon Bugge came to the crease at number five and departed run out, the identity of the fielder responsible left to the scorer's honest shrug of "Unsure." It was a plucky sort of dismissal, if a fruitless one, and it stands as his second duck's egg of the summer and the second of a career now twenty-four innings long. That places him seventieth of the six hundred and twelve names on the Club's roll of dishonour, a position he shares, as it happens, with one A S Day, who between 1944 and 1949 contrived to collect his own pair of noughts in a mere eleven innings. The two now sit level upon the tally of shame, kindred spirits separated by the better part of a decade but united in the art of not scoring. A quiet week all told. One duck's egg laid across two matches is a modest harvest by the Club's usual standards, and whether it speaks of improving technique at the crease or merely indifferent bowling elsewhere, the Committee is not minded to say. The tail, such as it was, wagged undisturbed. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - J Enfield — 2 innings, 2 ducks (100%) - Gordon Bugge — 3 innings, 2 ducks (66.67%) - E Goodall — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) - Gordon Fenner — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) - E Lockyer — 3 innings, 1 duck (33.33%) Mr Enfield continues to lead the field with a consistency of a very particular kind, and the Committee has every confidence the coming fixtures will furnish fresh candidates for the honours board. Members are cordially invited to the next match, where a sticky wicket, a rash stroke, or simple bad luck may yet add another name to the list.

The LPCC Duck Gazette — 12th to 14th May, 1951

8 ducks
Week 3 · 12 May 1951 – 14 May 1951
Eight batsmen surrendered their wicket for nought across three days of cricket, four at Bearsted and four more at Marden — proof once again that the eleven's lower order finds the art of not scoring comes rather more naturally than the art of scoring. 1st XI Bearsted CC, 12th May (away) - Gordon Bugge (6) fell to the bowling of B- Elswood — his 1st duck of the season, from a career of 23 innings, 168th of 612 on the Club roll. On this very day in 1906, one D H Luck also made a duck, against Town Malling CC — the calendar has a long memory for these things. - Bob Arnold (7) was stumped off the same bowler for his 3rd career duck from just 8 innings, a rate that has earned him a place among Ducks in a Row (four consecutive), Only Two Quacks with Alan Wilkes, and Quacking Together with John Thirkell. He too shares D H Luck's 1906 anniversary. - J Enfield (9), bowled by R- Spencer, notched his 2nd duck of the season already, from a career of a mere 3 innings — 76th of 612. - H Newport (11), also to R- Spencer, brought up his 2nd career duck from 9 innings, 71st of 612 — a long-standing member of the Retirement Duck honours from some past farewell. Marden, 14th May (home) - E Goodall (7), bowled by D- Heasman, marked his very first innings for the Club with a duck — a genuine Debutante Duck, and for 1951 a founding member of One and Done, joining - Gaskin of 1949 on a single career duck apiece. 142nd of 612. - Gordon Fenner (8), also to D- Heasman, brought up his 6th career duck from 49 innings — 11th of 612, level with D Sells, 1943's Duck of the Year. A family trade too, his brother Joe Fenner carrying five career ducks of his own. - Arthur Cradduck (9), bowled by S- Gurr, his 2nd career duck from 10 innings — fitting for a man already leading this season's Duck of the Year table. Level with A S Day on career tally. - E Lockyer (10), also to S- Gurr, his 3rd career duck from 12 innings, 42nd of 612 — level with A Kent, 1893's Duck of the Year. Three matches, eight ducks, and the bowling of S- Gurr and D- Heasman each claiming a brace at Marden alone. The lower order's resistance, such as it was, lasted rather longer at the crease than it did in the scorebook. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - J Enfield — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - E Goodall — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Gordon Fenner — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Gordon Bugge — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - Arthur Cradduck — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33% The season is young yet, and the Club's honours board never wants for candidates. All members are cordially invited to next week's fixture, where the eleven will no doubt add fresh names to this most exclusive of registers.

The Duck Club Gazette — 5th to 6th May, 1951

1 duck
Week 2 · 5 May 1951 – 6 May 1951
A quiet couple of days in the field, but the zero club is never wholly idle, and this week it welcomes one more name to the roll of honour. 1st XI J Enfield strode out at number six against West Farleigh CC on the 5th of May and was undone by George Reffell's bowling, clean bowled without troubling the scorers — though not, mercifully, first ball, so no golden ignominy to report here, merely the ordinary sort. This stands as his first season's duck and the second duck of a career now numbering two innings, placing him 177th of 611 in the club's long and honourable ledger of failure. He joins a considerable and eclectic fellowship on exactly one career duck apiece — from the venerable A Barker, who first achieved the feat between 1885 and 1904, down to the present-day Arthur Cradduck, still active and himself the reigning Duck of the Year for 1951. Fine company for a man just beginning to make his mark on the honours board of the unmarked. The Week in Brief Two fixtures played, and for all the eleven's application at the crease, only the solitary duck to show for it — a week in which the wicket, evidently, favoured application over abandon. West Farleigh CC can claim the credit, George Reffell the wicket, and the Duck Club a single, dignified new entry. No pairs, no family affairs, no golden ducks to speak of this time round — the eggs, it seems, proved harder to lay than usual. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - J Enfield — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A perfect record of imperfection so far this season, and nobody yet to challenge him for it. The table awaits fresh contenders, and with the season young there is ample opportunity yet for others to test their technique against the bowler's guile and their own concentration. The eleven takes the field again shortly, and the Duck Club, ever watchful from the boundary's edge, confidently expects further additions to its distinguished and dubious roster before long.

The Duck Club Gazette — 29th April, 1951

0 ducks
Week 1 · 29 Apr 1951
A quiet week to report, and for once the quiet is not our custom subject. One fixture was played in the period under review, and — remarkable as it may seem to the seasoned student of ignominy — not a single member of either eleven contrived to depart for a duck's egg. Every batsman who walked to the crease this week troubled the scorers, however modestly, before his eventual return to the pavilion. The exclusive zero club, so rarely short of new applicants, finds its books unopened this Sunday. Whether this reflects a sudden and alarming outbreak of competence, or merely a sticky wicket that favoured caution over adventure, your correspondent cannot say. We prefer to think of it as the calm before the storm — for a season is young yet on the 29th of April, and history teaches that the ducks are never far from home. The Committee views the development with polite suspicion and awaits next week's card with its usual keen appetite. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard The 1951 table stands empty at the time of writing — no innings yet posted to nought, no name yet entered upon the honours board for the current campaign. A blank page, gentlemen, and a challenge to us all. The season is but a single match old; there is time enough, and eleven need not fear for long. So to the players of Linton Park we say: enjoy the reprieve while it lasts, for the Duck Club's memory is long and its standards forgiving of nothing. The next fixture will surely furnish fresh material for these pages, and we shall be watching every ball with the keenest and least charitable of interest. Until then — play straight, and mind the honours board does not miss you for long.

1950 Season 11 reports

The Duck Club Gazette — the week ending 2nd September, 1950

2 ducks
Week 19 · 2 Sep 1950
A single fixture, a single afternoon at home to Bowaters CC, and yet the 1st XI's eleven found room enough for two duck's eggs to be laid before the same bowler. John Ibbotson, it seems, had their measure entirely. Let the record show it. 1st XI Brian Relf, promoted to first wicket down, was undone by John Ibbotson and sent back to the pavilion without score on what was, by the book, his very first innings for the club. A debut of the purest kind — he joins the Debutante Duck club on the strength of it, and all-time sits a respectable 117th of 610 in the club's long ledger of noughts. He is already down, too, as a paid-up member of the Quack-to-Quack fraternity and the Retirement Duck honours, though we trust those are honours earned in some earlier innings of the club's history and not a hint that we shan't see him again — Sunday next will tell. He shares, besides, a "Quacking Together" entry with Terry Whittaker from some previous rendezvous with nought. Curiously, this very day in 1945 saw D Clark similarly recalled to the pavilion without troubling the scorers against 1st Innings MCPC — five years apart, but evidently kindred spirits in the art of not scoring. Bert Buckoke followed at number eight, likewise accounting for John Ibbotson's figures, and made rather a habit of it — his third duck of the season and his tenth in a career now spanning forty-one innings. Third of all 610 in the club's history is no small distinction, and a man who already carries the Duck of the Year honour from 1928 must fancy his chances of adding the 1950 crown to the mantelpiece before the summer is out. As with his colleague, this same date in 1945 found D Clark similarly dismissed for nought against 1st Innings MCPC — the calendar, it seems, has long memory for these things. A modest week, all told: one match, two ducks, one common executioner in Mr Ibbotson, and the tail — such as it was at eight and three — offering little resistance either side of it. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. Bert Buckoke — 4 innings, 3 ducks, 75.0% 2. E Lockyer — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.3% 3. Joe Fenner — 9 innings, 2 ducks, 22.2% 4. John --'s Taylor — 11 innings, 2 ducks, 18.2% 5. - Hooper — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% The season's honours board continues to reshuffle itself most satisfyingly. Members are warmly invited to the next fixture, where further plucky knocks, sticky wickets and the occasional duck's egg may confidently be expected.

Week 10 · 1 Jul 1950
A record of the eleven's grander failures — 1st July, 1950 The ducks kept remarkably shy counsel this week, venturing out but the once, in a home fixture against Bearsted CC — yet what the week wanted in quantity it made up for in the quality of its victim, a name well known to the Committee. 1st XI Batting at eleven, where duty is expected rather more than runs, Bert Buckoke was bowled by Vic Pound for a duck's egg — his second such offering of the summer, and the ninth of a career now nine and thirty innings deep, good enough, or bad enough, for fifth place among all who have ever walked this particular road home, six hundred and seven strong. The Committee notes with some satisfaction that Mr Buckoke is already a two time laureate of the Duck of the Year, crowned in 1928 and, the ink scarcely dry, again in 1950 - a season not yet out and already spoken for. Curiously, on this very first of July back in 1903, one George Champion also strolled back for nought, against Yalding CC of all sides - a coincidence of the calendar the exclusive zero club treasures rather more than the players concerned ever did. The Week in Brief One match, one duck, one gentleman doing the honours for the second time this season already - a quiet week for the tally keeper, though Mr Buckoke shews no sign of relinquishing his grip on the summer's wooden spoon. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette

2 ducks
Week 9 · 24 Jun 1950 – 25 Jun 1950
A Chronicle of the Nought — for the week of the 24th to 25th June, 1950 Two matches, two ducks: a modest catch for the Club's watchful eye, but the register of dubious distinction never turns away a subscription however small, and grows steadier for it week upon week. The First Eleven Saturday, at home to Tovil, and Arthur Cradduck came to the crease at number six only to be run out before he had troubled the scorer, the confusion at the striker's end being a matter for the fielding side's conscience rather than his own. It is his first duck of the season, and the first of a career now five innings old — he takes his place 112th of the 607 gentlemen who have gone before him into this exclusive company, and joins - Gaskin, whose own single career nought (from one solitary innings back in 1949) sits him at exactly the same tally. A fine beginning to a collection, Cradduck, and may it grow no further this season. Sunday brought the Desert Rats to Linton Park, and Don Hartridge, holding the same number six berth, was given out leg before to the bowling of W Hall. A first duck of this season for him, though scarcely his first acquaintance with the Club — his fifth career nought from thirty-nine innings sees him installed 14th of all 607 on the all-time roll, a lofty and rather melancholy perch. He draws level on five career ducks with Allan Peach, who compiled his own quintet of noughts between 1903 and 1907 — good company for a man who evidently prefers his straight bat kept for other occasions. The Week in Summary A quiet week by the Club's usual bustling standards: two matches, two ducks, no pairs and no family gatherings to report. The rest of the eleven, it would seem, kept their straight bats about them and left only Cradduck and Hartridge to carry the Club's colours. Consistency, as ever, comes in a great many forms, and not all of them are welcome at the crease. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - E Lockyer — 4 innings, 2 ducks (50.0%) - Joe Fenner — 9 innings, 2 ducks (22.2%) - Hooper — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) - B Lloyd — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) - Bert Buckoke — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) The season's leading lights of the art of not scoring remain in fine and dismal form, and the Club awaits with quiet confidence the additions the next fixture will surely bring. Members are cordially invited to attend, bat in hand, and to trust that the eleven's luck at the crease will hold rather firmer than it has these past two days.

The Duck Gazette — Linton Park, 18th June 1950

1 duck
Week 8 · 18 Jun 1950
Only one soul answered the call of the zero club this week, but a lone duck flaps just as proudly as a flock, and the honours board takes note regardless of numbers. 1st XI, at home to Hambros Bank In strode Joe Fenner at first wicket down, and out he went again lbw to the bowling of F Chapman, without so much as a run to his name. It is his second duck of a summer already turning quackish, and the fifth of a career now thirty-three innings deep — enough to see him settle at 17th of 607 in the club's whole solemn history of the dismissed-for-nought. A Fenner trait, this: his brother Gordon sits on an identical five career ducks, so whatever it is that lands a Fenner back in the pavilion without scoring, it does appear to run in the blood. And by a pleasant quirk of the calendar, on this very day in 1949 John Thirkell was performing precisely the same trick against Bowaters CC — a small fraternity of the nought, scattered across the years but united in feeling. The week in brief One match, one duck, one Fenner walking back with his straight bat unrewarded. A quiet week for the club by its own modest standards, though quiet weeks have a habit of being followed by louder ones. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the week of the 10th to 12th of June, 1950

3 ducks
Week 7 · 10 Jun 1950 – 12 Jun 1950
Three fixtures were contested this week, and though two of them passed with every egg intact, the First Eleven's outing at Lloyds Social Club furnished the exclusive zero club with three fresh entries in a single sorry innings. 1st XI, away to Lloyds Social Club, 10th June Joe Fenner, promoted to first wicket down, was bowled by J. Stevens for a duck's egg — his first of the summer, and the fourth of a career now two-and-thirty innings deep, good enough for 28th place of all 606 names on the club's roll of dishonour. He keeps company with C. Amies, who played between 1867 and 1870 and sits on the very same tally of four, proof that the art of not scoring has never gone out of fashion. Cricketing kinship runs in the family too — his brother Gordon carries five career ducks of his own, so the Fenners are building quite the joint estate in nought. Down at number eight, Bert Buckoke was run out without troubling the scorers — his first duck of the season, and the eighth of an illustrious career, illustrious in this particular currency at any rate, leaving him fifth of all 606 in the club's history. A two-time Duck of the Year, in 1928 and again this very season of 1950, Buckoke wears his ignominy like a badge of office. George Champion, who turned out between 1886 and 1912 and gathered his own eight ducks across seventy-four innings, keeps him honest company on the same career total. At number ten, E. Lockyer departed caught by S. Jarrett off the bowling of J. Ibbotson — his second duck of the season, and remarkably his second career duck too, in only five innings played, a rate of failure that ought to have the selectors reaching for the smelling salts. That places him 63rd of all 606, level on career ducks with A. S. Day, who managed the same modest tally between 1944 and 1949 in eleven innings. The week in summary Three matches, three ducks, all laid in the one basket at Lloyds Social Club — the other two fixtures passed off without a single egg to report, which speaks either well of the batting or poorly of the bowling, depending on one's allegiance. A middle-order man, a lower-order man and a tail-ender all present at the same funeral suggests the Lloyds attack had the measure of the innings from top to bottom. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. E. Lockyer — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% 2. — Hooper — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 3. B. Lloyd — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 4. Bert Buckoke — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 5. Bob Arnold — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A perfect quintet of centurions at the foot of the table, though not the sort of century any of them will be framing for the clubhouse wall. The next fixture awaits, and with it, no doubt, fresh candidates queuing patiently for the pavilion steps. Week 4 · 20 May 1950 – 21 May 1950
A lean week for the connoisseurs of nought, two fixtures played and but a single egg laid between them. Still, quality over quantity, as any true student of the art of not scoring will tell you. The First Eleven Mr John Thirkell, at four in the order and away from home against Charles Arkcoll's eleven, was undone in the accustomed fashion — caught Humphrey Morris, bowled Stan Wratten — and trudged back to the pavilion to add his name to the season's roll of honour. It is his first duck's egg of the 1950 season, and the third of a career now twenty-four innings long, which plants him a solid 44th of 602 in the club's all-time list of dubious distinction. A long-serving member of several standing companies besides — the Ducks on the Road top ten, the Homebody Duck top ten, and the Lone Duck top ten among them — Mr Thirkell has twice before shared the ignominy in company, once with Mr Bob Arnold and once with Mr William Buck, though neither companion troubled the scorers alongside him on this occasion. He joins, on exactly three career ducks apiece, the name of A Kent, who managed the same tally for the 1893 eleven and was crowned that year's Duck of the Year for his trouble — kindred spirits fifty-seven years apart, bound by the same modest total. In Summary One duck, two matches, and precious little else to report — the ducks, it seems, mostly evaded the net this week. A quiet round for the club's least-wanted trophy, but the season is young yet. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - D Simmons — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - John Thirkell — 5 innings, 1 duck, 20% The eleven takes the field again presently, and the Duck Club's scouts will be watching every departing batsman with their usual keen and faintly ghoulish interest. Should the tail wag or a fresh name walk the plank, you may be sure it will be recorded here in due course. --- Separately, and only in passing: another machine on the team (turbosammy-Defiance-Pro-16) is well behind on skills sync and flagging unresolved problems — worth a nudge to whoever owns it to start a session so it pulls automatically, nothing needed from you here.

THE LPCC DUCK CLUB GAZETTE — 13th to 14th May, 1950

1 duck
Week 3 · 13 May 1950 – 14 May 1950
A quiet week upon the whole, with only two fixtures played and but a single name added to the register — though a solitary duck, dear reader, is no less an occasion for ceremony than a dozen. 1st XI At Bearsted, on the 13th, D Simmons strode to the crease at number seven and departed for nought, run out by a fielder whose identity the scorebook, in its wisdom, declined to record — "Unsure" being, on reflection, rather a fitting epitaph for the whole sorry business. This is the first duck's egg of the season for Simmons, and the second of a career now standing at six innings — a rate of failure that places him a very respectable 59th of 601 in the club's long and honourable roll of the dismissed. Not yet a name for the honours boards, but a promising apprenticeship in the art of not scoring is plainly under way. Curiously, on this very day in 1940 — a full decade before Simmons's own contribution — B Westover likewise trudged back for nought, against the George Fenner XI, one of nine such innings that yet sees Westover installed in fourth place of all time. The zero club, it seems, keeps its calendar as faithfully as its ledger. The Week in Summary One duck from two matches is a slim harvest by the Club's usual generous standards — the eleven, on the whole, appear to have played rather too straight a bat this week for our purposes. Still, where Bearsted is concerned, Simmons alone flew the flag for failure, and flew it with a certain understated dignity. No pairs, no families of ducks, no golden eggs to report — merely one plucky, if fruitless, contribution to the great tradition. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - D Simmons — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A leaderboard of one is, admittedly, an easy table to top, and Simmons finds himself there by simple virtue of being the only contender who troubled the scorers this week — in the wrong direction. Whether he can be caught, or indeed whether he shall wish to be, remains a question for the fixtures ahead. The season is young yet, and the wicket at the far end has a way of producing further candidates. Members are warmly encouraged to keep their bats straight — or, in the finer traditions of this Club, resolutely otherwise — for the next match promises the eleven every opportunity to add to this modest register.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — Tuesday, the 29th of April, 1950

0 ducks
Week 1 · 29 Apr 1950
A quiet week to report, and for once the quiet is the story. The eleven took the field on Saturday last, and by close of play not a single member of the batting order had contrived to depart for nought. A clean sheet. A whitewash of the wrong sort, from the Duck Club's point of view. We confess to a certain flatness in the clubhouse at this news. The exclusive zero club thrives on adversity nobly borne, and this week adversity simply declined to show up. Bats were played straight, singles were taken where ducks might once have been laid, and the tail — usually so reliable a source of comedy — wagged its way to respectable scores instead of the pavilion steps. One rather suspects the wicket was too kind for its own good. Still, the committee takes the long view. A team cannot manufacture failure to order, however much tradition might wish it, and a season is a long business with many a sticky wicket yet to come. The ducks have merely gone to ground this week, not retired from the field altogether, and past form suggests they will be back among us directly. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard Nothing yet to report here either — the season's honours board stands empty of any fresh entries, awaiting its first candidate for 1950. A blank ledger is a rare sight in these parts, and we shall watch with interest to see whose name is first to grace it. We look ahead, then, to the next fixture with the club's usual mixture of hope and mild anticipation of disaster. Someone, somewhere, is surely due a duck's egg before the season is very much older — and when he finds it, this gazette shall be first to mark the occasion with the ceremony it deserves. Until then, the members of the Duck Club remain, as ever, in cheerful reserve.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — the week ending Saturday, 28th August 1948

1 duck
Week 16 · 28 Aug 1948
A quiet week for the exclusive zero club, but a quiet week is not the same as an empty one, and the Duck Club is nothing if not attentive to detail. One duck's egg was laid at Bowaters CC, and it deserves its column inch. 1st XI Batting at number ten against Bowaters CC, L- Young was bowled by Roy Melhuish for a duck — his very first innings in senior colours, and thus a maiden knock in the truest and most unwelcome sense of the word. There is no shame in it. Every distinguished career on the honours board began somewhere, and Young's now begins here, at nought, in good and populous company — he takes up residence at 176th of 577 in the club's all-time list, with the whole of that table stretching invitingly above him. History, as it happens, keeps its own calendar: on this very day in 1893, one W W Tarrance likewise trudged back to the pavilion without troubling the scorers, also against The Mote CC — a coincidence separated by fifty-five years but united, as ever, by the art of not scoring. The Week in Summary One match, one duck, and a debut of the least celebrated kind. Young joins the roll of honour on his very first afternoon, which at Linton Park counts as a baptism of a particular sort — the eleven will no doubt remind him of it kindly, and often, for some seasons to come. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard Four names stand level atop this season's reckoning, each having faced but one innings and returned but one duck — a clean sweep of misfortune all round: - Sessions — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - C Newman — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - L- Young — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Richard Harris — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A sticky wicket for all four, and the season yet young enough for any one of them to break clear — or, in the fine tradition of this club, to be joined by rather more company before the covers go on for winter. Until Next Time The eleven takes the field again before long, and the Duck Club's ledger, as always, stands open and ready. Whether the next entry is a golden duck, a pair, or merely one more honest failure with the bat, this correspondent will be watching the scorebook with the keenest interest cricket has to offer.

The LPCC Duck Gazette — Sunday, the 25th of July, 1948

2 ducks
Week 11 · 25 Jul 1948
A quiet Sunday at Linton Park, and yet the eleven found room, as ever, for two additions to the club's most curious ledger. West Farleigh CC provided the opposition, and Kent hospitality, it must be said, extended rather too generously toward wickets taken. The 1st XI Mr Richard Harris, sent in at number six, played what one hopes was a straight enough bat before being taken by Harry Webb off the bowling of George Reffell. Not a first-ball departure, this — he troubled the crease a while before troubling nobody's figures — but a duck's egg all the same, his first of the season and the third of a career now numbering nine innings, which places him a respectable forty-fifth of the five hundred and seventy-six gentlemen who have ever walked back for nought at this ground. Curiously, this very date in 1925 saw a Mr W Turner similarly dismissed for a duck, against Bearsted CC of all sides — history, it seems, is fond of its small rhymes. Then came Mr C Newman, in at number ten, bowled by G Page without troubling the scorebook at all. A maiden appearance for the club, and what a maiden appearance — his very first innings yielding his very first duck, which is either the unluckiest or the most efficient way to begin a cricketing career, depending on one's temperament. He is welcomed forthwith into the club's roll of honour, sitting joint one hundred and eleventh of five hundred and seventy-six on debut alone. He keeps notable company on the calendar too: this same 25th of July, back in 1925, one W Turner also strolled back for nought against Bearsted CC, a full twenty-three summers before Mr Newman's own introduction to the art of not scoring. The Week in Brief One match, two ducks, both from the home eleven's middle and late order against West Farleigh — a modest bag by the club's standards, but every egg counts toward the season's basket, and a debutant duck is always worth a raised eyebrow in the pavilion. The Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Sessions — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - C Newman — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Richard Harris — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A tightly-fought summit this season, with the field level at a perfect record of failure. Whether any of the three can be dislodged from their unwanted throne remains to be seen. Until the next fixture, when the bowlers of the district will no doubt continue their quiet work of populating this register further — the eleven takes the field again, and the Duck Club watches on, ever hopeful of new members.

The Duck Gazette — Saturday, 15th May, 1948

1 duck
Week 1 · 15 May 1948
A single entry finds its way into the book this week, but a rare and memorable one for all that — a maiden appearance settled in the most economical fashion imaginable. 1st XI Away from home comforts and into the record books went Sessions, sent in first wicket down against Herne Bay CC and undone by the bowling of Gv Gethin before he could trouble the scorebook. A plucky attempt at a straight bat, no doubt, but the wicket proved sticky enough to see him back to the pavilion without a run to his name. What makes the occasion noteworthy is that this was no seasoned campaigner's misfortune but his very first innings for the club — a debut duck, and there can be few less auspicious ways to begin a cricketing career, nor few more splendid ways to begin a duck-hunting one. He enters the exclusive zero club at the first time of asking, his maiden knock now his maiden nought, career figures reading one innings, one duck, and a seat at number 87 of 571 on the all-time roll of honour. Early in the season it may be, but for now Sessions stands quite alone atop the ledger for Duck of the Year 1948 — a lead he holds only by virtue of being first through the gate, and one the rest of the eleven will no doubt be keen to contest before the summer is out. A pleasant curiosity of the calendar attends the occasion: on this very day in 1943, Gordon Fenner — who between 1941 and 1947 assembled four such noughts of his own, good enough for 24th of 571 on the all-time list — likewise made his way back to the pavilion without scoring, against Maidstone Fire Service. Certain dates, it would seem, carry a duck-shaped destiny all their own. The Week in Summary One match, one duck — a quiet week by the Club's usual standards, but quality over quantity has always been the Duck Club's watchword, and a debutant's egg is worth more column space than a dozen ordinary noughts from the regulars. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Sessions — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% The book stands open and the ink is barely dry. Members are warmly reminded that the next fixture offers every opportunity for further additions to this most select of registers — may the bowling be hostile and the concentration lapse where it matters most.

1947 Season 3 reports

🦆 The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 13th July, 1947 🦆

0 ducks
Week 6 · 13 Jul 1947
A Quiet Week in the Exclusive Zero Club Well now. The scorers may set down their pencils and the eleven may take a well-earned rest, for on this occasion the duck evaded every trap laid for it. Not a single member of the eleven troubled the honours board this week — a straight bat was played throughout, or else fortune simply looked the other way. The Club regrets to report that there is, this week, nothing whatsoever to report. One match was played in the period, and not a solitary nought was recorded from it. Whether this speaks well of the eleven's application at the crease, or merely of a wicket too placid to trouble anybody, the Committee declines to speculate. The art of not scoring, it seems, took the week off. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard Though the week itself yielded no fresh candidates, the season's roll of dubious honour stands as follows: - 🥇 Derek Pantony — 1 innings, 1 duck, a sobering 100.0% - 🏏 G Vince — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% Derek Pantony's solitary innings this season reads as a masterclass in brevity, while G Vince continues to flirt with the zero club at an even-money rate — the Committee watches both gentlemen with interest, and no small measure of sympathy. So there it is, members — a rare week of peace for the Duck Club's chroniclers, and doubtless all the more galling for it, since a quiet week merely postpones rather than cancels the inevitable. The eleven return to the field next fixture, and history suggests the zero club will not want for new members for very much longer. Until then, keep your bats straight and your eye on the ball — the ducks, we assure you, are merely biding their time.

The Duck Club Gazette

2 ducks
Week 2 · 15 Jun 1947
A Chronicle of the Nought — 15th June 1947 Fair skies over the ground on Sunday last, and the Eleven at home to Expense Accounts — a fixture that, on this evidence, gave rather more to the visitors' bowlers than to our own batting card. Two names go to the book this week, and the book, as ever, welcomes them with open arms. 1st XI - G Vince, in at eight, fell b Unsure — a bowler whose Christian name the scorer evidently despaired of, though his work needed no introduction. It is Vince's first duck's egg of the summer and the fourth entry of a modest career, taking him to 144th of 565 in the club's long and dishonourable roll. Curiously, on this very day in 1887, one Jack Fryer — second on that same roll with a dozen ducks to his name, and twice crowned Duck of the Year — also trudged back for nought, against 1st Innings East Peckham CC. Sixty years apart, the same calendar page, the same walk to the pavilion. - Derek Pantony, last man in at eleven, marked his very first appearance in a Club shirt with the most economical innings the game allows — out without troubling the scorer, on debut. A cruel welcome, but a distinguished one: this nought stakes an early and emphatic claim on the Duck of the Year 1947 honour, the season being but young and Pantony already first past the post. Like Vince, he finds himself keeping curious company with Jack Fryer of 1887 — proof, if any were needed, that the art of not scoring is no respecter of decades. The Week in Brief One match, one defeat of the scoreboard's ambitions, two ducks laid — both, fittingly, at the tail of the innings, numbers eight and eleven proving there is honour yet in going quietly. A modest sample this week, but every roll of honour begins somewhere, and young Pantony has begun his in memorable style. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Derek Pantony — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - G Vince — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% Level at the top of the table, then, though it must be said the bar for entry is not a high one. The season stands open, the wickets stand ready, and the Club looks forward with its customary mixture of dread and delight to whichever gentlemen the next fixture sees fit to induct. Until then, the eleven play on — straight bats where possible, sticky wickets where not.

The Duck Club Gazette — for the week of the 8th of June, 1947

0 ducks
Week 1 · 8 Jun 1947
A single fixture took the field this week, and — remarkable as it may seem to the connoisseur of the duck's egg — not one batsman among either eleven contrived to be dismissed for nought. The bowlers, for all their guile, went home with their appeals unanswered on this particular front, and the exclusive zero club must report, with no small disappointment, that its books remain unopened for the period. It is not for want of trying, one assumes. Every innings carries its share of jittery starts and playing-and-missing, yet on this occasion the tail wagged, the middle order held firm, and even the customary nervous newcomer seems to have got off the mark. A sticky wicket, evidently, was navigated by all with rather more application than the club prefers. We shall not pretend to be anything but a little put out. The pursuit of the duck's egg is, after all, the purest sport this club knows, and a blank week denies us both ceremony and comedy alike. Still, patience is a virtue long practised on the boundary's edge, and the season is young yet. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season's roll of dishonour has, as yet, no entries to publish. The honours board stands polished and waiting, its columns empty of both name and number — a state of affairs the committee trusts will not long persist. Members are reminded that the game continues, and with it the ever-present hazard of the first ball, the leaving stroke gone astray, and the confident forward defensive that meets rather more swing than bargained for. The next fixture will surely furnish the club with fresh material, and your correspondent awaits it with quiet and entirely unsporting optimism.

The Duck Club Gazette — the week of 20th July, 1946

5 ducks
Week 9 · 20 Jul 1946
A chastening afternoon at Gore Court, where the 1st XI's card was inked no fewer than five times with the duck's egg, and the home attack took what can only be called a proprietary interest in the business. 1st XI, away to Gore Court CC Bert Pierce, in at four, played on to Brian French — his first duck of the season and the second of an eleven-innings career, good enough for 53rd of the 559 names on the all-time roll. Pierce carries the Retirement Duck honour on his card, a distinction we trust describes some distant future rather than this one. On this very day in 1906, a certain R W Mitchell suffered likewise against the Royal West Kent Regiment's Officers XI — kindred spirits forty years apart. Frank Sutton, at six, was leg-before to Jack Whibley Jnr for his second duck of the season and a formidable fourteenth of his career, a mark that stands him alone atop the all-time table, first of all 559. A twice-crowned Duck of the Year, 1940 and now 1946 besides, Sutton wears his nought with the quiet authority of a man who has made a study of it. Mitchell's 1906 shade walked with him too. Bert Buckoke followed at seven, bowled by the same Whibley, for a fifth career duck and thirteenth of 559 — himself a Duck of the Year, 1928 vintage, and evidently still game for the honour. Mitchell, 1906, once more for company. At eight, N Young opened his innings account, such as it was, with a debut duck — bowled by Whibley for the third time that innings, and straight in at 178th of 559. A first taste of the club's particular hospitality, and, as it happens, on the same calendar date Mitchell once knew in 1906. Stuart Thirkell, in at nine, was bowled by Alec E Allsworth for a debut duck of his own, taking 197th place of 559 — two new members inducted in the one innings, a rare and generous double for the membership secretary. Mitchell's 1906 duck falls on this same date yet again. The week in summary Five ducks from one match is a harvest by any reckoning, and three of them fell to Whibley's bowling alone — the man might fairly be issued honorary membership himself. Two debuts, one duck's-egg apiece, and the eleven's lower order left looking distinctly threadbare by the close. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - Frank Sutton — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67% - Bert Pierce — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - K Vince — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - L Ricketts — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - N Young — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% The season's roll of dishonour stands ready for further entries, and the next fixture will doubtless oblige. Members are warmly invited to attend, bat bravely, and add to the count regardless.

We shall not pretend this is anything but an anticlimax. The committee notes it all the same, in the spirit of honest record-keeping, and looks forward with quiet confidence to sterner tests of technique in the matches ahead. On this very date in 1903, the Reverend W A Carr suffered precisely the same fate against Maidstone — proof, if proof were needed, that the art of not scoring respects no calendar. - Frank Sutton (No. 10), bowled J L Monk. Sutton needs no introduction to readers of this gazette, sitting as he does atop the all-time table — first of 555 — and reigning Duck of the Year both in 1940 and again this very season of 1946. By curious coincidence, on this same day in 1941 one Arthur Ash was despatched for nought against the splendidly named Home Guard's "Bungs Mob" — a fixture one imagines was not conducted with excessive solemnity. - K Vince (No. 11), lbw George W Farmer. A debut innings, and what an inheritance to begin one's career upon — nought, ranking him already 167th of 555 in a club that has been keeping this particular score since the last century. He may take some comfort, or none at all, in knowing that on this exact day in 1940 his own teammate Frank Sutton — the very gentleman dismissed two places above him in this report — first set down the foundations of the record he now so comfortably leads. Vince has a long road, and evidently a willing bowling attack, ahead of him. The week in brief One match, three ducks, and the tail bearing the brunt of it — Nos. 10 and 11 both walking back without so much as a run to their name. A sticky wicket for the lower order, though the eleven will doubtless take the view that these things even themselves out over a season. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - Frank Sutton — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - K Vince — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - L Ricketts — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% Early days yet, and the season's table is level all round — a state of affairs the committee fully expects will not last. Week 7 · 9 Sep 1944 – 10 Sep 1944
A quiet week for the exclusive zero club, the eleven's most enduring and dubious institution, but two gentlemen still found their way back to the pavilion before troubling the scorer. 1st XI Against the George Fenner XI at home on the Sunday, the 1st XI offered up a pair of victims to the same bowler, Mr J Jerman, who evidently found the home dressing room's timber to his liking. - A S Day, at number six, was bowled by J Jerman for a duck's egg — his second of the summer of 1944, and the second entry on a career sheet that now reads two ducks in six visits to the crease, good enough, in this parish, for 47th of 539 on the club's all-time roll of shame. He draws level on career ducks with one Arthur Ash, who plied his own trade between 1934 and 1941 and sits, fittingly, one place below him at 48th — kindred spirits of the straight bat gone wrong. - Two places further down the order, Gordon Fenner followed his teammate back with the identical dismissal, bowled J Jerman, for his first duck of the season and the fourth of a career now standing at thirty innings. That places him a very respectable 23rd of 539 on the all-time table — a position he shares, career-duck for career-duck, with the noted Bert Buckoke of 1928 to 1941, who claimed the Duck of the Year honour in his debut season and now finds Fenner drawing level with him at four apiece. It might be observed, purely as a matter of family interest, that Gordon's own brother Joe carries three ducks of his own upon the club's books — evidently a household not unacquainted with the art of not scoring. The Week in Brief Two matches, two ducks, one bowler doing rather more than his fair share of the damage — Mr Jerman may consider himself an honorary and unpaid officer of this club after such an afternoon's work. No pairs, no king pairs, and no family gatherings at the crease this week, so the honours boards may rest easy a little longer. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season's front-runners in the sport of not troubling the scorers, to date: - a- Gardener — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - W Bunting — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67% - A S Day — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.33% - E- Humphreys — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - D Sells — 4 innings, 1 duck, 25% A- Gardener continues to bat, or rather not bat, with a consistency of a very particular kind, and remains this season's most reliable supplier to the club's coffers. The eleven takes the field again shortly, and the club has every confidence that the batting order will continue its generous patronage of this most singular of honours. Until then, gentlemen — mind the straight ones.

The Duck Club Gazette — 3rd September 1944

2 ducks
Week 6 · 3 Sep 1944
A modest afternoon's harvest against the Home Guard's Royal West Kent 11th Battalion, but the exclusive zero club does not require a bumper crop to hold its ceremony. Two names are inscribed below. 1st XI - Jimmy Jameson, at number six, was bowled by L Wynn and made the long walk back to the pavilion for his season's first duck's egg — the third of a career now running to twenty-three innings, and good enough for 40th place on the club's all-time roll of the dismissed. He joins the venerable A Kent, Duck of the Year as long ago as 1893, on exactly three career ducks apiece — separated by half a century, united by nought. - W Bunting, sent in at nine, offered a catch to the same L Wynn off the bowling of Private Wilson, and departed for his second duck of the summer — his fifth in twenty innings, a tally that plants him 15th on the club's honours board of futility. He draws level on five with Allan Peach, whose own five ducks were compiled between 1903 and 1907, proof that the art of not scoring is no respecter of the calendar. Honourable mention to L Wynn, who had a hand — bowling one man, catching the other — in both misfortunes of the day. A sticky wicket for the home side's middle and lower order alike, though the Home Guard's XI will no doubt call it a straight bat well applied at the other end. Week in summary One match, two ducks, both in the same innings against the same attack, and both, in some fashion, at the mercy of the same fielder. A quiet week by the club's usual standards, but a quiet week is still a week the ducks came home to roost. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. W Bunting — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% 2. a- Gardener — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% 3. E- Humphreys — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% 4. D Sells — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33% 5. 2 ducks
Week 4 · 19 Aug 1944 – 20 Aug 1944
Being a true and faithful record of the weekend of the 19th and 20th of August, 1944 A quiet weekend for the collectors of noughts, but a quiet weekend is never a barren one, and the Eleven's ledger gains two fresh entries this Saturday and Sunday — one near the top of the order, one nearer the tail. 1st XI - Herbert Rayner, Saturday the 19th against R.A. Training Wing Wrotham, batting at four, held safely by McCulloch off the bowling of Emms and sent back to the pavilion without troubling the scorers. A first duck of the season for Rayner, and the fifth of a career now stretching to four and fifty innings, which places him twelfth of the five hundred and thirty-six names the club has ever welcomed into its dubious fellowship. He keeps distinguished company on that mark — one Allan Peach, who turned out for the club between 1903 and 1907, arrived at the identical tally of five in a rather brisker eleven innings. - W Bunting, Sunday the 20th against KCC Maidstone, batting at nine and clean bowled by Benger, done for nought on a wicket that gave him no quarter. A first duck of the campaign and the fourth of a career of nineteen innings, good enough, or ill enough, for twenty-fifth of the five hundred and thirty-six. A pleasing coincidence of the calendar attends him — on this very day in 1892, two and fifty years past, one G Knight likewise trudged home for nought, against Town Malling CC. A modest weekend by the club's usual standards of catastrophe: one duck at four, one at nine, top order and tail alike finding a sticky patch. Two matches played, two eggs laid, no pairs and no family gatherings in the book this time — the honours board must wait for livelier days. Members are reminded that the wicket offers no favours to anyone, batsman or eleven alike, and the club looks forward, as ever, with keen anticipation to the next fixture's fresh contributions to the register.

The Duck's Egg Gazette — 13th August 1944

2 ducks
Week 3 · 13 Aug 1944
A single fixture at home to the National Fire Service Overseas Contingent, and the eleven did not emerge from it unscathed from the gentle art of not scoring. Two of our number were called upon to make the short, familiar walk back to the pavilion. 1st XI D Sells, sent in at number seven, was bowled by Buxton for a duck's egg — his sixth in a career now spanning twelve innings, and the seventh name on the club's all-time roll of 534. Sells is no stranger to this particular parade ground, being a titled holder of Duck of the Year for 1943 and a paid-up member of the rare Ducks in a Row board, four consecutive noughts to his name — a run of misfortune that a lesser man might resent and that Sells appears, by now, to have made rather his own. He stands level on career ducks with F Danells, who compiled his own half-dozen across eighteen innings between 1881 and 1904 — good company for a bad habit, separated by sixty years and united by nought. At number ten came a- Gardener, undone by MacIldowie without troubling the scorers, his second duck of the season and second in a slender five-innings career — a striking rate of failure that places him 83rd on the all-time list, though with 1944 barely half run he must already be reckoned a serious contender for this year's Duck of the Year. He draws level on career ducks with Arthur Ash, who managed the same modest tally in fourteen innings between 1934 and 1941. In summary A single match, a single innings apiece for the unfortunate two, and two entries duly logged in the book of dubious distinction. The middle order held reasonably firm; it was the tail, once again, that wagged its way straight back to the pavilion. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - a- Gardener — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - E- Humphreys — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - A S Day — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - D Sells — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The eleven take the field again before the week is out, and the Duck Club's scorers stand ready with pencils sharpened for whatever fresh triumphs of adversity may follow. Members are warmly invited to add their names to the list — the exclusive zero club welcomes all comers, provided they arrive with nothing to show for it.

The Duck Report — 2nd August 1944

3 ducks
Week 1 · 2 Aug 1944
A modest gathering this week, but the 1st Eleven contrived three fresh entries to the Zero Club against the National Fire Service Overseas Contingent, and the honours board has taken due note. 1st XI Opening the innings and, alas, opening the book of misfortune too, E- Humphreys was bowled by MacIldowie without troubling the scorer — a duck's egg to lead off proceedings. It is his 1st duck of the season and the 122nd of 532 in the club's long and distinguished record of failure, drawn from a career of seventeen innings that has evidently seen sunnier afternoons. Curiously, this very date in 1882 saw no fewer than four different gentlemen fall to a duck against 1st Innings Boxley CC — Humphreys keeps company across the decades with W H Fryer, whose own six ducks earned him ninth place in the all-time table. At number six, A S Day marked his first appearance for the club in the manner the club best appreciates — with a duck on debut. Bowled by the same relentless MacIldowie, he becomes the 95th name of 532 upon the roll, and joins the exclusive company of A S Smith, who once claimed the Duck of the Year honour in 1934 on precisely the same tally of one. A gentle welcome to the fold, Mr Day — the eleven salutes a foundation stone well and truly laid. Down at number ten, a- Gardener was caught by S- Scott off the bowling of S- Hill, adding his own modest contribution to the afternoon's proceedings. This is his 1st duck of the season, his 1st in a career of four innings, and sits him at 215th of 532 all time — though he may take some quiet pride in already holding the Duck of the Year 1944 board, a standing honour for a season not yet concluded. Like his fellow duckers, he finds himself keeping historical company with the Boxley CC quartet of 1882. The Week in Summary Three ducks from a single fixture, all falling to the Fire Service bowlers, and all from the home eleven — a sticky wicket indeed against the Overseas Contingent. No pairs, no families of ducks, and mercifully no king pairs this week, though with A S Day's arrival the club's rolls grow ever longer. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - A S Day — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% - E- Humphreys — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% - a- Gardener — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% A tight field at the top this season, gentlemen, with the entire leaderboard playing a perfect if unwanted average. The eleven takes the field again shortly, and the Duck Club awaits its next candidates with the patience of a mid-off. Until then — mind your straight bat, and beware the sticky wicket.

1943 Season 15 reports

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette

0 ducks
Week 17 · 5 Sep 1943
A Chronicle of the Nought — 5th September, 1943 A single fixture was played this week, and — remarkable to relate — not one soul among either eleven was persuaded back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer. The zero club, so often busy with new subscriptions, finds its ledger unchanged this week. Whether this speaks of straight bats generally applied, or merely of the bowling having an off day, the Gazette shall not speculate. The art of not scoring, it seems, was set aside in favour of the plainer art of scoring something. We shall not pretend to mourn overlong. A quiet week for the duck's egg is no bad thing, and the exclusive zero club can certainly bear one Saturday's want of new members. Let it be recorded, for the curious, that the ducks were abroad somewhere in Kent that afternoon, merely not at Linton Park. The season's roll of dubious honour, however, stands undisturbed and worth admiring all the same: Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard — 1943 - D Sells — 10 innings, 5 ducks, 50.0% - B Westover — 12 innings, 5 ducks, 41.67% - Herbert Sunley — 14 innings, 5 ducks, 35.71% - Frank Sutton — 20 innings, 5 ducks, 25.0% - W Bunting — 14 innings, 3 ducks, 21.43% D Sells leads the field by the finest of margins, sitting at an even half of his innings surrendered for nought — a consistency of a very particular kind, and one the rest of the eleven might privately envy even as they publicly commiserate. Herbert Sunley and Frank Sutton continue their steady, patient accumulation of noughts across a long season, proof that the duck's egg is a dish best served often. W Bunting brings up the rear of this select company, though with the season yet to run its course there is time enough for him to close the gap, should fortune or the bowling favour him. The Gazette must record, too, that a quiet week is rarely a lasting one. History and the LPCC batting order both suggest the ducks are merely gathering themselves for the next appointment. Members are warmly invited to attend the following fixture, where the zero club will no doubt be pleased to welcome fresh candidates to its ranks, and where the eleven's tail — as ever — stands ready to wag or to fold as the wicket dictates.

The Duck Club Gazette — the week of 28th August, 1943

2 ducks
Week 16 · 28 Aug 1943
A modest week for the eleven, but the exclusive zero club welcomed two new entries all the same, both falling to the same tormentor with the ball. 1st XI Against the Home Guard's Royal West Kent 11th Battalion, B Westover, sent in at eight, was taken by X Chambers off the bowling of X Graves for a duck's egg. It is his fifth of the season and the ninth of a career now twenty-seven innings long — a record that sees him sit fourth of all 528 names ever to have graced this dubious honours board, a position most men would sooner not hold but which he occupies with a certain grim distinction. Curiously, on this very day in 1893, one W W Tarrance strolled back to the pavilion in identical fashion against The Mote CC — the calendar, it seems, has long had a fondness for late August. One place down the order, C- Pierce followed him back, caught by Private Wilson off the same relentless X Graves — who may fairly claim the day's honours with both wickets. It is Pierce's first duck in only three innings for the club, and though his name is a newer one on the board, he is not to be mistaken for a debutant; he simply joins the great unscoring tradition rather later than some. He too shares his fate with history: the same W W Tarrance, back in 1893 against The Mote CC, once made exactly this same walk on the very same date. Week in summary One match, two ducks, and both surrendered to the same bowler — a plucky performance with the ball that the batting could not answer in kind. The tail, on this occasion, did not so much wag as fall quietly still. A sticky wicket for the eleven's lower order, and a fine reminder that the art of not scoring remains alive and well even against wartime opposition. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard 1. D Sells — 10 innings, 5 ducks, 50.00% 2. B Westover — 12 innings, 5 ducks, 41.67% 3. Herbert Sunley — 14 innings, 5 ducks, 35.71% 4. Frank Sutton — 20 innings, 5 ducks, 25.00% 5. W Bunting — 14 innings, 3 ducks, 21.43% D Sells continues to lead this season's field with a consistency of a very particular kind, and B Westover presses close behind after this week's addition. The season is far from finished, and with X Graves evidently in such fine form, further candidates for the zero club may well present themselves before the eleven next takes the field. All members are warmly invited to attend the next fixture and, should fortune desire it, to add their own name to the register.

A quiet week for the exclusive zero club, and no mistake. Whether this reflects a sudden outbreak of straight bats and sound judgement, or merely that Fortune was looking the other way, the Gazette cannot say. Old hands will know better than to celebrate too heartily — the art of not scoring has a way of reasserting itself the very next Saturday, and the club's most distinguished members are rarely kept from the pavilion door for long.
