The LPCC Duck Gazette — Sunday, 8th August 1943

2 ducks
Week 13 · 8 Aug 1943
A modest gathering of the exclusive zero club this week, as the eleven met RA Wing at home and yielded but two entries to the roll of dishonour. Small mercies, and no doubt Durden thought Christmas had come early. 1st XI — v RA Wing (home) - Frank Sutton, in at seven, played on to Durden for a duck's egg that scarcely troubled the scorer. His fifth duck of the summer, and the twelfth of a career now spanning six-and-forty innings, a return that plants him, with a certain grim majesty, at the very head of the club's all-time roll — first of five hundred and twenty-six names who have ever walked back for nought. A past holder of the Duck of the Year honour in 1940, he adds this latest failure to an already distinguished ledger. Curiously, on this very day in 1892, one Jack Fryer likewise fell for a duck, against the Royal Engineers, proof that the calendar has long had a fondness for this fixture. - Gordon Fenner, last man in at eleven, was trapped leg-before to the same relentless Durden without troubling the umpire's patience for long. A third duck of the season, and a third of his career in but two-and-twenty innings, he now stands thirty-sixth of five hundred and twenty-six on the club's roll — respectable ignominy for a young player, and one shared, curiously enough, with his own brother Joe, who carries an identical three career ducks of his own. As it happens, the eighth of August has form here too: Jack Fryer made a duck against the Royal Engineers on this very date back in 1892. A brief but pointed afternoon's work for Durden, who accounted for both departures, top and tail of the order alike, in a display of what one might call democratic hostility. Two ducks from a single match is no epidemic, but the club's ledger grows regardless, as it always does. 5 ducks
Week 12 · 31 Jul 1943 – 2 Aug 1943
31st July – 2nd August, 1943 Three fixtures, five ducks laid down for the record — the honours board grows heavier by the week. 1st XI At home to the RAF on the 31st, Herbert Rayner played on to Jerman for nought, his second duck of the season and the fourth of a career now stretching to forty-six innings, the twenty-first most prolific egg-layer among our five hundred and twenty-five. On this very day in 1895, Ernest Cruttenden was likewise trudging back against Headcorn CC, proof that late July has always had a taste for feathers. Down at number ten in that same innings, B Westover fell to the same bowler for the same reward, his fourth duck of the summer and eighth of a career now standing fourth in the club's entire history, a distinction few would covet and fewer still could match. Cruttenden's shade of 1895 walked beside him to the pavilion once more. Against the 53rd Divisional Signals on the 1st, opener W Bunting was caught behind off Skilton without troubling the scorers, his third duck of the season and his career total besides, the forty-fourth name on the roll. The Reverend F A Leveson-Gower kept him company across the decades, having done precisely the same against Maidstone Conservative Club in 1910. At the other end of that innings, D Sells was bowled by Skilton for his fifth duck of the season, and remarkably his fifth in only eight innings played, a rate of failure so pure it already carries him to this season's Duck of the Year, with the Ducks in a Row now standing at four in succession. Eleventh of all who have ever turned out for the club, and young yet in his cricketing life. The good Reverend's 1910 shade attended this dismissal too. Completing the week's misfortune, against H Murray's XI on the 2nd, Bert Pierce was bowled by Moore for his very first duck, entering the list at ninety-eighth of all comers. He joins, on the honours board if not yet in practice, the ranks of the Retirement Duck club, a distinction earned by others' farewells, and no cause yet to fear for Bert's continued service with the bat. On this day in 1882, W H Fryer suffered similarly against Boxley CC. The Week in Brief Five ducks across three matches, and the tail seemed rather fonder of the pavilion steps than the crease — three of the week's five fell at number ten or below. The Signals match alone furnished two, Skilton claiming both with commendable economy. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. D Sells — 8 innings, 5 ducks, 62.5% 2. Herbert Sunley — 13 innings, 5 ducks, 38.46% 3. B Westover — 10 innings, 4 ducks, 40.0% 4. Frank Sutton — 16 innings, 4 ducks, 25.0% 5. W Bunting — 11 innings, 3 ducks, 27.27% The eleven takes the field again before long, and the Gazette has little doubt the list above will want updating. The Duck Club Gazette — a week of note, 24th–25th July 1943

4 ducks
Week 11 · 24 Jul 1943 – 25 Jul 1943
🦆 A wet ball and a straighter one from the Home Guard bowlers, and the exclusive zero club welcomes four new subscriptions this week. The tail did not so much wag as fall clean off, and the honours board creaks under fresh dubious distinction. 1st XI Saturday against Tovil brought Dennis Smith to the crease at number eight, only to depart bowled by Alexander for his 1st duck of the season, the 3rd of an accomplished career now standing 32nd of 525 all-time. A paid-up member of the Retirement Duck club from some past and presumably premature farewell — though nobody is suggesting he is bowing out now. Curiously, on this very day in 1909 one Charles Wycherley also trudged home for nought, against Barming Asylum CC of all opponents — some dates simply attract the duck's egg. Sunday's fixture against Home Guard D Company was a sticky wicket indeed, claiming three wickets for nothing at all. Gordon Fenner, caught by Sergeant Smith off X Elwell, notched his 2nd duck of the season and his 2nd of the career — 55th of 525 on the all-time roll, and a chip off a duck-shaped block, his sibling Joe Fenner carrying three career noughts of his own. Frank Sutton followed, bowled by L Wynn, for his 4th duck of the season — a plucky sequence of failure that brings his career total to 11, good enough (or bad enough) for 2nd of 525 all-time, and a returning name on the Duck of the Year 1940 board. And D Sells completed the rout, lbw to Wynn, for his 4th duck of the season and, remarkably, his 4th career duck from a mere seven innings — 17th of 525 all-time, freshly minted onto both the Duck of the Year 1943 board and the rare Ducks in a Row (4 consecutive) honour, a run of futility so unbroken it deserves its own regimental colours. All three Sunday duckers share their on-this-day cousin in the 1925 vintage, when W Turner also fell without scoring against Bearsted CC. The week in summary Four ducks in two matches — a quiet week by the standards of a club that treasures its failures, but a concentrated one, with three of the four falling in a single innings against the Home Guard. The art of not scoring was practised with particular conviction on Sunday. The First Eleven Against the Royal Army Service Corps at home on the 17th, two of the Eleven found the scorebook thoroughly unaccommodating. 🦆 The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 11th July 1943 🦆

4 ducks
Week 9 · 11 Jul 1943
A Report on the Week's Additions to the Exclusive Zero Club The Royal Artillery Wing paid a visit to the ground on Sunday, and while the eleven acquitted themselves with the usual mixture of pluck and misfortune, four of the home side's number found the art of not scoring rather too easy for comfort. A grave day for the scorebook, and a fine one for the Club. 1st XI Opening the innings and, alas, opening the Club's account for the day, Stan Wratten was taken by Steel off the bowling of Tiplady without so much as troubling the scorers 🍩. His second duck's egg of the season and the second of his career in a dozen visits to the crease — he now stands 77th of 525 in the club's long and dishonourable roll, and remains, by virtue of past company, a paid-up member of Quacking Together with John Ames. He joins the venerable Arthur Ash, of the 1934–41 vintage, in sitting on exactly two career ducks apiece — kindred spirits level on noughts, though separated by the better part of a decade. At number two, George Winter was run out in circumstances the scorer records only as "Unsure" — a fitting epitaph for a first career duck, his maiden entry into the Club after five innings of otherwise blameless service. He arrives at position 135 of 525 all-time, and finds instant company with the newly-minted "- Mill", also on a solitary duck this very season. Down at number nine, W Bunting played on to Tiplady via a catch to Phillips 0️⃣, his first career duck in ten innings — a long and patient wait for infamy, now rewarded, and he takes his place at 194th of 525. And last man in, Gordon Larking, went the way of so many number elevens before him — trapped leg-before to Tiplady for his first career duck in only three innings 🏏. He joins the same crowded ledger as Winter and Bunting on one apiece, and enters the all-time list at 137th of 525. Tiplady, it must be said, had rather a field day — three of the four ducks bear his name in the wicket column, a spell the Club salutes with considerably more enthusiasm than the batting side will muster. Week in Summary Four ducks from a single fixture is a solid week's work by the Club's standards — none of them golden, all falling to a straight ball, a sharp bit of fielding, or the umpire's raised finger. No pairs, no king pairs, and no family affairs to report this time; simply four honest men undone by four honest deliveries. The Duck Club Gazette — a chronicle for the week of the 22nd and 23rd of May, 1943

4 ducks
Week 2 · 22 May 1943 – 23 May 1943
Two fixtures, four eggs laid, and the exclusive zero club welcomes its latest subscribers with the usual mixture of ceremony and sympathy. The First Eleven At Bearsted CC on the Saturday, the last pair went in quick succession to the bowling of W E Weber, each man contributing nothing but his wicket. N- Parr, at number ten, was bowled for his very first innings in senior colours — a debut duck's egg, no less, and one that sets him down at 160th of 510 in the club's long and undistinguished roll. He joins A Barker, of the 1885 to 1904 vintage, on precisely one career duck apiece — Barker, it might be noted, once carried off the Duck of the Year honour in 1885, so N- Parr keeps distinguished if unfortunate company. B Westover followed him back to the pavilion at number eleven, bowled by the same hand — a tidy piece of bowling by Weber, and a tidier collapse by the Eleven. This was Westover's sixth career duck in seventeen innings, and his second of the season already, which places him a lofty sixth of 510 on the all-time list — level with F Danells, who managed the same feat across eighteen innings between 1881 and 1904. The Sunday brought the Royal Artillery Wing 48 to the home ground, and the home side found the art of not scoring just as readily as the visitors had. K- Symonds, first wicket down at number three, was leg-before to a Dillon delivery for nought — his maiden innings for the club, and thus a debut duck to match Parr's, good enough for 151st of 510 on the roll and the same one-duck company of A Barker. Later, at number six, Herbert Sunley was caught by Peach off the bowling of Black, his first duck in three innings for the club, ranking 136th of 510 — a paid-up member of the same one-duck fraternity, though Sunley arrives an established hand rather than a new face. The Week in Brief Four ducks from two matches is a fair week's work for the club's recruiting officer, and the Saturday's last-wicket pairing at Bearsted — both men undone by W E Weber within the same passage of play — will not be forgotten quickly by whoever keeps the Eleven's batting averages. No pairs and no family affairs to report this week, just four honest eggs laid in the ordinary course of cricket. The Duck Gazette — a chronicle for the 15th and 16th of May, 1943

3 ducks
Week 1 · 15 May 1943 – 16 May 1943
A brief innings this week for the Zero Club's recruiting sergeant — three eggs laid across two fixtures, each a tale of its own in the ancient art of not scoring. The First Eleven Saturday's engagement against the Maidstone Fire Service saw the middle and late order do their level best to douse the innings before it caught light. Gordon Fenner, promoted to number eight, was bowled by Andrews for a duck — his first blob of the summer and the first of his career in five innings, placing him 129th of 508 in the club's long and honourable roll of failure. He is not alone in the family trade, either — his sibling Joe Fenner carries three career ducks of his own, so a certain talent for ignominy plainly runs in the blood. Gordon keeps distinguished company besides: A Barker, who turned out for the club between 1885 and 1904 and was crowned Duck of the Year in 1885, sits on precisely the same solitary career duck. One place further down the order, B Westover followed him back to the pavilion, bowled by Porter without troubling the scorers. It was the fifth duck of a career now sixteen innings deep, and it lodges him a lofty tenth of 508 on the all-time list — rarefied ground indeed. He draws level on career ducks with Allan Peach, who plied his trade for the club from 1903 to 1907 and racked up his own five in eleven innings. Sunday brought the eleven up against the Royal Army Service Corps' 533 Division, and here the honour fell to L- Breedon, stumped by Gaines off the bowling of Golder for nought. It was his maiden innings for the club — a debut duck in every sense, and a fine, if unwanted, way to announce oneself to the honours board. He joins A Barker too, on one apiece, in what is fast becoming a well-populated corner of the ledger. The Week in Summary Three ducks, two matches, and not a repeat egg among them — a clean sweep of single failures rather than any grim double this week. The Fire Service accounted for two of the three in one innings, which one imagines they considered fair exchange for whatever blaze they might otherwise have been called to attend. Breedon's arrival is the tale of the week — there can be few gentler introductions to a cricketing life than a stumping for nought on one's very first appearance. Five ducks were laid down for the exclusive zero club this week — a place of dubious distinction, but never short of new members. 1st XI - Herbert Rayner — in at four against the Royal Army Ordnance Corps on the 17th, and undone by Brierley for his first duck's egg of the season. His second of a career now nineteen innings deep, and it lodges him at 51st of 493 in the club's long roll of the dismissed. He draws level on two career ducks with B W Haynes, a name from the club's Edwardian heyday who compiled his own identical pair somewhere between 1891 and 1910 — proof, if any were needed, that this particular failing spans the generations undiminished. - B- Vince — arrived at the crease for the very first time in claret and gold, at nine against the RAOC, and departed for nought before he had properly arrived at all, bowled Brierley. A debut duck, and with the season young he stands, for now, the leading claimant to the club's own Duck of the Year 1941. He joins A Barker, of the 1885 vintage, on a single career duck apiece. But the story did not end there — the very next day, at ten against the Home Guard's Bungs Mob, he was caught off A Stevens for nought once more, completing a grim pair inside forty-eight hours of his arrival. Two innings, two ducks, a full house already — a baptism as chastening as any this correspondent can recall. - R Dann — run out for nought at five against the Home Guard, his tale a touch confused (the striker's end remains, charitably, "unsure"). His first career duck in two innings, placing him 156th of 493. Curiously, on this very day in 1940, Joe Fenner also strolled back for a duck's egg, against Staplehurst CC — the calendar, it seems, has its own sense of humour. - Don Hartridge — stumped by P Richmond off the bowling of George Winter, also against the Home Guard, for his third career nought in fifteen innings, and 28th of 493 on the all-time list. He shares his duck's anniversary with the same Joe Fenner of 1940, who was evidently no stranger to a Saturday spent walking back early. The week in brief Two matches, five ducks, and the Home Guard's Bungs Mob proved especially fond of the eleven's lower order, claiming three of the five between run-out, stumping and catch. The standout performance, if that is the word, belongs to B- Vince, who turned up, introduced himself to the crease twice, and left it twice without troubling the scorer — a pair to mark a debut that will not soon be forgotten. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - B- Vince — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - Herbert Rayner — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Don Hartridge — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - R Dann — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The season is young and the wickets, by all accounts, still a touch sticky. Members are warmly invited to the next fixture, where no doubt further candidates for the honours board await — the eleven's tail has shown it can wag, but rarely for long.

LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 17th August 1940

0 ducks
Week 16 · 17 Aug 1940
A quiet week at Linton Park, and for once the eleven have nothing to answer for. The Week's Ducks Not a single egg was laid this Saturday. The bowlers hunted, no doubt, with their usual cunning, but every batsman at the crease this week found a way to troouble the scorer for at least one run — a sticky wicket, evidently, for the ducks rather than the ducked. The exclusive zero club, so used to welcoming new members most weekends, must for once content itself with admiring its existing roll of honour from a respectful distance. Week in Summary One match played, nought ducks laid — a rare and faintly suspicious state of affairs for a club whose very purpose is the chronicling of noughts. Whether this reflects a sudden and alarming outbreak of good form, or merely that the bowling wanted its usual sting, the committee declines to speculate. The Duck Club's records remain, this week, entirely undisturbed. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Frank Sutton — 10 innings, 4 ducks, 40.0% - B Westover — 14 innings, 4 ducks, 28.57% - W- Barton — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100.0% - Phil Bowles — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.0% - Joe Fenner — 9 innings, 2 ducks, 22.22% Frank Sutton continues to lead the chase with quiet consistency, while young W- Barton's perfect record of two innings and two ducks remains, for the moment, a rather remarkable achievement of pure, unblemished failure — a hundred per cent is a hundred per cent, after all, whichever direction one takes it. The Club extends its commiserations to no one this week, and its congratulations to the eleven for a job, in the strictest sporting sense, well done. Normal service — a straight bat undone, a plucky knock cut short, the tail wagging briefly before subsiding — will no doubt resume at the next fixture, and the committee awaits fresh nominations to the zero club with its customary and undimmed enthusiasm.

Whale — a tidy piece of work by the visitors that returned him for his fourth duck of the summer and the fifth of a career now seventeen innings long, a standing that holds firm at ninth in the club's roll of four hundred and eighty seven. Berry, brought up his fourth duck of the season, level with his career tally after thirteen innings — good enough for twelfth place in the club's long records. A sticky sort of session for the lower order, though the eleven will doubtless reflect that a duck's egg or two is simply the game's way of keeping a man humble. 0 ducks
Week 9 · 29 Jun 1940
A quiet week to report, and for once the news is that there is no news at all. One fixture was played in the period under review, and — remarkable as it may seem — not a single member of the Eleven troubled the scorer with a duck's egg. The exclusive zero club, so often swollen with new arrivals, admits no one this week. Whether this reflects a sudden and alarming outbreak of application at the crease, or merely a sticky wicket that favoured the bowlers too evenly to discriminate, the Committee declines to speculate. The ducks, in short, evaded capture — a state of affairs the Club trusts will prove temporary, for a Duck Report with nothing to report is a poor advertisement for the art of not scoring. Let it not be said, however, that the season's honours board stands empty. The following gentlemen continue to hold their heads — or rather, their bats — in the particular manner that has earned them their standing among this summer's foremost practitioners of the well-tried and the swiftly departed. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Frank Sutton — 7 innings, 3 ducks, 42.86%. A batsman evidently determined to make a habit of it, and doing so with real consistency. - W- Barton — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100%. A quiet week by the Club's usual standards, but a memorable one for two young men now permanently enrolled among the eleven's most select company — those who have played a straight bat to nothing at all. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 18th May, 1940

4 ducks
Week 3 · 18 May 1940
A modest afternoon at Staplehurst brought the eleven no fewer than four fresh entries to the roll of dishonour. The visiting side's attack found rather more success with the ball than our willow-wielders found with theirs, and the pavilion clock ticked round for four short walks back. Let it be recorded properly below. 1st XI at Staplehurst CC Opening the innings and opening the ledger, Joe Fenner was trapped leg-before to W Tipples without so much as a run to his name — his first duck's egg of the season, and the fourth of a still-young career. He joins the goodly company of A Barker, that stalwart of 1885 to 1904, on exactly one career duck apiece — kindred spirits separated by fifty-five years and united in nought. Not to be outdone, W- Barton fell at first wicket down, bowled by the same relentless Tipples, for his second duck of the season and, remarkably, his second in as many innings played for the club — a career average of failure that would make a mathematician wince. He keeps company with B W Haynes of the 1891-1910 vintage, level on two career ducks. At number six, Bert Buckoke was bowled by D Bearsby, his first duck of this season but the third of a distinguished career spanning fourteen innings — distinguished, that is, by his place on the Duck of the Year honours board for 1928, a title he holds still. He and the venerable A Kent of 1893 stand shoulder to shoulder on three career ducks each. And last but not least, Frank Sutton was caught behind off R Munn without scoring, his second duck of the season and third of his career — a career, one notes, that has already earned him this very season's Duck of the Year honour. A paid-up member of that particular club, and level with A Kent on three career ducks besides. The Week in Brief One match, four ducks, and the Staplehurst bowlers thoroughly enjoying their afternoon's work. A fairly one-sided procession to and from the crease, though it must be said the eleven bore it all with the customary good grace the game demands — there being, after all, a certain nobility in the art of not scoring. 0 ducks
Week 4 · 8 Jul 1939
🏏 Well now. The eleven took the field, the willow was wielded, and — most unusually for these pages — not a single duck's egg was laid to report. A match played, evidently, without incident of the ignominious variety. There is, in truth, precious little for your correspondent to embellish this week. No batsman walked back before troubling the scorer, no golden duck was hatched, no pair was suffered, and no unhappy family gathered twice at the pavilion gate. The exclusive zero club, it seems, held no meeting this Saturday — its members, one presumes, all found their timing, or at least their luck. One might almost call it a disappointment. The art of not scoring is a fine and testing discipline, practised by only the bravest of souls, and this week the willow-wielders of Linton Park declined the invitation entirely. We trust it shall not become a habit. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - E Hayes — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - X Rayner — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% Slim pickings atop the table this season, though E Hayes sits at a rather emphatic full house, and X Rayner is not far removed. Plenty of season left, gentlemen, for the ducks to make their return. Until the next fixture, then — when we trust the eleven will oblige us with rather more material. The pavilion gate awaits its next pilgrim.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 17th June, 1939

2 ducks
Week 1 · 17 Jun 1939
Two more names are inscribed upon the honours board this week, both claimed at Castle Hill CC, Kent, where the eleven's lower order once again proved rather better at walking off than staying in. 1st XI — away to Castle Hill CC X Rayner, sent in at number eight, was stumped by Albert Perryman off the bowling of Edward Knight and thereby enrolled himself in the exclusive zero club on his very first outing for the eleven — a debut duck, the purest kind of welcome the game can offer. It is his 1st duck of the season, and, being his maiden innings, his 1st in a career now formally begun, leaving him 178th of 458 upon the club's long roll of dubious distinction. He arrives, too, already a name upon the Retirement Duck board, that solemn register reserved for those whose final recorded innings ended in nought — though we trust Rayner's own farewell lies a good many summers off yet, and that this is merely the first chapter of a longer story. Curiously, on this very date in 1899, one F Smith likewise trudged back to the pavilion for nought against Sutton Valence School, the calendar drawing the two gentlemen together across forty years of shared misfortune. E Hayes, last man in at number eleven, was bowled by David Hodges without so much as troubling the scorer, and racks up his 1st duck of the season and 3rd of his career — a duck in every one of his three innings to date, a consistency few could hope to rival and fewer still would wish to. He stands 25th of 458 on the all-time list, and carries the Duck of the Year honours for both 1937 and, most pertinently, the present season of 1939 — a title he seems intent on defending with unusual thoroughness. He too shares his day with F Smith's duck of 1899, forty summers gone but evidently not forgotten. Week in summary One match, one duck's egg apiece for the bottom of the order — the middle order played the straighter bat, leaving positions eight and eleven to carry the club's honour, such as it is. Early days in the season yet, but with Mr Hayes averaging a duck an innings and Mr Rayner already keeping distinguished company on the honours boards, the tail shows every sign of being this year's chief source of entertainment. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - E Hayes — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - X Rayner — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% Early honours shared evenly between our two contributors. The eleven takes the field again before long, and the zero club stands ready, as ever, to welcome new members with open arms and straight faces. 1937 Season 1 report

The Duck Club Chronicle — Saturday, 29th May 1937

1 duck
Week 1 · 29 May 1937
A single fixture, a single sacrifice to the great god of nought — but where the Duck Club is concerned, one is quite enough to warrant the trumpet. 1st XI - E Hayes, sent in at number eleven and asked to do little more than see out the innings, instead saw out his stumps — caught E A Brooks, bowled L Roberts, for a duck's egg that will not trouble the scorebook further. It is the first blot of the season for Hayes and, sobering thought, the second of a career that has run to just two innings — a strike rate for nought that would make a statistician blush. He takes his place 39th of 453 in the Club's roll of the dismissed-for-nothing, drawing level on career ducks with the venerable B W Haynes, who between 1891 and 1910 contrived the very same brace of two in nineteen innings — kindred spirits separated by the better part of half a century but united, as the honours board has it, in the art of not scoring. Given that this is 1937's own vintage, Hayes may already fancy his chances for the Duck of the Year sash that carries this season's name upon it — early days yet, but a promising start in the wrong direction. The Week in Brief One match, one duck — a modest yield by the Club's usual standards, but a duck's egg is a duck's egg, and the ledger must be kept regardless of season or scarcity. No pairs, no king pairs, and no family gatherings at the crease this week — the Hayeses, whoever they may be elsewhere, kept their noughts to themselves. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - E Hayes — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A short list this early in the summer, but the season is long and the eleven is willing. Members are warmly reminded that the wicket cares nothing for reputation, and the next fixture will doubtless furnish further candidates for these hallowed and inglorious pages. Until then — mind your off stump.

1936 Season 3 reports

The Duck Club Gazette — Saturday, 29th August, 1936

3 ducks
Week 10 · 29 Aug 1936
A single fixture at home to Charles Arkcoll on this last Saturday of August, and the Zero Club opens its ledger three times over. No golden ducks to report this week — each of our three victims at least troubled the scorer's pencil for a ball or two before the long walk back, which in this fellowship counts as a plucky knock of sorts. 1st XI Opening the innings and opening the account for ignominy, E Cheeseman went for a duck at first wicket down, bowled J W Rowe. It is his second career duck in six innings — thirty-eighth of all 450 upon the roll — and a Duck of the Year laureate of 1935 besides, so the fellow knows his way to the pavilion by now. He draws level with the venerable B W Haynes (1891-1910), also on two career ducks, kindred spirits in the art of not scoring. At four, N Tiley fell to E A Brooks, bowled, his second career duck from a mere five innings — fifty-third of all 450. Like Cheeseman he joins B W Haynes on two career ducks apiece, proof that history repeats itself down the batting order as readily as up it. Down at nine, Frank Sutton was caught C Leeson, bowled E A Brooks, his maiden career duck from four innings, one hundred and seventh of all who have ever walked this particular plank. He joins A Barker (1885-1904), also on a single duck, among the Club's newer initiates — every great collection must start somewhere. The week in brief One match, one duck's egg apiece for three unlucky batsmen, and Charles Arkcoll's bowlers did the damage between them, E A Brooks claiming two of the three for his afternoon's work. A tidy little haul, and the tail wagged not a jot. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - E Godden — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - E Cheeseman — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33% - Frank Sutton — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33% - N Tiley — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33% - O Fryer — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33% The season's sorriest table remains keenly contested, and E Godden's early lead upon a single innings is one every member will be hoping to see challenged, or indeed spared, before too long. The eleven return to the field next Saturday, and the Club stands ready, as ever, to welcome new members into its exclusive and dubious fellowship. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette

1 duck
Week 1 · 22 Jun 1935
Recording the week of Saturday, 22nd June 1935 A quiet week for the exclusive zero club, but a duck's egg is a duck's egg, and one gentleman of the 1st XI has duly been elected to its ranks for the occasion. 1st XI Percy Brattle, sent in at first wicket down away to Bearsted CC, departed caught by L Monckton off the bowling of Frank Harnett — a plucky enough dismissal, and no golden duck to be recorded against his name, for the scorebook has him surviving at the crease before his luck ran out. It is his first duck of the present season, and his first in a career now standing at two innings, which places him a respectable 137th of 440 upon the club's long and honourable roll of those who have played and missed. A fellow of pleasant company there, it might be said, for by curious coincidence it was on this very day in the year 1881 that one W H Fryer, of the 1867 to 1885 vintage and no stranger himself to the art of not scoring — six ducks to his name, and 7th of 440 upon the same roll — likewise strolled back to the pavilion for nought, against Boxley CC's first innings. Fifty-four years apart, and the wicket claimed its due on the selfsame date. There is something almost providential in that. The Week in Summary One match played, one duck recorded, and Mr Brattle carrying the whole burden of ignominy upon his own shoulders this week — a solitary sort of triumph through adversity, but triumph of a kind nonetheless. The eleven may take some comfort that the tail, on this occasion, was not required to wag, there being only the one wicket of this particular description to report. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Percy Brattle — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent A modest table this week, with room enough upon it for others to make their mark, or rather to fail to make one, in fixtures yet to come. The eleven takes the field again before long, and the zero club stands ready, as ever, to welcome whichever gentleman the bowlers next persuade back to the pavilion with nothing to show for his visit to the crease.

3 ducks
Week 1 · 1 Sep 1934
🏏 A modest afternoon at the crease against Charles Arkcoll, but a fruitful one for the exclusive zero club — three gentlemen of the Home Eleven found their way back to the pavilion without so much as troubling the scorer. The art of not scoring was practised with some diligence this day. 1st XI Bert Buckoke, sent in first wicket down, was undone by J Parsons and departed for a duck's egg — his second of a career now standing at two in as many innings, placing him 34th of 434 in the club's grand and dubious ledger. A Duck of the Year man from 1928, he remains a paid-up member of that select company, though this particular knock added nothing to the honour beyond confirming old habits die hard. He joins B W Haynes, of the 1891–1910 vintage, in sitting on exactly two career ducks apiece — kindred spirits across the decades, united by nought. A Smith, first innings ever pulled on for the club, walked to the crease at first wicket down and walked straight back again, also to J Parsons' bowling — a debut duck of the purest and most immediate variety, and thus his very first entry on the honours board, Duck of the Year 1934 already secured before he has troubled the scorers even once. A fine start, in its way. He draws level with A Barker of 1885–1904, also on a single career duck. J Barker, at number eight, played a plucky knock of nought, bowled by L Roberts for his second career duck in four innings — the tail, one might say, wagged only briefly. He sits 45th of 434 on the all-time list, level on two career ducks with the venerable B W Haynes among a long and distinguished company of others similarly becalmed. The Week in Summary Three ducks, one match, all falling to the home eleven against Charles Arkcoll, and all three bowled — a sticky wicket for the willow-wielders, or perhaps simply a good day for the bowlers. No pairs, no golden ducks, no family affairs this week — merely honest, straightforward failure, thrice repeated. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - A Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) - Bert Buckoke — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) - J Barker — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) A three-way tie atop the season standings, gentlemen all equally devoted to the cause. The Duck Club Gazette — the week ending the 29th of June, 1910

1 duck
Week 1 · 29 Jun 1910
A modest week upon the roll of the exclusive zero club, with but a single gentleman required to make the long walk back for nought. Let the record show it properly. Midweek XI Mr Tom Peach Jnr, going in at number ten against the 1st Innings of Boxley CC away from home, was bowled by W L Reading and returned to the pavilion having troubled the scorer not at all, though he is credited with having faced his share of the bowling before the timbers went — no golden duck this, merely the ordinary and thoroughly respectable art of not scoring. It is his first duck of the present season, and the fifth of a career now numbering fourteen innings, which places him ninth upon the club's all-time roll of three hundred and ninety-seven names — a standing not lightly come by. Members will recall he remains a laureate of some distinction, having carried off the Duck of the Year honours as long ago as 1902, a garland that loses none of its lustre for having been won in another age. It may interest the eleven that upon this very date in 1907, Mr Ernest Cruttenden — second upon our all-time roll with ten ducks to his name, and himself Duck of the Year in 1895 — likewise failed to trouble the scorer, against Town Malling CC. History, it seems, is fond of an anniversary. The Week in Summary One match played, one duck recorded, and the Midweek XI may count themselves fortunate that the ducks did not multiply further upon foreign soil. A quiet week for the club's registrars, but a week is a week, and the ledger must be kept regardless of how thin the pickings. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Tom Peach Jnr — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent A leaderboard of but one name this week, Mr Peach standing entirely alone at its head, though whether this reflects distinction or simply an absence of competition, the correspondent leaves to the reader's judgement. The eleven return to the field presently, and the club's registrars stand ready, pencils sharpened, to record whatever further ciphers the coming fixture may yield. Members are reminded that the art of not scoring spares no one, however illustrious, and the honours board awaits new names with its usual patience.

This being his maiden innings for the eleven, it is his first, his only, and consequently his season-defining duck to date, and stands as his maiden entry in the honours book — 77th of 395 in the club's all-time roll of dishonour. He may console himself that the season's silverware for scorelessness already bears his name, Duck of the Year 1909 being his for the taking so far. And by a pleasant coincidence of the calendar, on this very day in 1899 one P T Oyler likewise strolled back for a duck's egg, against Rochester CC — a full decade separating the two gentlemen, united only in the art of not scoring. Week in summary Two fixtures played, and but a single wicket fell to the great leveller of nought. The eleven, on the whole, kept remarkably good order at the crease this week — whether through improved application or simple good fortune, the correspondent declines to speculate. Mr Stevens carries the week's honours alone, and carries them well. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. C Stevens — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% 2. Charles Wycherley — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% Both gentlemen sit level atop the season's table of dubious distinction, each having faced but a single innings and made rather less of it than they might have hoped. A quiet week for the exclusive zero club: but one gentleman was required to make the short walk back, and he did so with a certain dogged consistency that our readers will find not unfamiliar. 1st XI - Charles Wycherley, sent in at number five in the away fixture against Barming Asylum CC, was bowled by Dr Lewis and returned to the pavilion for a cipher. This is his first duck of the present season, and the fourth of a career now running to ten innings — a record that places him eleventh among the three hundred and ninety gentlemen who have, over the club's long history, achieved this particular species of distinction. He finds himself in close and honourable company with C Amies, who between 1867 and 1870 also compiled precisely four such innings, proving that the art of not scoring has never wanted for practitioners. It may further be recorded, for the historically minded, that Mr Wycherley was Duck of the Year as long ago as 1906, a laurel earned in a season quite separate from this one, and no less becoming for its age. In summary, one match was played and one duck secured — a modest yield, though the club's chroniclers would observe that a single well-turned nought, bowled clean by the good doctor himself, wants for nothing in quality what it lacks in quantity. The ducks, in the main, evaded the net this week, and our correspondent is not ashamed to say he was glad of the one that did not. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - Charles Wycherley — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% The season is yet young, and the eleven take the field again before long, at which time the club has every confidence that further candidates for this dubious honour will present themselves. 1908 Season 3 reports

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — Saturday, the 12th of August, 1908

0 ducks
Week 11 · 12 Aug 1908
A quiet week, gentlemen, and no cause for the honours board to trouble itself. Our correspondent has scoured the scorebook from every corner of the ground and must report, with something approaching regret, that not a single member of the eleven presented his wicket for a cipher this week. The timbers stood unmolested, the leather went unrewarded, and the art of not scoring was, for once, left entirely unpractised. One match was played, and in it every batsman troubled the scorer at least once — a state of affairs the Duck Club can only note with wry disappointment, for it is rather the business of this gazette to celebrate failure, and failure has this week declined the invitation. We trust our members will not take this as encouragement. The exclusive zero club stands ready to receive new subscribers the moment application is made, and a place of such dubious distinction is never short of interest for long. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. S H Hills — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% Mr Hills leads the field this season by the simplest of arithmetic, having faced the scorer's pencil but once and been sent back to the pavilion on that solitary occasion. A perfect record, of a kind, and one his fellow members are cordially invited to challenge at the earliest opportunity. We look ahead with confidence, if not quite optimism, to the next fixture, where the willow may yet fail our men as reliably as it has failed them in seasons past. The Duck Club awaits its next candidates with open arms and a well-thumbed ledger.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — Week Ending the 8th of June, 1908

1 duck
Week 2 · 8 Jun 1908
A single fixture graced our books this week, and a single wicket fell for nought — but what it lacked in number it makes handsomely up for in ceremony. To the wicket, then. The 1st Eleven Opening the innings against Maidstone Cricket Club, Mr S H Hills strode out first to face the bowling and was, alas, promptly caught by E Buss off the bowling of W Simmonds without so much as troubling the scorer. We are given to understand he did survive at least one delivery before his dismissal, so no golden duck attaches to the affair — a small mercy. What does attach is rather grander: this being the very first innings of Mr Hills's career with the club, he has thus been admitted, on his maiden appearance, to the exclusive zero club — a distinction some men labour a decade to earn and he has secured before luncheon on his first day. The honours board records him already for Duck of the Year 1908, a laurel earned this very week and one he may wear, we trust, with the appropriate mixture of pride and mortification. His name now stands 136th of 386 in the club's long roll of the dismissed, a single nought to his single innings — a purity of record, if nothing else. We note also that a Mr A Barker, who turned out for the club between 1885 and 1904 and was himself Duck of the Year in 1885, sits on the very same career tally of one — Mr Hills may consider himself in respectable, if scoreless, company. The Week in Summary One match, one duck, one debutant received into the fold with unusual promptness. There is something to be said for efficiency, even in failure, and Mr Hills has demonstrated it admirably. The bowling figures of Mr Simmonds and the safe hands of Mr Buss are noted with the courtesy due to gentlemen who did their office well. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. S H Hills — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0 per cent A leaderboard of one is, admittedly, an easy table to top, and Mr Hills has done so in a single stroke of misfortune. We look forward with keen anticipation to the season's next fixture, when the bowling attacks of our opponents will no doubt continue their diligent efforts to add further names to this esteemed and ever-growing register. The eleven are cordially reminded that the timbers wait for no man, and that the art of not scoring remains, as ever, very much alive at Linton Park.

The Duck Club Gazette — Saturday, the 30th of May, 1908

0 ducks
Week 1 · 30 May 1908
A single fixture was contested this week, and it is my melancholy duty to report that the ducks proved elusive quarry throughout. Not one gentleman of either eleven was dismissed for a cipher — the timbers stood, the willow connected, and the leather was, on this solitary occasion, denied its usual harvest. One may search the honours boards in vain for a fresh entry this week. The exclusive zero club, that place of dubious distinction to which so many of our members have in seasons past been unwillingly admitted, gained no new subscriber on this occasion. Whether this reflects a sudden and uncharacteristic outbreak of application at the crease, or merely the ordinary caprice of the game, this correspondent will not presume to say. Consistency, it seems, took the week off — even consistency of the particular kind for which the Club exists to celebrate. We trust our members will not take this as any diminishment of the art of not scoring, which remains as noble and as democratic a pursuit as ever, open to novice and veteran alike, and merely resting this week rather than retired. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season's returns stand as they were — no fresh figures to report this week, the tally sheet undisturbed by the day's play. Members presently of note in the season's reckoning will find their standing unchanged, and are cordially invited to consider whether such a state of affairs is entirely to their liking. We look with quiet confidence, and no small measure of hope, to the next fixture, at which normal service — by which we mean the entirely abnormal service of being sent back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer — may reasonably be expected to resume. The Club's doors, as ever, remain open to all comers.

2 ducks

A modest bag from the fixture against Town Malling CC, yet a bag all the same: two of our number were obliged to make the long walk back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer. The First Eleven - Mr Ernest Cruttenden, at number six, was bowled by W Hickmott and returned for a duck's egg — his first cipher of the present season, and the tenth of a long and distinguished career now numbering seven and sixty innings, a return that places him second of all 383 gentlemen ever to have graced the club's roll of dubious distinction. He remains, and has long remained, a Duck of the Year laureate of 1895, an honour undimmed by the passing of a dozen summers. It may interest the curious that upon this very date in the year 1896, one G M Style was likewise dismissed without score, against the eleven of Mr H Wilson-Smith. - Mr F E Wallis, batting at number eight, was taken by G H Adam off the bowling of W R Stratton, recording the fourth duck of a career spanning six and twenty innings, and standing eleventh in the club's ancient order of nought. He tops this season's table already, and presently holds the club's Duck of the Year honour for 1907 — a distinction the season yet has time to snatch from him. By a curious coincidence, this too was the anniversary of G M Style's duck of 1896, against that same Wilson-Smith eleven — the date would appear to have something of a talent for producing ciphers. The Week in Summary One fixture, two ducks, both from the First Eleven's middle and lower order. No great surprise, perhaps, but a fitting demonstration of the club's founding principle — that failure, properly and repeatedly borne, is itself a kind of distinction. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - F E Wallis — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - Ernest Cruttenden — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent - Allan Peach — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.3 per cent The club awaits, with its accustomed patience, the next fixture and whatever fresh additions to the roll it may furnish. Members are reminded that the willow spares no reputation, and the timbers least of all.

The Duck Report — 25th May 1907

1 duck
Week 1 · 25 May 1907
A quiet week at Linton Park, the eleven engaged in but a single fixture, and the exclusive zero club obliged with only one new member. Modest fare, but not without its dignity. 1st XI — v Town Malling CC (home) Mr Allan Peach, sent in at first wicket down, was undone by the bowling of W R Stratton and returned to the pavilion, the timbers rearranged behind him, though he had at least troubled the crease for a ball or two before his dismissal — no golden duck to record here, merely the ordinary variety, of which he is now a most practised collector. This stands as his fifth indiscretion of a distinguished career spanning ten innings, and lodges him at the respectable position of seventh in the club's all-time roll of dishonour, a table of some three hundred and eighty names. He carries no honours-board memberships as yet, though on the present showing the committee may wish to keep a place warm. Of interest to the statistically minded: Mr Peach's tally of five now sits precisely alongside that long amassed by Mr F S W Cornwallis, who plied his trade between 1885 and 1906 across four-and-fifty innings before settling on the very same figure — a coincidence of the ledger that the correspondent is only too pleased to record, the two gentlemen now drawing level upon the honours board of nought, separated by but a single place in the all-time reckoning. The Week in Summary A single duck from a single fixture — the willow, on this occasion, proved rather more obliging than usual, and the art of not scoring was practised but the once. Whether this reflects a temporary want of application among the bowling fraternity, or merely good fortune among the batting order, the correspondent declines to speculate. Suffice it to say the ducks proved elusive this week, and the hunting was thin. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Mr Allan Peach — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0 per cent A leaderboard of one is, admittedly, scant sport, but the season is young and the correspondent has every confidence the ranks will swell before long. In Closing The eleven take the field again shortly, and the committee trusts further candidates for the zero club shall present themselves in due course, as they invariably do. Members are cordially reminded that a duck's egg, however unwelcome to the batsman, is always warmly received by this correspondent. Until the next fixture, then — may your bat find the middle, and may Mr Peach find some company at the foot of the table.

3 ducks

A single fixture at home to Boxley Cricket Club furnished the eleven with three fresh entries upon the club's roll of dubious distinction, and a productive afternoon it was for Mr W. Coveney, who accounted for two of the three unaided. The season of 1906 finds him already inscribed upon the Duck of the Year board, and on this showing the honour may yet be his to defend before September is out. He finds companionship in adversity with one A. Kent of 1893, likewise a career total of three, and himself similarly garlanded in his day. At number four, Mr C. L. Pemberton met the same bowler and the same fate, lbw b Coveney — his very first appearance at the wicket for the club thus concluding upon a cipher, a debut conducted with scarcely any ceremony at all. He takes his place at the seventieth rung of the all-time roll, in the company of one A. Barker, whose solitary career duck, recorded between 1885 and 1904, stands at precisely the same modest total. Sent in at six, Mr Tom Peach Jnr was bowled by G. Laurence for his fourth career duck in a innings tally now standing at thirteen, no stranger to this ledger, being already a name from 1902's Duck of the Year board. He shares his present total of four with one Allan Peach, whose career runs from 1903 to the present season. The Week in Summary One match, three ducks, and a single bowler answerable for two of them — the leather plainly found the timbers to its liking this Saturday. No pair of misfortune was recorded, nor any family united in nought this week, each duck being a solitary affair, however keenly felt by the gentleman concerned. 8 ducks

A solitary fixture against Leeds Castle CC yielded no fewer than eight ciphers for the club's ledger this week — a splendid harvest for one afternoon's play, and business enough to keep the scorers' pencils sharp. 1st XI (away, Leeds Castle CC) - Jack Fryer, second man in, was bowled by W Betts for the season's first addition to his account and his twelfth career duck in 67 innings, a tally that stands first of 367 upon the club's roll of dishonour. Sent in again the same day, he was run out without addition, completing a pair and his season's second duck, his career tally now standing at two in a mere four innings — level with C French Snr, who managed the same modest feat between 1860 and 1864. - C Kneller, playing his very first innings for the club, was run out without scoring, opening his career account with a duck in his second innings played, level upon one career duck with A Barker, ranked 68th of 367. - H Wilson, likewise making his debut, was caught De Uphaugh, bowled Betts, and, sent in again, was bowled by Betts a second time without troubling the scorers — a pair upon his very first afternoon in the eleven. Not one of our men departed first ball, each contriving to survive a delivery or more before submitting to the inevitable cipher, which the club's historians will note as consistency of a most particular and unremunerative kind. Week 11 · 25 Aug 1904
A single fixture is recorded in the period under review, our eleven meeting Leeds Castle Cricket Club, and the willow yielded to the club's collection two further ducks' eggs of note. House Team Mr T Woollett, walking to the wicket at number eight for his very first innings in this eleven's colours, was caught by T Sparks off the bowling of R Startup, and thus took his introduction to the game's sterner disciplines in the most unceremonious fashion available to a debutant — dismissed for a cipher before he had properly taken his guard. It is his maiden innings and, by the same stroke, his maiden duck, a coincidence the honours board records rather less kindly than we do here. He enters the all-time列, or rather the all-time list, at 135th of 359, and in doing so draws level upon a tally of one with the venerable A Barker, whose own solitary duck was taken back in 1885 and earned that gentleman the Duck of the Year garland for his trouble — Mr Woollett may take some comfort in such distinguished, if modest, company. Mr G Pearce, sent in at number ten, was bowled by B Tillman without scoring, his third innings for the club and his first acquaintance with the duck's egg, a distinction he had until now been spared. He stands 93rd of 359 upon the all-time roll of dishonour, and he too finds himself level upon a single duck with the aforementioned A Barker of 1885 vintage — two gentlemen, nineteen years apart, united by the same modest arithmetic. The week in summary Two ducks from a single match, both falling to the lower order of the House Team's innings against Leeds Castle, suggests our tail found the leather rather more troublesome than the top order — no partnerships, no pairs, and mercifully no family misfortune to report this week, the ducks confining themselves to individual, rather than dynastic, disappointment. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season being yet young, five gentlemen stand together at the summit, each having faced the bowling once this season and each having been dismissed without score, for a season average of nought and a duck percentage of a full 100: - Mr Arthur Cornwallis — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Mr C H Style — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Mr C Reid — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Mr G Pearce — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Mr T Woollett — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A crowded summit, and an early one, but the season is long and the willow fickle. Members are cordially invited to attend the next fixture, where no doubt further candidates shall present themselves for admission to this most exclusive and least sought-after of clubs.

The Duck Club Gazette — a Report for the Week of the 6th to the 9th of August, 1904

1 duck
Week 9 · 6 Aug 1904 – 9 Aug 1904
A quiet week for the timbers, gentlemen, with but a single egg laid across two fixtures — the ducks, it would seem, took their ease this week and left the eleven largely untroubled. House Team - Jack Fryer, first wicket down against Leeds Castle Cricket Club on the 9th, in the away fixture, was bowled by W Thorndycraft for a cipher, and returned to the pavilion with the ledger unimproved. This being his first duck's egg of the 1904 season, and his eleventh in a career now standing at sixty-five innings, he remains ensconced at the very head of the club's all-time roll — first of some three hundred and fifty-five names who have known the particular ignominy of nought. Mr Fryer will further be remembered as a past holder of the Duck of the Year honour, claimed in both 1891 and 1900, proof, if proof were needed, that the art of not scoring may be practised at the very highest level, and practised more than once. A Week in Summary Two fixtures were played in the period under review, and but a single duck's egg was laid between them — a scarcity that will please the batting order rather more than it pleases this correspondent, whose columns are ever the poorer for a quiet week. Mr Fryer alone flew the club's sorry colours, and flew them, it must be said, rather briefly. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - Arthur Cornwallis — 1 innings, 1 duck, a full 100 per cent - C H Style — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - C Reid — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - Allan Peach — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent - Jack Fryer — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent The season's leading three gentlemen have, it will be observed, achieved a perfect record of imperfection, having faced but the one innings apiece and failed on each occasion to trouble the scorer. Whether such consistency may be sustained, or whether the willow shall yet find its mark, remains a matter for the coming weeks to determine. We commend the eleven to their next fixture, in the confident expectation that the ducks, presently in hiding, shall shortly be flushed once more from cover. The correspondent remains, as ever, at the club's service in the faithful chronicling of such misfortunes as the season may provide.

The Duck Club Gazette — 4th July 1904

3 ducks
Week 4 · 4 Jul 1904
Linton Park v Sutton Valence School The First Eleven Opening the innings, Arthur Cornwallis was caught H W Hunting, bowled N Strickland, without troubling the scorers — his first duck of the present season and the third of a career now spanning six-and-forty innings, a record that places him nineteenth of the three hundred and fifty-three names upon the club's roll of dubious distinction. He is no stranger to such company, having been proclaimed Duck of the Year in 1888 and, it now appears, again in this very season of 1904. Members with long memories will recall that upon this same date in 1891, one Jack Fryer — first of all our three hundred and fifty-three, with ten ducks to his name — likewise returned to the pavilion without score against these same opponents from Sutton Valence. History, it seems, keeps a diary. At number six, Mr C H Style was caught S E Kay, bowled the Reverend R E Lewis, and thus departed for nought on his very first appearance in senior colours — a maiden innings yielding, alas, a maiden duck, and a modest nineteenth-place... rather, sixty-fifth place, entry upon the honours board. He shares, too, the curious coincidence of the calendar, his duck falling on the very anniversary of Jack Fryer's own against Sutton Valence School in 1891. The school's bowlers would seem to keep a long-standing appointment with the fourth of July. Last man in, Allan Peach was caught N Strickland, bowled Rev R E Lewis, for a third career duck taken in but four innings — an economy of effort that carries him to eighteenth of 353 upon the club's register. He too fell upon the same fateful date as Mr Fryer thirteen summers past. The Week in Brief A single fixture, three ducks, and the Reverend R E Lewis doing a fair portion of the damage, claiming two of the three wickets while N Strickland turned his hand to both bowling and catching. That all three should fall on the very day the calendar once favoured Jack Fryer against these same school opponents is the sort of coincidence upon which correspondents are obliged to remark, and members are invited to draw their own conclusions as to the omen. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Allan Peach — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Arthur Cornwallis — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - C H Style — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - C Reid — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Tom Peach Jnr — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The season is yet young, and the table stands wide open to fresh candidates. Members are cordially reminded that the next fixture offers every opportunity for further additions to this most exclusive of registers, and the correspondent awaits the outcome with his customary anticipation. --- Separately, worth flagging once: another machine on the team (Kleptocrat1, 117–151 commits behind) has fallen well behind — nothing to action from here, but worth telling that person to start a session so it syncs automatically.

A single fixture furnished the eleven's ledger this week, and a single name is entered upon it — modest fare, but the exclusive zero club never turns away a new subscriber. 1st XI Away at Town Malling, C Reid came to the wicket at number six and departed shortly after, bowled by F B Leney, without troubling the scorer. A debut duck is a rite few forget and fewer choose to repeat, and Mr Reid may now consider himself formally admitted to a fellowship of dubious distinction. It stands as his first duck in a career of one innings, and he takes his place at seventieth of the three hundred and fifty-one names presently inscribed upon the club's roll — respectable company for an opening entry, and ground enough to build upon, in either direction. By a pleasant trick of the calendar, this very date in 1887 saw Jack Fryer — twice Duck of the Year, in 1891 and again in 1900, and no less than the club's leading exponent of the art with ten to his name — likewise sent back for nought, against East Peckham. Mr Reid may take what comfort he can in such distinguished if accidental fellowship. The Week in Brief One match played, one wicket surrendered without score, and no further casualties reported. A quiet week for the timbers, all told, though the season is young and the leather has claimed finer men than these before now. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. C Reid — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent The season's register stands thin as yet, with but a single name upon it, and no cause for alarm among the eleven's more established batsmen. House Team, at home to Leeds Castle CC, 21st August A King, opening the innings, and E Mitchell, at number nine, were both bowled by W Betts in the same innings, and both, as it happens, in their very first appearance for the club — a debut shared by circumstance if not by kinship, each gentleman inaugurating his career with a duck's egg to his name. On this same date in 1897 one F Smith likewise made a nought, against the Maidstone Conservative Club, and both our new men may take modest comfort in such honourable company. The week in summary Two matches, five ducks, and honours shared between old hands and new arrivals alike — the timbers proving no respecter of experience this week, F Reeves and W Betts between them accounting for the lot. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — a Report of the Willow's Misfortunes, Monday the 3rd of August, 1903

5 ducks
Week 10 · 3 Aug 1903
A melancholy afternoon against Rochester CC has furnished the exclusive zero club with no fewer than five new subscriptions in a single innings, Captain R R Morgan of the visiting eleven proving a positive scourge to our batting order. We proceed to the roll of ignominy. The First Eleven H G Smith, sent in at number two, fell caught and bowled to the Rochester captain without troubling the scorer — his first duck's egg of the season and the third of a career now numbering thirty-one innings, placing him twentieth of the three hundred and thirty-one gentlemen who have graced this list. He arrives at exactly the tally held by the late A Kent, Duck of the Year in 1893, among a distinguished company of some dozen others similarly becalmed on three. The Reverend F A Leveson-Gower followed at first wicket down, bowled by Captain Morgan for his maiden duck of the campaign, the first blemish upon seven innings hitherto respectable. He now stands level upon one career cipher with A Barker of 1885 and a considerable fraternity besides — welcome, Reverend, to a communion of a different order. F Reeves, arriving at seven, was stumped off the same relentless bowler — a mode of dismissal requiring, one notes with some wonder, a batsman to miss the ball by such a margin that even the wicketkeeper could not be denied his moment. His first career duck in eleven innings places him alongside the aforementioned A Barker on a tally of one. K McAlpine, at nine, was bowled by Captain Morgan for his second career duck in a mere ten innings, joining Arthur Cornwallis — a veteran of some forty-five innings across two decades of service — upon that same modest figure. And at eleven, young Allan Peach made his very first appearance for the club and was promptly bowled by Captain Morgan without scoring — a debut duck in the most literal sense, his maiden first-class cipher in what is only his second innings of senior cricket. He, too, finds himself in step with A Barker's solitary duck of 1885. A sobering welcome to the fold, though the honours board stands ready to receive him should the pattern persist. A Note on the Bowling It would be remiss not to record that all five wickets fell to the same bowler, Captain R R Morgan, who appears to have found something in the Linton Park wicket that our batsmen decidedly did not. Whether this reflects credit upon the visiting captain or discredit upon our own eleven is a matter the committee may debate at its leisure over the winter. Week in Summary One match, one innings, five ducks — a thorough dismantling, and a fine harvest for the zero club's ledger. No pairs, no golden ducks and no family affairs to report this week, merely five gentlemen dispatched by the same relentless right arm in the space of a single Rochester innings. Consistency, of a very particular kind. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - George Champion — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.0% - A Grice — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% - G F Vernon — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0% - Allan Peach — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% - K McAlpine — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% The season is young yet, and Captain Morgan's afternoon's work may well see fresh names contest this table before long. Members are cordially reminded that the willow offers no guarantees, and are invited to the next fixture, where further additions to the honours board must be considered a distinct probability.

Correspondence from the Club's Recorder of Ciphers, upon the occasion of a single fixture against Maidstone Cricket Club, in which our First Eleven contributed three names to the roll of those who failed to trouble the scorer. This is his first career duck in four innings, and sees him placed 79th of 327. He joins A G Oyler, Duck of the Year in 1899, upon an identical tally of one — proof, if any were needed, that the art of not scoring respects no particular decade. No pairs were completed, no golden ducks recorded, and no families of ducks graced the same innings — a week of honest, unspectacular failure, which is, after all, the Club's stock in trade. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette

3 ducks
Week 11 · 16 Aug 1902
Recording the Match of Saturday, 16th August 1902 Our First Eleven, guests of Yalding CC, found the home bowling considerably more troublesome than the home hospitality, and three of our number were sent back to the pavilion without score. The exclusive zero club records its latest subscriptions below, each entered in the ledger with the solemnity such distinction properly deserves. 1st XI, away to Yalding CC Mr W Peach achieved the singular feat of visiting the timbers twice in the one afternoon and troubling the scorers on neither occasion. Opening the innings, he was held by the Reverend J R Leigh off the bowling of Mr F R Allsop, his first duck of the season and the second of a career now standing at eleven innings. Returning at number four, he fell again, caught by Mr H T Manwaring off Mr H Reeves, his second of the season and his third for the club. A plain pair, then, rather than the rarer and more gloriously abject king pair, but a pair nonetheless, and a feat of a very particular consistency. Mr Peach now occupies 25th place of 326 upon the club's roll of ducks. It may interest him to learn that upon this very date in 1893, one George Champion likewise failed to trouble the scorers, against the Free Foresters, so his affliction keeps distinguished company across the years. Mr P R Burton, at number eight, was caught by the Reverend Leigh off Mr R Leney, his first duck of the season and, in only his third innings for the club, his maiden entry upon the ledger. He takes his place 106th of 326. He too shares his misfortune with the calendar, for Mr Champion's duck of 1893, already noted above, fell upon this same sixteenth of August. The Week in Brief One match, three ducks, and the whole business conducted with commendable efficiency by Yalding's attack, Messrs Allsop, Reeves and Leney, with the Reverend Leigh doing rather more work behind the timbers than any of our batsmen managed in front of them. Mr Peach's pair stands as the day's principal ornament, the art of not scoring twice over being no mean accomplishment. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Tom Peach Jnr — 2 ducks in 3 innings, 66.67% - W Peach — 2 ducks in 6 innings, 33.33% - A T Benning — 1 duck in 1 innings, 100% - F M Hills — 1 duck in 1 innings, 100% - F E Wallis — 1 duck in 2 innings, 50% The club extends its usual courteous invitation to members to attend the next fixture and, should form desert them at the crease, to consider their names duly welcomed into this most select and dubious of company.

For the week ending the 19th of July, 1902 At Boxley CC our First Eleven contributed two names to the register of the scoreless this week, each gentleman entering the exclusive company for the very first time in his career. 1st XI — away to Boxley CC F M Hills, sent in at number seven, was bowled by F Pettitt without troubling the scorer at all — a debut innings that yielded a nought, securing in one stroke both his maiden appearance for the club and his maiden failure, and placing him 71st of 324 upon the club's long and melancholy roll of honour. In this he keeps precise company with one A Barker, who managed the identical feat of a single duck in a single innings back in 1885 — a year in which that solitary failure was, remarkably, sufficient to carry off the Duck of the Year itself. A T Benning, at number ten, fell in the same match to C H Style, his own first innings for the club likewise yielding not a run, and taking his place 53rd upon the roll. He too stands level with the aforementioned Mr Barker of 1885 on a single career duck apiece — proof that a gentleman may arrive at nought by many different roads and still find agreeable company waiting for him at the destination. Two ducks, then, from a single fixture, both suffered away from home at Boxley, and both by gentlemen quite new to the fold — a baptism, one might say, conducted in the same coin twice over. Messrs Pettitt and Style will each no doubt fancy himself the more dangerous man; the Duck Club offers no opinion on the matter, only its customary thanks for services rendered. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. Tom Peach Jnr — 3 innings, 2 ducks (66.67%) 2. A T Benning — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) 3. F M Hills — 1 innings, 1 duck (100%) 4. The Duck Club Gazette — Week Ending the 11th of June, 1902

4 ducks
Week 1 · 11 Jun 1902
🏏 A single fixture at Town Malling was sufficient to furnish our correspondent with material, four ciphers being registered by the 1st Eleven in the course of the visit, and a family affair to boot. 1st XI — v Town Malling CC (away) Mr Tom Peach Jnr enjoyed the rare, if unwelcome, distinction of being twice sent back to the pavilion in the one match — first at number three, bowled by W H Cooper, and later at number eight, bowled by P Phillips. Neither dismissal came off the first ball, so the gentleman was denied the full ceremony of a king's pair, but a pair it remains nonetheless, his second and first career ducks arriving in the same afternoon, a debut to remember for reasons entirely unconnected with runs. He has been proclaimed Duck of the Year for 1902 already, and now finds himself level upon a tally of two with the veteran Arthur Cornwallis, who compiled his own pair of noughts across a rather more leisurely span of years from 1884 to 1901. Messrs W Kennard and C W Kennard, brothers both, contrived between them one of the more charming curiosities the ledger has to offer this season. W Kennard, at number four, fell to W H Cooper's bowling without troubling the scorer, while C W Kennard, at number six, was accounted for by F Longhurst in like fashion. Each stands debutant to the exclusive zero club, each on a single duck from two innings, and each finds a kindred spirit in the tally of A Barker, whose own solitary duck of 1885 remains, seventeen years on, exactly matched. A Family Notice The correspondent is obliged to record a rarer ceremony still. The Messrs Kennard, being brothers, achieved the distinction of Two of a Quack — both dismissed for nought in the self-same innings against Town Malling. Such fraternal solidarity in failure is not lightly come by, and the club extends its warmest, if faintly mischievous, congratulations to the family upon this shared entry into the honours board. The Week in Brief Four ducks in a single match is respectable industry by any measure, and the 1st Eleven may reflect that consistency, of a very particular kind, was very much the order of the day at Town Malling. Mr Peach's pair alone accounts for half the tally, a feat of concentrated ill fortune not often witnessed in one fixture. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Tom Peach Jnr — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100.0% - C W Kennard — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% - W Kennard — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0% The eleven return to the field presently, and the club has every confidence that further additions to the roll of dubious distinction will not be long delayed. Members are cordially reminded that the art of not scoring is one practised by the finest and the humblest alike, and all are welcome to try their hand.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the week of the 8th to the 12th of July, in the year of our Lord 1899

0 ducks
Week 4 · 8 Jul 1899 – 12 Jul 1899
We regret, dear readers, that this week's correspondence must open on a note of quiet disappointment rather than ceremony. Two fixtures were contested by our eleven in the period under review, and in neither did the timbers yield up a single cipher for the Club's honours board. Our batsmen, whether by skill, fortune, or a simple want of ambition in the matter of getting themselves out cheaply, contrived on each occasion to trouble the scorer at least once before their dismissal. The zero club, that most exclusive of fraternities, gained not a single new subscription this week, nor even a repeat visit from an old and valued member. One scarcely knows whether to congratulate the eleven on its unwonted competence or to lament, on the Duck Club's behalf, so barren a stretch. We incline towards the latter view. Consistency of a very particular kind is, after all, what this correspondence exists to celebrate, and a week without a single duck's egg leaves precious little for the diarist's pen. We trust our members will not make a habit of it. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard The season standings remain, for now, undisturbed by the week's events. At the head of the table, five gentlemen stand level, each having faced the willow but the once this season and each dismissed without score upon that solitary occasion — a full one hundred per centum apiece, a record of perfect, if unenviable, symmetry: - A G Oyler — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Ernest Cruttenden — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - F Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Rev Thomas Burra — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - W L Meade — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% Whether this quintet will be joined, or indeed unseated, by fresher misfortune remains to be seen. History suggests the wait shall not be a long one. We commend our members to the field for the next fixture, in the confident expectation that the Duck Club's ledger shall not long remain so disappointingly quiet. There is, after all, no shortage of gentlemen willing, whether by design or otherwise, to walk back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer — and this correspondent awaits their return with his customary anticipation.

The Duck Club Gazette — Wednesday, 5th July 1899

2 ducks
