A modest fixture against Brenchley CC yielded but two visits to the exclusive zero club this week, yet each name carries its own quiet distinction. 1st XI — v Brenchley CC (at home) - Mr Ernest Cruttenden, in at number five, was run out before he could trouble the scorer, the fielder responsible being, we are informed, a matter of some uncertainty, though the outcome is not. This is his first duck of the current season and the eighth of a career now spanning forty-two innings, a tally that places him first of all two hundred and eighty-four names upon the club's roll of honour, a distinction he shares with no other gentleman living or departed. He remains besides a name of record upon the Duck of the Year board of 1895. We note that upon this very date in the year 1882, one W Wilson likewise returned to the pavilion without score, against 1st Innings Collier Street CC — history, it would seem, is fond of an anniversary. - Mr A G Oyler, at number seven, was bowled by R E Marchant, similarly without addition to the total. It is his first duck of the season and but the first of his career, in a mere five innings to date, ranking him forty-fourth of two hundred and eighty-four. He is already inscribed upon this year's Duck of the Year board for 1899, a distinction not lightly come by so early in the season. By a curious coincidence of the calendar, the fifth of July 1882 was likewise the date of W Wilson's dismissal for nought — the ledger appears to hold this date in particular esteem. The Week in Summary One fixture, two ducks, both delivered inside the same afternoon at home to Brenchley — a fair return for the bowlers, and a sobering one for our eleven. No pairs, no king pairs, and no family gatherings at the crease this week; the club's rarer ceremonies must await their turn. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - A G Oyler — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Ernest Cruttenden — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - F Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Rev Thomas Burra — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - W L Meade — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A perfect record of imperfection at the head of the table, five gentlemen yet to trouble the scorer this season. The willow awaits its next volunteers, and the club shall follow the coming fixture with its customary keen and cheerful interest.

3 ducks

A modest afternoon's work for the eleven against Sutton Valence School furnished the Club with three fresh entries for the honours board, all falling to the school's bowling within the same innings. He joins Mr C Amies, who turned out for the Club between 1867 and 1870, in sitting upon exactly four career ducks — a fine piece of company across the decades. - W L Meade (No. 7), appearing for the first time in Club colours, was caught by the Reverend R E Lewis off the bowling of J K Blackmore, and thus opened his career's account with a duck's egg — a debut of the most emphatic kind, and one that plants him at once at 108th of 284 in the all-time table. He finds himself level, on a single career duck, with a Mr A Barker, who achieved the same modest distinction in the solitary season of 1885 and was thereupon named Duck of the Year for his trouble. - The Reverend Thomas Burra (No. 9) likewise fell to J K Blackmore, bowled outright, and failed to trouble the scorer for the third time in a career of twelve innings — a showing that holds him at 20th of 284 all time. He stands shoulder to shoulder with Mr A Kent, whose three ducks in the brief season of 1893 earned him that year's Duck of the Year honours. The week in summary Three wickets fell for nought, all in the one fixture, and Mr J K Blackmore of Sutton Valence School may fairly claim the lion's share of the credit, having accounted for two of the three gentlemen himself. A tidy afternoon's work for the school's bowling, and a rather less tidy one for our own batting order — though the Club, ever generous in defeat, records each with due ceremony. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard With the season yet young, our three subscribers arrive level at its summit: - F Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - Rev Thomas Burra — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - W L Meade — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% A perfect record of imperfection, and no doubt one that will not survive the season's further fixtures unaltered. The Club looks forward, as ever, to the next match and whatever fresh additions the willow and the leather may conspire to provide.

🦆 A modest notice to the members of the exclusive zero club 🦆 Well now. We are given to understand our men acquitted themselves with the bat well enough to deny the club its customary tribute. The Duck Club Gazette — a Record of the Match Played the 18th Day of June, 1898

3 ducks
Week 3 · 18 Jun 1898
Our First Eleven took the field against Yalding Cricket Club and returned, as is so often the way of this pursuit, with three names newly entered upon the ledger of nought. The First Eleven Opening the innings, George Champion marched out and was bowled by a delivery the scorer, in his uncertainty, could only record as "Unsure" — a fitting cipher for a ciphered innings. This is the fifth occasion of Mr Champion's career upon which he has failed to trouble the scorer, in eight-and-twenty innings all told, placing him sixth of the two hundred and six-and-seventy names upon the club's roll of dubious distinction, and a holder of the Duck of the Year honour for 1897. He finds fellowship in adversity with F Danells, of the 1881 to 1891 era, who across fifteen innings arrived at the identical total of five — kindred spirits upon nought, separated by near a score of years. Sent in at first wicket down, B W Haynes likewise fell "b Unsure", the bowler's identity lost to the scorebook though his work plain enough. This was Mr Haynes's maiden duck of the present season, and but the first of his career in ten innings, ranking him one-and-fiftieth of the two hundred and six-and-seventy. He now stands level upon a single career duck with A Barker, whose solitary innings of 1885 yielded the very same tally, and who was himself crowned Duck of the Year that season. Batting at number eight, C S Smith was also dismissed "b Unsure" for nought, his second duck of the season and the second of a career yet only four innings old — a rate of failure that places him five-and-twentieth of all who have gone before, and sees him among those who bear the Duck of the Year honour for the present season of 1898. He shares his career tally of two with C French Snr, who achieved the same across three innings between 1860 and 1864, and who likewise once wore that crown, in 1864. A Week in Summary Three ducks were laid in the single fixture played, all at Yalding, and all, curiously, to bowling the scorer declined to name. Whether this speaks of a modest bowler or an unsighted scorer we leave entirely to the reader's judgement. The willow, on this occasion, was thoroughly silenced. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. C S Smith — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.0 per cent 2. A J Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0 per cent 3. C Marsh — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100.0 per cent 4. B W Haynes — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.0 per cent 5. F Smith — 4 innings, 1 duck, 25.0 per cent The club awaits its next fixture with the customary mixture of dread and anticipation, confident the honours board has not yet seen its final entry this season. A quiet week for the chronicler, but not an idle one, for the roll of the exclusive zero club has gained a new name. What lends the occasion its particular interest is that this was Mr Smith's very first innings for the Club. He arrives, then, at the wicket of history in the most direct manner possible, inscribed forthwith as the 44th name of 273 upon the club's roll of those acquainted with nought. A debut duck is ever a matter for ceremony rather than commiseration, and the Club extends its solemn welcome. The correspondent cannot pass over a curious circumstance of the calendar: upon this very day in the year 1887, one Jack Fryer — a gentleman who played from 1881 to 1898, who stands first of all 273 upon the club's roll with eight ducks to his credit, and who was crowned Duck of the Year in 1891 — likewise walked back without score, against the First Innings of East Peckham CC. Whether this be a happy augury for Mr Smith's future upon the willow, or merely the calendar's own dry jest, the correspondent leaves to wiser heads than his. The Week in Summary One match played, one egg laid. A modest return by the Club's usual standards of failure, but a debut duck is worth more column space than a dozen ordinary ones, and Mr Smith's name shall not want for good company upon the honours board in seasons to come. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the week of the 4th to the 6th of June, 1898

3 ducks

Three of our number were sent back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer this week, across two fixtures. The exclusive zero club welcomes its latest subscribers. 1st XI Against Sutton Valence School on the 4th, at home, our innings yielded a most economical pair of dismissals from the same hand. Mr C S Smith, in at number nine, was bowled by H Goodban for a cipher — his very first appearance at the wicket in senior colours, and thus a debut of the most particular sort. The Gazette records him at once upon the Duck of the Year board for 1898, a swift elevation to dubious distinction. He stands 54th of 271 in the club's all-time reckoning. Curiously, on this very date in 1886, one Tom Peach Snr likewise returned for nought against The Mote CC — history, it seems, is fond of an anniversary. Following him at number ten came Mr C Marsh, caught H C Pearson off the same Mr Goodban, and likewise dismissed for a duck's egg on his first outing — Goodban may fairly claim a brace of debutants in one afternoon's work. Mr Marsh takes his place at 52nd of 271. He too finds himself in curious company with Tom Peach Snr's duck of the 4th of June 1886 against The Mote CC, the calendar repeating itself twelve years on almost to the hour. Two days later, away at Brenchley CC, Mr F Smith was bowled by R Larkin at number six for a duck — no stranger to this fate, it being his third career nought in seven innings, and his season's first. He rests handsomely at 17th of 271 on the all-time list, level on three career ducks with Mr A Kent of the class of 1893, himself no less than the Duck of the Year for that season. Kindred spirits in the art of not scoring. The week in brief Two matches, three ducks, and a curious symmetry — Sutton Valence School accounted for two of our men in successive deliveries from Mr Goodban, while Brenchley CC claimed the third at the far end of the week. All three fell to the bowler rather than to any misadventure of their own making, which is, we are assured, some small comfort. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the days 2nd to 4th August, 1897

7 ducks
Week 8 · 2 Aug 1897 – 4 Aug 1897
A fixture against Rochester CC on the 2nd, and a further engagement at Headcorn on the 4th, have furnished the Club with no fewer than seven fresh additions to its roll of dubious distinction. The willow was, on several occasions this week, wielded to no visible purpose whatever. 1st XI Against Rochester, our innings yielded three ciphers in short order. Mr K McAlpine, sent in first wicket down, was smartly taken by H Newsome off X Fellowes for his first duck of the season and the first of his career in five completed innings — 81st of 261 in the club's long roll. On this very day in 1882, one W H Fryer likewise returned a duck's egg, against 1st Innings Boxley CC, a coincidence separated by fifteen years and no improvement in fortune. George Champion followed, bowled by J B Finlayson without scoring, his second duck of the present season and his fourth in a career of three-and-twenty innings — a tally that places him ninth of all who have ever failed to trouble the scorer for the Club, and sufficient, it seems, to have already secured him the Duck of the Year board for 1897. He, too, shares the anniversary with Mr Fryer's 1882 nought. The Reverend Thomas Burra, promoted to bat at nine, was caught by Finlayson off Fellowes for a duck — his second of a career now numbering eleven innings, and the 37th such performer of all time. The reverend gentleman keeps, it might be observed, distinguished company on this same calendar date. At Headcorn on the 4th, the rot continued in earnest. Tom Peach Senior, at number seven, was bowled by E Holland without scoring — his third career duck in seventeen innings, the 21st of all time, and, by pleasant coincidence, a duck struck on this same date in an earlier year of 1869 by one W H Fryer against Horsmonden CC. Mr A Heathfield, appearing for the very first time in club colours, was bowled by W Clinch for a nought on his maiden appearance — a debut duck of the purest and most immediate kind, and one that places him at the modest but respectable rank of 42nd of 261 all-time. R Tree, following at ten, was likewise bowled by Clinch without scoring, his first career duck in a brief innings of two, ranking 92nd of all time. And to close proceedings, R Giles, also making his first appearance for the Club, was bowled by Clinch for nought — a second debutante duck in the very same innings, ranking 88th of all time. Messrs Heathfield, Tree and Giles were all despatched by the same bowler's hand, a fact the correspondent notes without further comment, beyond observing that Mr Clinch appears to have found something in the wicket that our lower order did not. A Word on the Week Two matches, seven ducks — a rate of failure the Club's honours board will record with its customary solemnity rather than alarm. Three wickets fell without score inside a single Headcorn innings, all to the one bowler, which is either misfortune or a want of application, and the correspondent, ever charitable, inclines toward the former. Week 4 · 3 Jul 1897
A single fixture furnished the eleven with but one occasion for the exclusive zero club this week, yet one occasion is all the ceremony requires. The First Eleven Number ten, S Smith, went to the wicket against Sutton Valence School and returned to the pavilion caught F B Thornhill off the bowling of the Reverend J C Wilson, his name entered upon the season's ledger for the first time this year. It is his third duck's egg in nine innings for the club, a record of consistency of a very particular kind that places him eighteenth of two hundred and fifty-two in the club's long roll of the dismissed. In this he now stands shoulder to shoulder with Mr A Kent, whose own three ducks in five innings back in 1893 were sufficient, that season, to carry off the Duck of the Year honour itself — no small society for Mr Smith to find himself keeping. The Week in Summary One match, one wicket surrendered without score, and the leather may fairly be said to have had the better of the willow on this occasion. A modest week for the club's chroniclers, but the timbers are ever patient, and Sutton Valence School will doubtless furnish further opportunity before the season is out. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - S Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent A leaderboard of one is, admittedly, a leaderboard easily led, and we trust the remainder of the eleven will not long permit Mr Smith to stand there unchallenged. The club awaits the next fixture with its customary mixture of dread and anticipation, confident that further ciphers will not long delay themselves.

The Duck Report — 23rd June, 1897

0 ducks
Week 2 · 23 Jun 1897
Gentlemen, a curious week for the annals. Our correspondent must report, with something approaching regret, that the timbers went undisturbed this week — not a single wicket fell to a duck's egg, and the exclusive zero club welcomes no new members from the fixture just played. Whether this speaks to a sudden and uncharacteristic soundness of technique among our batsmen, or whether the bowling on offer was simply not equal to the task of inducing failure, this correspondent cannot say. Triumph through adversity requires, at minimum, some adversity, and none seems to have presented itself at the crease this week. We trust it is merely a lapse, and that our men will return to the art of not scoring in due course. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season standings remain undisturbed by this week's want of material, no returns having been furnished for the present table. The correspondent notes, for the benefit of members anxious about the club's ongoing health, that a quiet week of scoring is no cause for alarm — the ledger merely awaits its next contribution. Members are warmly reminded that the next fixture stands ready to supply what this one so ungenerously withheld, and the committee remains confident that dismissal for a cipher shall return to its rightful place in the club's affections before very long. Until then, we remain, as ever, hopeful.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — Wednesday, the 16th of June, 1897

0 ducks
Week 1 · 16 Jun 1897
A quiet week, gentlemen, and we confess ourselves almost disappointed by it. One fixture was played upon the appointed day, and not a single member of either eleven troubled the scorer with a cipher against his name. The timbers stood, the leather was struck, and — most vexingly for this correspondent — every man who walked to the wicket contrived to leave it having scored. The exclusive zero club, that place of dubious distinction, gained not one new subscriber this week. We are informed the bowling was respectable and the batting sounder still, which is a fine thing for the fixture and a rather barren one for these pages. Even our most reliable friends of the nought appear, this week at least, to have mislaid the knack. The Season's Honours The Duck Hunting Season ledger for 1897 stands, as yet, unopened. No gentleman has claimed a place upon it, and the leaderboard is consequently a blank page awaiting its first entrant. We trust this happy state of affairs — happy for the batsmen, if not for the correspondent — shall not endure a second week running. In Closing We commend the eleven on a match played without ignominy, while noting privately that the art of not scoring is a discipline this club exists to honour, and honour it we shall resume at the very next opportunity. Members are reminded that the timbers care nothing for reputation, and that the next fixture will very likely furnish this Gazette with rather livelier material. Until then, we remain hopeful, watchful, and only a little disappointed. --- One quick note outside the report: a change from the team (skills#27) is waiting in your review queue whenever you'd like to go through it — happy to pull it up on request.

The Duck Club Gazette — the 22nd of August, 1896

4 ducks
Week 16 · 22 Aug 1896
🏏 A modest offering from Maidstone on Saturday, where the visitors' willow proved unequal to the task on four separate occasions. The zero club welcomes its latest subscribers with the usual grave ceremony. 1st XI — dismissed for a cipher against Maidstone CC - S Smith, at four, was caught and bowled by W C Betts — a tidy piece of work by the bowler, and a less tidy one by the batsman. This stands as his second duck of the season and his second in a career of eight innings, placing him thirty-fourth of the two hundred and forty-nine names on our roll of dishonour. He now sits level with C French Snr, whose own pair of ducks was recorded between 1860 and 1864 — kindred spirits across two generations, united by nought. - W Edwards, batting eighth, was taken by wicketkeeper Betts off the bowling of H Waghorn. A second duck of the season for Mr Edwards, and his second in a career still young at but five innings — a promising start to a less promising ledger. He, too, joins the gentlemen sitting on two career ducks, C French Snr among them. - D H Kennard, at ten, was stumped by A Large off W C Betts — undone by a step too far down the wicket. This is his third duck of the season, his third in a career of only four innings, and it earns him fifteenth place of all who have gone before, together with a place on the Duck of the Year 1896 board — an honour he appears determined to defend without challenge. He joins A Kent, whose identical tally of three was compiled in 1893. - R Kennard, last man in, was bowled outright by W C Betts. His second duck of the season and his second in a career of but two innings — a start of remarkable uniformity. He, too, keeps company with C French Snr on the ledger of twos. A family affair — the brothers Kennard, D H and R, both departed without score in the same innings against Maidstone, a rare domestic double the club records with particular satisfaction as a Two of a Quack. Between them they carried the Kennard name to the crease and back again with nothing to show for either journey — one imagines the walk to the pavilion was, at least, companionable. The week in summary — four ducks in a single match, two of them shared by brothers, and W C Betts alone accounting for three of the four dismissals. A bowler in inspired form, and an innings the eleven will be glad to leave behind them. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 15th August 1896

2 ducks
Week 15 · 15 Aug 1896
🏏 A modest bulletin this week, but a noteworthy one for the family concerned. This stands as his second career cipher in but three innings, placing him twentieth of the two hundred and forty-nine gentlemen who have graced this particular register. Curiously, on this very day five years since, one R Norton likewise returned to the pavilion without troubling the scorer, against the Eton Ramblers — a coincidence of the calendar we are pleased to record. Hard upon his heels came Mr R Kennard at number ten, held by W French off the same F Gilbert, and similarly dismissed for nought. This being his maiden first-class innings, we are obliged to note it as his debut — an inauspicious one, though he joins the club in good and populous company. His name now stands at the eighty-third position of all-time ignominy, itself a curious echo of Mr Norton's own standing at eighty-fourth, and, as with his brother, this day in 1891 saw an identical fate befall the aforementioned Norton against the selfsame Ramblers. We should be remiss not to observe that Mr D H Kennard and Mr R Kennard are brothers, and their twin failures this day at Westborough constitute what the club records as Two of a Quack — a shared and simultaneous descent into scorelessness that we are pleased to solemnise. It is not every week that one family may boast two ducks laid in the same afternoon, and the Kennard household has this day secured that dubious distinction with room to spare. The Week in Summary A single fixture yielded two ducks, both from the same family, both from the same bowler's spell — Mr Gilbert may take some private satisfaction in a family double, though we shall not encourage him further. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — the 3rd of August, 1896

0 ducks
Week 13 · 3 Aug 1896
It is with a curious mixture of relief and disappointment that your correspondent must report a want of material this week. The eleven took to the field, the willow was wielded, the leather was bowled with every customary vigour — and yet not a single cipher was recorded against any name. The exclusive zero club, so often swollen by the misfortunes of our batsmen, gained not one new member this week past. One scarcely knows whether to offer congratulation or condolence. A week without a duck is, for the club proper, a week without incident, and the honours boards must remain, for the present, undisturbed. Whether this reflects a sudden and alarming outbreak of competence at the crease, or merely the leather's own want of application, this correspondent shall not speculate. The art of not scoring is, after all, a discipline requiring constant practice, and even our most devoted exponents cannot be expected to maintain their standards in every match. We are assured, however, that the season is young yet, and that the ducks, though they evaded the net this week, are unlikely to remain at liberty for long. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard, 1896 - Ernest Cruttenden — 6 innings, 2 ducks, a return of 33.33 per cent, and thus the season's most industrious contributor to the club's cause - H W Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, a perfect century of failure at 100 per cent, and a start to the season that could scarcely be more emphatic - W Edwards — 1 innings, 1 duck, likewise perfect in his ignominy, and welcomed accordingly - X Gilbert — 1 innings, 1 duck, a third gentleman to open his season's account at the first time of asking - A L Woodhouse — 2 innings, 1 duck, a return of 50 per cent, and evidence that the timbers found him out soon enough Mr Cruttenden remains the season's leading light, if light be the word for so dim an achievement, and the club watches his continued progress with an interest bordering on the proprietorial. Members are respectfully reminded that the next fixture is expected to furnish the usual crop of candidates, and the correspondent awaits, with his customary patience, the opportunity to record their names in due course. Until then, the eleven may enjoy this brief and no doubt temporary reprieve from the scorer's cruellest entry.

The Duck Club Gazette — Headcorn CC, 29th July 1896

5 ducks
Week 12 · 29 Jul 1896
A single fixture furnished the Club with five ducks apiece worthy of the honours board, Headcorn's bowlers proving uncommonly parsimonious throughout. 1st XI Ernest Cruttenden did Headcorn the signal courtesy of failing to trouble the scorer twice in the one afternoon. In the first innings he was taken by F Norris off the bowling of the Reverend A C Scott, his fifth career duck in five and twenty innings, and a sitting Duck of the Year for 1895. He shares that exact tally with F Danells, who retired upon it between 1881 and 1891. Sent in again in the second innings, Mr Cruttenden fell lbw to G Knight for his sixth, drawing level with W H Fryer of the 1867-85 vintage, and so completed what the Club terms simply a pair — twice dismissed without score in a single match, a feat demanding rather more application than it might appear. He remains third of all who have ever taken guard for this purpose, out of two hundred and forty-seven. S Smith, at number ten, was held by F E Foreman off G Knight for nought, his first duck in a modest six innings to date. He joins a long and honourable company sitting on the same single duck, among them A Barker, who managed the identical feat in 1885 and was that year's Duck of the Year. H L Andrews, appearing in the eleven for the first time, was bowled by the Reverend A C Scott without troubling the scorer — as warm a welcome to senior cricket as the Club knows how to extend. He too keeps company with A Barker's tally of one, though with his career scarcely begun he may yet better it, for good or ill. D H Kennard, at nine, was bowled by G Knight for a duck on his earliest outing for the Club, and finds himself already proclaimed Duck of the Year for 1896 — an honour arriving rather sooner in the season than he can have hoped for. He stands alongside Messrs Smith and Andrews on a single career duck, level with A Barker's mark of 1885. The afternoon's bowling honours belong chiefly to Headcorn: Mr G Knight accounted for three of the five ciphers and the Reverend A C Scott for the remaining two, a display of the willow's opposite number at its most eloquent. One match, five ducks, and the Reverend proving that the cloth is no bar to menace with the ball. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - Ernest Cruttenden — 5 innings, 2 ducks, 40.0% - H W Smith — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - W Edwards — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - X Gilbert — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - A L Woodhouse — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The Club extends its condolences to those named above and its quiet confidence that the coming fixture shall furnish further candidates for these pages. Recording the 21st and 22nd of July, in the year of grace 1896 To the members of the club it falls once more to your correspondent to record, with the customary mixture of solemnity and quiet amusement, those gentlemen of the First Eleven who this week joined the exclusive zero club — a place of dubious distinction to which admission is granted, entirely without ceremony, the moment the timbers are disturbed before a run is troubled from the scorer. The First Eleven - Mr H W Smith, promoted to number nine against the Royal West Kent Regiment CC on the 21st, was bowled by Captain G Marshall and returned to the pavilion for a duck's egg on his very first appearance at the wicket for the club. In this he now stands level with one Mr A Barker, whose own single duck, recorded as long ago as 1885 and sufficient that year to carry off the Duck of the Year itself, shows that a solitary nought may yet be a distinguished one. - Mr W Edwards, at number seven in the home fixture against Maidstone CC on the 22nd, was smartly caught by Mr H Waghorn off the bowling of Mr A Large, and departed without registering a run. This is his first cipher of the current season, though by no means his first acquaintance with the art of not scoring, his career tally now standing at one from four completed innings, and placing him 92nd of 243 upon the roll. Members of a historical bent may care to note that upon this very date in 1887, Mr C Pocock likewise walked back for nought, on that occasion against The Mote CC — the calendar, it seems, has its own sense of humour. The Week in Summary Two fixtures, two ducks, and the ignominy shared with commendable fairness between number seven and number nine. No gentleman troubled the wicket twice this week, and no families were embarrassed in company, so the roll of shame remains, for once, a modest one. LPCC Duck Club Gazette — the 10th day of August, 1895

3 ducks

A single fixture at Maidstone brought the eleven three additions to the club's roll of the dismissed, the exclusive zero club welcoming two new subscribers to go with one old and familiar face. The 1st Eleven J Lampard, at number five, was bowled by H Waghorn after giving the bowling due consideration, only for the timbers to be disturbed all the same. It is his season's first cipher and his first in a senior career now numbering four innings, placing him sixty-sixth of two hundred and twenty-five in the club's honours roll of the dismissed — respectable company, if not company one seeks out. A debut duck is a bold beginning, and Mr Kenward may console himself that he has, at a stroke, secured his place forty-fourth of two hundred and twenty-five on the all-time list without troubling the bowlers in the slightest. He, too, finds himself in step with Mr Richards's exploit of 1891. F Smith, following at number seven, likewise fell to H Waghorn — the same bowler claiming his second victim of the innings — on his own first appearance for the club. Two debutants, two ciphers, one bowler enjoying rather more success than either newcomer would have wished. Mr Smith rests fifty-third of two hundred and twenty-five, and shares, as did his colleagues, the distinction of the tenth of August's historical partiality to nought. The week in summary One match, three ducks, the whole of the misfortune falling upon the 1st Eleven at Maidstone. Of note, two of the three dismissed were making their maiden appearance in club colours, and H Waghorn's bowling accounted for fully two of the three — a fine afternoon's work for Maidstone, and rather a chastening one for the eleven. 1893 Season 2 reports

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — for the day's play of 28th August, 1893, versus The Mote CC

3 ducks
Week 3 · 28 Aug 1893
A modest but by no means unworthy showing for the club's exclusive society this week, our men contributing three additions to the roll of dubious distinction in the single fixture played. 1st XI Mr W W Tarrance, promoted to the number four position, was undone caught by F G Stenning off the bowling of A J Thornton — a debut innings, and thus his maiden entry upon the ledger, first of the season and first of a career now standing at one, placing him 85th of 214 in the club's long and melancholy roll. He joins good company on that particular figure: A Barker of the 1885 season, whose solitary duck earned him the Duck of the Year honour that summer, sits level with him at one apiece. At number ten, Mr C A Whittaker fell leg-before to the same indefatigable Mr Thornton, without troubling the scorer. This too was his first appearance upon the club's honours board, his maiden duck in only his second innings for the eleven — an inauspicious beginning, though he keeps distinguished company at one career duck, level again with Mr A Barker of 1885. Mr H Waghorn, at first wicket down, was caught and bowled by the same Mr Thornton, whose afternoon's work read like a benefit performance for the Duck Club. This was no debut mishap but the second nought of an established career now numbering five innings, placing him 26th of the all-time list. He draws level on two career ducks with Mr C French Senior, whose own pair between 1860 and 1864 earned him the Duck of the Year in the latter season. One is bound to observe that Mr A J Thornton, of The Mote CC, appears to have enjoyed a thoroughly satisfactory afternoon at our expense, accounting for all three dismissals himself — a hat-trick of sorts, though not one this correspondent is obliged to celebrate. The Week in Summary Three ducks in the single match played, all falling to one visiting bowler, and all from the 1st XI. No pairs, no golden ducks, and no family ceremonies to report this week — merely three gentlemen returning to the pavilion in steady, unspectacular succession. A quiet week for the club by its own exacting standards, though the timbers and the scorebook alike bore witness to the visitors' evident command of the conditions. The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 14th to 18th August, 1893

10 ducks
Week 1 · 14 Aug 1893 – 18 Aug 1893
A full week of misfortune with the willow: three fixtures played, and no fewer than ten ciphers entered upon the club's rolls. The exclusive zero club welcomes its usual mixture of new arrivals and seasoned campaigners. 1st XI Against the Royal Engineers CC on the 14th, the innings unravelled handsomely for our men. A Kent, introducing himself to first-team cricket, was twice sent back to the pavilion without score — bowled by Captain Hamilton, then caught and bowled by A J Woodroffe — a pair on his very arrival that few gentlemen would wish upon themselves. H Waghorn followed at number seven, bowled by A J Woodroffe on his own first outing, and takes his place beside the estimable A Barker of 1885 on a solitary career blemish, 57th of 206 on the club's all-time roll. Further down, Jack Fryer, stumped off Corporal Bayfield in a manner suggesting the willow was scarcely required, recorded the seventh cipher of a career now level with the redoubtable A Startup of the 1870s and 80s — Fryer remains top of the all-time table, 1st of 206, and a past holder of the Duck of the Year honour in 1891. F S W Cornwallis, last man in, fell to Corporal Bayfield for his fourth career duck, keeping distinguished company with C Amies of the 1860s, and stands 7th of 206. Two days later, against the Free Foresters CC, George Champion contrived to be dismissed twice for nought in the one encounter — bowled, then caught by G W Ricketts, both off the bowling of W E W Collins — a grim pair to open his season's account, drawing him level with C French Senior of the 1860s on two career ciphers, 24th of 206. Major Rawson, at number eight, also fell to Collins without troubling the scorer, his maiden duck for the eleven, and joins A Barker's modest company on one, 67th of 206. The Eton Ramblers CC, on the 18th, completed the week's misery. Jack Fryer was bowled by C Heseltine for his second duck of the period and eighth of an ever-lengthening career. A Kent, closing out a week entirely his own, was likewise bowled by Heseltine for a third duck in five short days, drawing level with A Tapsfield of the early 1880s — Kent now stands 12th of 206, and already occupies a place upon this year's Duck of the Year board for 1893. In summary Ten ducks across three matches is a rate of failure the eleven will not care to repeat, though the honours boards are rather better furnished for it. A Kent's three ciphers make him the week's undisputed champion of adversity, with George Champion's pair in a single match running him a close second. 4 ducks

This stands as his third career duck in two-and-twenty innings, placing him twelfth of the two hundred and one names on our roll of honour — a tally shared exactly by A Tapsfield of the 1881 vintage, among a distinguished company of fellow sufferers. At number four, G Knight fell to the bowling of T Carr, his solitary duck of the season and the first of his career in five innings — forty-first of the two hundred and one, and drawing level on a single career cipher with the late A Barker, that gentleman's name forever bound to Duck of the Year 1885. Number seven brought G D Hale to the wicket and swiftly away again, caught by Captain Stratford off X Brooker — his first career duck in a brief three-innings apprenticeship, keeping him level with Mr Knight on a solitary nought apiece, forty-ninth upon the roll. And at number eight, F King made his first appearance for the club and, alas, his first acquaintance with the duck's egg in the same afternoon, bowled by T Carr without scoring. The week in summary One match, four ducks, and Town Malling's bowlers — Messrs Carr and Brooker chief among them — evidently in fine and unforgiving form. A tidy illustration that the art of not scoring remains, as ever, within reach of veteran and newcomer alike. The Zero Club Gazette — Tuesday, 8th to Friday, 12th August, 1892

3 ducks
Week 1 · 8 Aug 1892 – 12 Aug 1892
Three visits to the pavilion without troubling the scorer are recorded this week, the whole sorry business confined, as it happens, to the First Eleven. The exclusive zero club welcomes its latest subscribers below. The First Eleven Mr Jack Fryer opened proceedings on the 8th, at home to the Royal Engineers CC, going the way of all willow-wielders at the hands of Mr F G Guggisberg, bowled without addition to the total from the number six position. This is his season's first cipher and his sixth in a career of nineteen innings, a record of consistency that secures him second place of 197 in the club's roll of honour, and he may reflect, with whatever comfort the fact affords, that he was named Duck of the Year for 1891. He finds himself level, on exactly six career ducks, with a Mr W H Fryer, who plied his trade for the club between 1867 and 1885 — a namesake, so far as the records show, rather than a relation, though the coincidence of surname is a pleasing one for the historian. The Eton Ramblers CC proved a most obliging visitor on the 12th, claiming two of our men in the same fixture. Captain Bowles, sent in first, was bowled by Mr C Heseltine without scoring — a maiden innings and a maiden duck together, the gentleman's very first appearance for the club yielding nothing but a cipher, and thereby securing him the Duck of the Year honour for the present season of 1892 at the first attempt. It is recorded that on this very day in 1867, a Mr G a K Simpson likewise returned to the pavilion for nought, against the 1st Innings of Leeds Park CC — history, it seems, is fond of an anniversary. Batting at seven in the same innings, Mr S Christopherson was bowled by Mr G J Foljambe for nought, his first duck of the season and the first of his career, in a modest eight innings to date, placing him 67th of 197 in the club's long ledger of the dismissed. He shares his parallel with the same Mr Simpson of 1867, who made his own duck on this date against Leeds Park CC — a distinguished, if unwitting, anniversary companion. The Week in Summary Three matches, three ducks, and two of our batsmen despatched in a single afternoon by the Eton Ramblers — a fixture that shall not soon be forgotten by those concerned. No pairs, no families of ducks, and no king's ransom of ignominy this week, merely the steady, dependable arithmetic of nought. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - Captain Bowles — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100 per cent - Jack Fryer — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50 per cent - S Christopherson — 3 innings, 1 duck, 33.33 per cent The season is young and the willow treacherous. The Duck Club Gazette

3 ducks

A Chronicle of the Willow's Misfortunes, 10th to 12th August, 1891 To the members of the Club is offered this week's modest harvest — three eggs laid across two fixtures, the eleven having found the art of not scoring practised with its customary devotion. The First Eleven - Mr L M Richards, going in at number nine against the Royal Engineers CC on the 10th, was bowled by Captain Rice without addition to the total. This is his first cipher of the present season and the second of a career now numbering seven innings, placing him 28th of 186 in the Club's roll of dishonour. In this he keeps close company with Mr C French Snr, whose own two career ducks — struck between 1860 and 1864, and crowned that latter year with the Duck of the Year itself — stand at exactly the same figure. A worthy fellowship, separated by some thirty years and not one run. - Mr L Friend, opening the innings against the Free Foresters CC on the 12th, was taken by the bowler's own hand off his own bowling, Mr J A Turner accounting for him before the scorers had troubled themselves to sharpen their pencils. It is his second career duck in seven innings, and he stands 27th of 186. Curiously, this very date in the calendar has form: on the 12th of August 1867, one G a K Simpson likewise departed for nought, against Leeds Park CC — history, it seems, keeps a diary. - Mr R H Pemberton followed him to the crease at number seven that same afternoon, and was undone by the identical Mr Turner, bowled without scoring. It is his maiden duck of the campaign and his first in a career of seven innings, ranking him 62nd of 186. He shares Mr Friend's curious anniversary, for the same Mr Simpson's duck of the 12th of August 1867 stands as his parallel also — a fine thing, to be accompanied into ignominy by one's own teammate and a gentleman three decades departed alike. It will not escape the attentive reader that Mr Turner of the Free Foresters enjoyed a most productive afternoon's bowling, accounting for both home ducks inside the same innings — a spell our batsmen will not care to recall, nor Mr Turner soon forget. The Week in Summary Three ducks were laid across two matches, all by the First Eleven, and none golden — each gentleman troubled the bowling for at least one delivery before his dismissal, which is, we are assured, some small comfort. The Royal Engineers and the Free Foresters may both congratulate their bowling attacks on a satisfactory afternoon's work. The Duck Report — Linton Park CC, 27th June 1891

4 ducks
Week 1 · 27 Jun 1891
A modest fixture against Hunton CC on Saturday last has furnished the club's zero register with a fresh quartet of entries, our first eleven contributing the whole of the day's misfortune between them. 1st XI at Hunton CC (away) - F Danells, in at first wicket down, was stumped by the watchful Dr Smart off the bowling of J Foord, and returns to the pavilion for his first duck's egg of the season — his fifth in a career of fifteen innings, placing him third of the club's one hundred and seventy-six honorands. He now sits level upon five with W Goad, whose own accumulation was gathered between 1864 and 1872 — kindred spirits in the art of not scoring, separated by some twenty-seven years but united upon the same solemn total. - Jack Fryer, at first drop, fell caught by H Hubble off the same J Foord — evidently a bowler in fine and unwelcome form — for his first duck of the current season and the fourth of an already distinguished career spanning sixteen innings. He is, be it noted, the reigning holder of the Duck of the Year honour for 1891 itself, a title he may consider well and truly defended by this latest contribution. He draws level upon four with several distinguished names of seasons past, among them J Sedgwick of 1881 and W White of 1869, each themselves former Ducks of the Year. - S Ruck, promoted to the crease at number seven, was bowled by T Hards without troubling the scorer, and does so upon the very occasion of his debut for the club — a duck's egg to mark his arrival, which places him sixty-fourth of one hundred and seventy-six on the all-time roll. He shares his solitary tally with a great many who began thus, among them A Barker of 1885. - H Graves, at number nine, was likewise bowled, by W Galpin, for a duck upon his own first appearance in club colours — a debut shared in ignominy with his colleague Ruck, the pair entering the honours board together. He too stands upon one, in fellowship with A Barker and the long roll of those whose careers began at nought. The Week in Summary Four wickets fell for nought in the single fixture played, the whole harvest gathered by Hunton's bowlers Foord, Hards and Galpin between them — Foord accounting for two of the four, a performance the visiting batting card will not remember fondly. Two debutants and two established campaigners shared the day's disappointments in equal measure, a fair distribution of misfortune by any reckoning. A quiet week at the wicket, gentle readers. The Duck Club's committee records this with a measure of relief tempered by mild disappointment — for it is, after all, in the art of not scoring that our members find their truest glory, and a week without a nought is a week the honours board must go without fresh laurels. We are assured the ducks have merely gone to ground, and not retired from the field altogether. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season standings are, alas, not to hand this week — no returns have been lodged. The committee trusts the usual suspects remain in good and scoreless health, and will publish the table the moment the figures are recovered from the pavilion ledger. A quiet week, then, but the season is young yet, and Linton Park's willows have shown before that a duck's egg is never more than one indiscreet stroke away. Members are cordially reminded that the next fixture offers every opportunity for redemption, or its opposite, and the committee awaits the results with its customary keen and slightly mischievous interest. Until then, we remain, as ever, watchful for the cipher.

Week 10 · 31 Jul 1886
A single fixture was played this week, and it is with a measure of mixed feeling that your correspondent reports the timbers were spared their usual visitors. Not a single member of the eleven was sent back to the pavilion for a cipher — the ducks, it seems, evaded capture entirely on this occasion. Whether this speaks to a sudden and uncharacteristic soundness of technique, or merely to the ball declining to find the edge, this correspondent shall not speculate. The exclusive zero club held no induction ceremony this week, and its roll of dubious distinction remains, for now, unchanged. Members may take what comfort they can in a fixture passed without ignominy, though old hands will know such quiet spells rarely last. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - J F Cornish — 2 innings, 2 ducks, a scarcely believable 100%. A gentleman apparently unable to trouble the scorer at all this season. - F S W Cornwallis — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50%. Consistency, of a very particular kind. - A M Streatfield — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50%. - Hon J B Brownlow — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50%. A creditable showing for a gentleman of rank, in the art of not scoring. - Tom Peach Snr — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50%. The season's honours board stands ready to receive fresh entrants, and your correspondent has little doubt it shall not wait long. Members are cordially reminded that the willow shows no mercy, and the next fixture will surely furnish the Gazette with rather livelier material. Until then, the club rests, somewhat unusually, without a fresh duck's egg to its name.

The LPCC Duck Gazette — the Match of Wednesday, the 14th of July, 1886

2 ducks
Week 7 · 14 Jul 1886
A modest fixture at The Mote CC yielded, as these things will, two additions to the Club's roll of honour — that most exclusive of fraternities reserved for gentlemen who faced the bowling and had nothing whatsoever to show for it. House Team Mr L Friend, sent in first wicket down, was bowled by K McAlpine and returned to the pavilion for a duck's egg — not, it should be recorded, upon the very first delivery, so he may claim to have inspected the bowling before declining to trouble the scorer. It is his first duck of the season and, in but his third innings for the Club, the first of his career, placing him 52nd of 151 in the club's long and undistinguished ledger. He now sits level, at one duck apiece, with Mr A Barker, who was crowned Duck of the Year in 1885 on the strength of a single such visitation — an honour Mr Friend may in time aspire to, or, one hopes, avoid. Batting at number nine, the Reverend Thomas Burra was bowled by A J Thornton and likewise dismissed for nought — his first duck of the campaign and, remarkably, the first of a three-innings career, which places him 58th of 151 upon the all-time list. He too joins the fellowship of Mr A Barker's single duck, a reminder that the cloth offers no especial protection against the leather. The week in summary A single match, a single fixture lost to the willow, and two ducks laid — both, curiously, maiden ducks in the career sense if not the cricketing one, each gentleman's first. The Mote CC's bowlers, Messrs McAlpine and Thornton, may consider their afternoon's work satisfactorily concluded. Duck Hunting Season leaderboard - J F Cornish — 2 innings, 2 ducks, a faultless 100% - F S W Cornwallis — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67% - A M Streatfield — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - Hon J B Brownlow — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - Tom Peach Snr — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The season's leading exponents of the art of not scoring remain in fine fettle, and the Club awaits the next fixture with its customary mixture of dread and anticipation. Members are cordially reminded that the timbers care nothing for reputation, and that the pavilion door swings open for gentleman and cleric alike.

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 3rd and 4th June, 1886

7 ducks
Week 1 · 3 Jun 1886 – 4 Jun 1886
A brisk fixture against The Mote CC on the 4th has furnished the exclusive zero club with no fewer than seven fresh entries, our men finding the art of not scoring rather more congenial than the art of scoring. Let the ledger speak. House Team Batting at seven, Tom Peach Snr was run out without addition, his end unsure but his cipher perfectly certain — a 1st season duck, and his 2nd of a modest career spanning five innings, placing him 27th of 145 in the club's grim roll of honour. He now sits level with C French Snr, that veteran of 1860 to 1864 and Duck of the Year 1864, on an identical career tally of two. F S W Cornwallis, at nine, was first bowled by A J Thornton for nought, and — the innings evidently agreeing with him — returned later in the day to be caught by K McAlpine off the same bowler, again without troubling the scorer. A pair, gentlemen, the grim double so beloved of this establishment, taking him from his 1st to his 2nd season duck in a single afternoon, and to 2 career ducks in four innings, 20th of 145. He joins the estimable C French Snr on that same tally of two. J F Cornish, opening his career at number ten, was leg before to A Hearne for a cipher on his very first appearance at the wicket — a true debutante duck to mark his arrival. Not content with one, he returned to be bowled by A J Thornton for a second, completing his own pair and, being brand new to these pages, arriving already a Duck of the Year 1886 nominee with 2 career ducks from just 2 innings, 24th of 145 — level company indeed with C French Snr on two. A M Streatfield, at four, was run out for a duck, his end likewise unsure. His 1st season duck stands as his 1st career duck from four innings, 30th of 145, drawing level with A Barker, Duck of the Year 1885, on a tally of one. The Hon J B Brownlow, at six and also new to the fixture list, was caught by A Hearne off F M Atkins without scoring — his maiden innings and, fittingly, his maiden duck. His 1st season and 1st career duck from two innings places him 45th of 145, keeping A Barker company on a tally of one apiece. The Week in Brief Seven ducks from two matches, every one of them furnished by the House Team against The Mote CC, and two gentlemen — Cornwallis and Cornish — managing the singular feat of a pair apiece in the same fixture, proof that lightning may strike twice in an afternoon, though never, mercifully, first ball. A fixture to be filed under triumph through adversity, if adversity may be said to triumph twice. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - F S W Cornwallis — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - J F Cornish — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - A M Streatfield — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - Hon J B Brownlow — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - Tom Peach Snr — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The season stands young and the willow has spoken plainly this week. Members are cordially invited to the next fixture, where the timbers will doubtless be rattled afresh and further names added to this most dubious of distinctions. --- One other matter, unrelated to the willow: two machines on the team have fallen behind the shared skills and prompts — one well over a hundred commits adrift — so it may be worth a word to whoever owns them to start a session and let it pull automatically.

1885 Season 2 reports

The Duck Club Gazette

3 ducks
Week 8 · 12 Aug 1885
A Chronicle of Ciphers — the 12th of August, 1885 Intelligence reaches us of a single fixture played against Hunton CC, in which our First Eleven's willow-wielders contributed no fewer than three additions to the exclusive zero club. A day, in short, in which the art of not scoring was practised with some diligence. 1st XI, away to Hunton CC Mr A Barker opened proceedings at the wicket, only to be run out — the identity of the fielder responsible left, we are told, unrecorded, which is perhaps the kindest mercy the innings afforded him. It marks his very first appearance in senior colours, and what an overture: a maiden innings closed at nought, his name entered at 26th of 137 in the club's roll of dubious distinction. The season bearing his own birth year, 1885, his effort stands credited toward this year's Duck of the Year honours, a race very much open. We note, with the solemnity such coincidences demand, that on this very day in 1867 Mr G a K Simpson likewise departed for a duck's egg, against Leeds Park CC. At number eight, Mr X Latter fared no better, caught by W Crump off the bowling of W Hodges without troubling the scorer. Like Mr Barker, this was his debut innings — a baptism of ciphers, if ever one was witnessed — and he takes his place at 65th of 137 on the all-time list. He too shares his misfortune with the calendar, Mr Simpson's duck of the 12th of August 1867 standing as company for him also. Then, at number nine, came Mr F Danells, no stranger to these proceedings, caught by W Best off the bowling of W Crump. This being his fourth career duck in but fourteen innings, he climbs to a lofty fifth of 137 on the club's all-time register — a veteran, one might fairly say, of the noble failure. His name too falls under the shadow of that same August afternoon in 1867 when Mr Simpson made his own contribution to the calendar of ciphers. The Week in Summary Three ducks from a single fixture is no mean haul, and that two belong to gentlemen quite new to the fold suggests Hunton CC's bowling gave our newer men rather more to consider than they might have wished. Mr Danells, for his part, continues to demonstrate a consistency of a very particular kind. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - A Barker — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - F Danells — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - X Latter — 1 innings, 1 duck, 100% - F J Barmby — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - F J Richardson — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% We commend all five gentlemen to the club's continued attention, and await, with our customary mixture of dread and delight, whatever further ciphers the next fixture may add to the register.

A Chronicle of Ciphers — Linton Park Cricket Club, week ending the 26th of June, 1885

5 ducks
Week 1 · 26 Jun 1885
Our fixture against The Mote CC on the 26th proved a fertile afternoon for the ledger of nought, five of our men returning to the pavilion without ever troubling the scorer. The House Eleven F J Barmby, in at four, fell to a catch by G Marsham off the bowling of A Hearne, his maiden entry in the club's books of failure. By curious chance the almanack records that this very date in 1872 also claimed E Skinner for a cipher in the first innings against Sutton Valence CC. Tom Peach Snr, following at five, was run out, the fielder responsible going unrecorded by our scorer, a fate perhaps crueller than dismissal by skill, for it leaves no bowling figures to console him. The date, as before, carries its history, E Skinner having met an identical fate in 1872. N T Nickolls, at seven, was bowled by L E Bligh, his stumps rearranged in a manner permitting no appeal. The 26th of June continues its long acquaintance with the duck's egg, E Skinner having set the precedent some thirteen years before. F J Richardson, at nine, was taken by G Marsham off L E Bligh, Marsham's second catch of the innings and a tidy one by all accounts. Once more the calendar obliges with company from 1872, when E Skinner suffered likewise. O M Leigh, last man in, was caught by the Hon V Parnell off A Hearne, completing the quintet of ciphers for the innings. That this same date in 1872 should furnish a fifth precedent, in the person of E Skinner once again, is a coincidence the club's historians will doubtless wish to note down. In summary A single fixture yielded five ducks, a testament to the home bowling of A Hearne and L E Bligh, who claimed two apiece, and to G Marsham's safe hands, taken twice. All five gentlemen record their first duck of a young season, and indeed the first entered against their names in the club's proper books, each having but one prior innings behind him. The Season's Ledger of Ciphers At this early hour of the season all five ciphered gentlemen stand level at the head of affairs, each with one duck from two innings, a rate of fifty per centum apiece: F J Barmby, F J Richardson, N T Nickolls, O M Leigh and Tom Peach Snr. The next fixture awaits, and with it, no doubt, fresh candidates for this most select and unenviable of confraternities. Members are cordially invited to attend, willow in hand, and try their fortune against the leather.

1884 Season 1 report

The Duck Report — 16th July 1884

0 ducks
Week 1 · 16 Jul 1884
A quiet week at the crease, if quiet is the word for an absence of the very thing this correspondent exists to record. No Ducks to Report Our sole fixture of the period passed off, remarkably, without a single member of either eleven troubling the pavilion gate before troubling the scorer. Not a cipher, not a duck's egg, not so much as a nervous single dot ball worth remarking upon — the willow, on this occasion, was wielded with a wholly uncharacteristic competence. The Duck Club's honours boards remain, for one week only, unvisited. Whether this reflects a sudden and alarming improvement in the batting generally, or merely that the bowling was not quite equal to the task, the correspondent declines to speculate. We trust it is a passing aberration, and that our eleven will return to their more familiar habits before the season is much older. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season's honours board stands untroubled this week and, the records showing nothing further to hand, must rest as it was. Watchers of the ledger are invited to consult it at the next occasion of note. A gentle word to our batsmen: complacency of this sort cannot be allowed to stand. The Club looks forward, with its usual mixture of dread and delight, to the next fixture furnishing rather more material for these columns.

1883 Season 1 report

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — 18th July, 1883

5 ducks
Week 1 · 18 Jul 1883
A single fixture graced our books this week, the eleven at home to the Maidstone Junior Liberal Association, and the exclusive zero club welcomed five new entries into its ledger of dubious distinction. Two completed innings were played in the day, and one of our number contrived to visit the pavilion twice before tea. 1st XI - W Wilson, sent in first to face the bowling, was undone lbw to A E Hickmott without troubling the scorer. His fourth duck in eighteen innings of a career, which places him eighth of all our 120 honoured members. He draws level, curiously enough, with C Amies, who compiled his own four ciphers between 1867 and 1870 in a mere nine innings, and now finds a companion in adversity across the years. - B Small, appearing for the club for the first time, was caught by F Wallis off Hickmott for a maiden duck, a debut of the quieter sort. He enters at 27th of 120, and stands upon the very same mark as A R Simpson of 1881 to 1882, a fellowship of one apiece. - J Danells achieved the rarer distinction of a pair upon his very first appearance for the club, batting at number ten in both innings. First he was taken by R T Nicholson off F Wallis, then, evidently unconvinced by the merits of a second attempt, bowled outright by A E Hickmott. Two ducks in an afternoon and two in a fledgling career, a beginning of the most emphatic kind, and one that earns him a place already among the season's foremost, being a name entered upon the Duck of the Year board for 1883. He now shares his tally with C French Snr, whose own pair of ciphers were gathered between 1860 and 1864, a member of the 1864 Duck of the Year board himself. - F Simmons, last man in, was bowled by F Knight for a debut duck of his own, entering the roll at 33rd of 120, and keeping A R Simpson company at one apiece alongside Master Small. A tidy afternoon's work for the opposing bowlers, then, five ciphers from one match, all confined to the 1st XI, and the singular curiosity of a young debutant contriving to fail twice before luncheon was properly digested. The art of not scoring, it seems, was practised with uncommon thoroughness this week. The Season's Duck-Hunting Ledger - J Danells — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100% - B Small — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - F Simmons — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - W Wilson — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The committee trusts the eleven will contrive fresh entries at the earliest opportunity, and looks forward to greeting the next fixture's arrivals into this most select and inglorious of fellowships.

1882 Season 5 reports

The LPCC Duck Club Gazette — Tuesday, 2nd August, 1882

5 ducks
Week 11 · 2 Aug 1882
A day at the wicket against Boxley CC that will be remembered less for runs scored than for runs conspicuously absent. Five of our men returned to the pavilion without troubling the scorer, and the Club's exclusive zero club welcomes its latest — and, in one case, repeat — subscribers. 1st XI W H Fryer, going in at first wicket down, was undone by C Chambers for a cipher — his second duck of the season and the sixth of a distinguished career now spanning four-and-twenty innings, second only on the all-time roll of dishonour. He arrives level with A Startup on six career ducks apiece, a meeting of kindred spirits neither gentleman is likely to toast. Speaking of Mr Startup, his afternoon deserves a paragraph of its own. Bowled by F Atkins for his first duck of the day — the season's first, the career's sixth — he had barely regained the pavilion steps before being sent out again and bowled once more, by F B Hallatt this time, for his second of the match and seventh of his career. A pair, gentlemen, and a chastening one, though we are assured the willow itself bears no blame. Mr Startup may console himself with the season already named in his honour not once but thrice — 1868, 1870 and now 1882 — and a run of five ducks in a row that stands as a monument to consistency of a very particular kind. A R Simpson fell to F B Hallatt for his maiden career duck, a modest debut in the art of not scoring that places him twenty-fifth on the club's roll — good company, for he joins a positively crowded field of gentlemen similarly becalmed on a single nought apiece. J Gurney completed the afternoon's misery, caught by A G Mannering off H Foster's bowling for his first career duck in eight innings, drawing level with Mr Simpson on that same solitary figure — two men, one shared distinction, acquired within minutes of each other. In Summary One match, five ducks, and Mr Startup's pair the undoubted feature of the day — a gentleman who went out to bat twice and returned twice without so much as troubling the umpire's patience. Boxley CC's bowlers, it must be said, appear to have found something in the conditions that suited them handsomely. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard - A Startup — 2 innings, 2 ducks, 100.00% - A Tapsfield — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67% - W Wilson — 6 innings, 2 ducks, 33.33% - F Foster — 8 innings, 2 ducks, 25.00% - W H Fryer — 8 innings, 2 ducks, 25.00% The Club extends its compliments to all five contributors and looks forward, with an entirely proper sense of anticipation, to whatever further additions the next fixture may bring to this most select of registers.

The Duck Club Gazette — a Record of Notable Failures at the Wicket, Wednesday the 14th of June, 1882

7 ducks
Week 4 · 14 Jun 1882
Our correspondent is pleased to report a most fruitful afternoon in the field against Boxley CC, in which no fewer than seven of our men found their way back to the pavilion without so much as troubling the scorer. A season of some promise, it must be said, for the art of not scoring. 1st XI C Gibbs, sent in at first wicket down, was bowled by K McAlpine for a cipher — his maiden duck of the season, and the first blot upon a card that had stood at a modest one from three innings. He now draws level with E J Rook on a career tally of one duck apiece. W Wilson followed at number nine, likewise bowled by McAlpine, and enters his second duck of the campaign — his career total now standing at two from thirteen innings, a figure shared with the venerable C French Snr, Duck of the Year in 1864. J Mallard, at number ten, was run out for nought, his third career duck from a mere seven innings — a rate that places him ninth of the 106 gentlemen who have ever graced this dubious register, level on tally with A Tapsfield. Speaking of whom — A Tapsfield, last man in, was himself run out without scoring, his second duck of this very afternoon's proceedings and his third of the career, seventh on the all-time roll. A curious business, two run-outs in close company, though the record does not suggest collusion. F Foster, at number four, was bowled by E Hickmott for nought — his second duck of the season and of the career alike, from a young career of only four innings, keeping company with C French Snr on a tally of two. Jack Fryer, number six, fell in the same manner to Hickmott, his second career duck from ten innings, level with C French Snr once again — that gentleman keeps distinguished company this week. And E J Rook, batting at seven, was bowled by Hickmott for a nought on what our records show to be his very first innings for the club — a debutante's duck, no less, and about as warm a welcome to first-class ignominy as the game allows. He joins C Gibbs on the season's ledger at one apiece. A Week in Summary A single fixture, seven ducks — a rate of failure our correspondent ventures Boxley CC's bowlers, Messrs McAlpine and Hickmott between them, will recall with some satisfaction. The lower order bore the brunt of it, numbers four through eleven contributing the full complement, which may say something of our batting order or nothing at all. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard 1. A Tapsfield — 3 innings, 2 ducks, 66.67 per cent 2. F Foster — 4 innings, 2 ducks, 50.00 per cent 3. C Gibbs — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.00 per cent 4. E J Rook — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.00 per cent 5. Ernest Cruttenden — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50.00 per cent The Club extends its compliments to all seven contributors and looks forward, with some confidence, to further additions at the next fixture. Members are reminded that the willow shows no favour, and the timbers care nothing for reputation.

The Linton Park Duck Club Gazette — Saturday, the 24th of May, 1882

5 ducks
Week 1 · 24 May 1882
A single fixture only this week, away to Collier Street CC, yet the first innings there contrived to return no fewer than five of our men to the pavilion with a duck's egg against their names. A meagre harvest of runs, but a bountiful one for the Club's own particular ledger. 1st XI — away to Collier Street CC - Ernest Cruttenden opened proceedings and closed them almost as swiftly, bowled by C Martin without troubling the scorer. His first duck of the season, and the second of a career now numbering eleven innings, placing him fourteenth of the hundred and three gentlemen who have achieved the distinction. He finds a kindred spirit in A Tapsfield, who sits upon the self-same tally of two. - G Sedgwick followed at the second wicket, bowled by W Hodges, recording his first duck of the season and third of his career in seven innings, a standing of seventh in the club's roll. One J Sedgwick, of an earlier season, was similarly troubled on three occasions and carried off the Duck of the Year honour in 1881, though whether the name denotes any kinship the Gazette does not presume to say. - F Foster, at three, offered his wicket to a smart catch by F Savage off the bowling of W Hodges, his very first innings under the Club's colours thus beginning, most memorably, with nought. A debut duck secures him twenty-fourth place of the hundred and three, level with the long-retired E M Owens, who managed but the one duck in six innings between 1869 and 1875. - W H Fryer, at four, was adjudged leg before to C Martin without score, his fifth career duck in eighteen innings, and a most exalted third of the whole club. He draws level with none other than A Startup, a three-time Duck of the Year and holder of the club's mark for five ducks in a row, whose own tally of five stands near the very summit of the art of not scoring. - A Tapsfield, last man in at eleven, was bowled by C Martin to complete the innings' collection, his first duck of the season and second of his career in but four innings, a lofty tenth of the hundred and three. He keeps close company, as noted above, with Mr Cruttenden on identical figures. Three of the five fell to the bowling of C Martin, who may fairly claim to have done Collier Street's work for them single-handed, with W Hodges accounting for the remaining two. Duck Hunting Season Leaderboard The season being yet young, the following gentlemen lead the field, each with a single duck from two innings and so, for the present, a discomfiting fifty per cent: - A Tapsfield — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - Ernest Cruttenden — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - F Foster — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - G Sedgwick — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% - W H Fryer — 2 innings, 1 duck, 50% The Club looks forward, as ever, to its next fixture, confident that further candidates will present themselves for enrolment in this exclusive and ignominious company.

1881 Season 5 reports

LPCC Duck Club Gazette

8 ducks
Week 10 · 17 Aug 1881
Week ending the 17th of August, 1881 A single fixture against Leeds Nil Desperandum this week, and yet the timbers proved remarkably hospitable, no fewer than eight of our number being sent back to the pavilion without troubling the scorer. 1st XI - Jack Fryer, at number four, was bowled by G Gibbon for his first nought in the Club's book, a modest opening entry that places him 32nd of 101 upon the all-time roll, level with A Tapsfield on a single career cipher apiece. - A Startup, ever prompt to arrive and depart, contrived the rarer feat of falling twice in the one match — bowled by A Hollands in the earlier innings, run out amid some confusion in the latter — a pair, and no small addition to a record already unrivalled at the head of the all-time table. His tally advances from four career ducks to five, drawing him level first with C Amies and then with W Goad, and sits comfortably beside his standing honours as Duck of the Year for both 1868 and 1870, and his place among the five-in-a-row. - W H Fryer followed, caught W Chambers bowled A Hollands, his third duck's egg of the season and fourth of a career now sixteen innings deep, good enough for fifth upon the all-time table, level with C Amies. - A Tapsfield, bowled A Hollands, has the peculiar distinction of making his very first appearance in senior colours a scoreless one, a genuine duck on debut, and finds himself level with E M Owens on career noughts. - W Lamb followed him back almost directly, caught J Edmed off A Hollands, likewise dismissed without score upon his own first outing, two debutants and two ducks in the very same innings. He presently keeps company with A Tapsfield on a single career duck. - W Eggar, last man but one, was caught A Betts bowled G Gibbon for his second duck of the season, his career total now standing at two, level with C French Snr, whose own second nought, by curious coincidence, arrived in the season that brought him the Duck of the Year honour in 1864. - J Sedgwick closed the procession, caught W Ambrose bowled A Hollands, his third duck of the season and of his career alike, and already carries the Duck of the Year honour for the present season of 1881, a title he may consider himself keeping warm rather handsomely. He draws level with T Tomson on three career ducks. Of the eight ciphers recorded, no fewer than five fell to the bowling of A Hollands, who might fairly claim to have had rather the better of the exchanges with the willow this week. Two debutants departing without score in the same innings is a coincidence worth remarking upon, as is Mr Startup's pair, achieved with the minimum of fuss and the maximum of consistency.
